Part: Combinatorial optimization problems (301)

1. Combinatorial optimization problems (48)

oc-f-001 · level facile · notes
How many distinct cyclic orderings do $n=6$ elements have, if a sequence, its rotations and its reverse are the same cyclic ordering?
  1. $64$
  2. $60$
  3. $720$
  4. $120$
Explanation. The number is $\frac{(n-1)!}{2}=\frac{5!}{2}=60$: the first element is fixed ($n$ rotations) and every sequence is identified with its reverse. $6!$ counts the orderings, $2^6$ the subsets.
oc-f-002 · level facile · notes
In a combinatorial optimization problem in maximization form, let $z(I)$ be the optimal value of instance $I$. The value $f(\bar S)$ of a feasible solution $\bar S$ is:
  1. a primal bound, i.e., a lower bound on $z(I)$
  2. a dual bound, i.e., an upper bound on $z(I)$
  3. a primal bound, i.e., an upper bound on $z(I)$
  4. a dual bound, i.e., a lower bound on $z(I)$
Explanation. A feasible solution gives a primal bound; in a maximization problem $f(\bar S)\le z(I)$, hence it is a lower bound. In minimization problems the roles are exchanged.
oc-f-003 · level facile · notes
For an instance of a combinatorial optimization problem in maximization form we know $\mathrm{LB}=16$ (value of a feasible solution) and $\mathrm{UB}=20$ (dual bound). What is the relative gap?
  1. $20\%$
  2. $4$
  3. $80\%$
  4. $25\%$
Explanation. The relative gap is $\frac{\mathrm{UB}-\mathrm{LB}}{|\mathrm{LB}|}=\frac{4}{16}=25\%$. The value $4$ is the absolute gap; dividing by $\mathrm{UB}$ gives $20\%$.
oc-f-004 · level teorema · notes
In a combinatorial optimization problem with objective function $f$, let $\beta$ be a dual bound on the optimal value $z(I)$ of an instance $I$ ($\beta\ge z(I)$ in maximization form, $\beta\le z(I)$ in minimization form). Which statement is correct?
  1. In maximization form $\lfloor\beta\rfloor$ is always a dual bound, even if $f$ does not take integer values
  2. If $f(S)\in\Z$ for every feasible solution $S$, in minimization form $\lfloor\beta\rfloor+1$ is also a dual bound
  3. If $f(S)\in\Z$ for every feasible solution $S$, in maximization form $\lfloor\beta\rfloor$ is also a dual bound
  4. If $f(S)\in\Z$ for every feasible solution $S$, in maximization form $\lceil\beta\rceil-1$ is also a dual bound
Explanation. With an integer objective, in a maximization problem $f(S)\le\beta$ implies $f(S)\le\lfloor\beta\rfloor$; in a minimization problem one rounds up, $\lceil\beta\rceil$. Without the integrality of $f$ the rounding is not allowed.
oc-f-005 · level facile · notes
In the knapsack problem (KP) with $n$ items and integer capacity $c$, an algorithm executes $\Theta(nc)$ steps. How is it classified with respect to the input size?
  1. Strongly polynomial, because it does not depend on the profits
  2. Pseudo-polynomial: polynomial in the value of $c$, not in the number of digits of $c$
  3. Polynomial: the number of steps is a polynomial in $n$ and $c$
  4. Exponential in $n$, because it examines the subsets of the items
Explanation. $c$ is written with $\log c$ digits: $\Theta(nc)$ is polynomial in the value of the largest number, not in the size of the instance. This is the definition of a pseudo-polynomial algorithm.
oc-f-147 · level facile · notes
For a combinatorial optimization problem in maximization form, with objective function $f$, what does its decision version ask?
  1. What the optimal value $z(I)$ of the instance is
  2. To find a feasible solution of maximum value
  3. Whether all feasible solutions have value at least $k$, for a given integer $k$
  4. Whether some feasible solution has value at least $k$, for a given integer $k$
Explanation. The decision version has a yes/no answer: «is there a solution with $f(S)\ge k$?». A solution of value at least $k$ is a certificate checkable in polynomial time.
oc-f-148 · level teorema · notes
An NP-hard problem is strongly NP-hard if it remains NP-hard even when all its numbers are bounded by a polynomial in the instance size. If $P\neq NP$, which statement is correct?
  1. A strongly NP-hard problem has a pseudo-polynomial algorithm, but no polynomial one
  2. A strongly NP-hard problem is polynomial if its numbers are bounded by a polynomial
  3. A strongly NP-hard problem has no pseudo-polynomial algorithm
  4. A strongly NP-hard problem has no exact algorithm
Explanation. With numbers bounded by a polynomial a pseudo-polynomial algorithm would become polynomial, and would solve a problem that is still NP-hard in that case. Exponential exact algorithms always exist (for example brute force).
oc-f-149 · level facile · notes
An NP-hard problem is weakly NP-hard if it admits a pseudo-polynomial algorithm (polynomial in the size and in the value of the largest number). Which of the following problems is only weakly NP-hard?
  1. The travelling salesman problem (TSP)
  2. The 0-1 knapsack problem (KP)
  3. Bin packing (BPP)
  4. Vertex coloring (VCP)
Explanation. The KP is solved by dynamic programming in $\Theta(nc)$, a pseudo-polynomial time; bin packing, coloring, maximum clique and the TSP are strongly NP-hard.
oc-f-150 · level facile · notes
The decisions of combinatorial optimization problems fall into five categories: IN/OUT, counting, assignment, ordering, configuration and partitioning. Which category does a bin packing solution (items in interchangeable bins of capacity $c$) belong to?
  1. Configuration and partitioning: a partition of the items
  2. IN/OUT: a subset of the items
  3. Ordering: a permutation of the items
  4. Counting: a vector of integer quantities
Explanation. The bins are interchangeable: only the grouping of the items matters, that is, a partition into groups respecting the capacity.
oc-f-151 · level facile · notes
In an assignment decision every element $i$ is assigned to exactly one of several distinct resources $j$ (for example tasks to different people). Which variables describe it naturally?
  1. $x_i\in\{0,1\}$, equal to $1$ if and only if element $i$ is selected
  2. $x_i\in\Z_{\ge0}$, the number of units of element $i$ to use
  3. A permutation $\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ of the elements
  4. $x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}$, equal to $1$ if and only if $i$ goes to resource $j$, with $\sum_j x_{ij}=1$ for every $i$
Explanation. An assignment is a function from the elements to the resources: one binary variable per pair and one equality constraint per element. The others are the IN/OUT, counting and ordering variables.
oc-f-152 · level facile · notes
For $n=20$ elements four numbers of candidates are compared: $n^3$, the subsets $2^n$, the partitions $B(n)$ (Bell number) and the cyclic orderings $\frac{(n-1)!}{2}$. Which increasing order is correct?
  1. $2^n<n^3<B(n)<\frac{(n-1)!}{2}$
  2. $n^3<B(n)<2^n<\frac{(n-1)!}{2}$
  3. $n^3<2^n<B(n)<\frac{(n-1)!}{2}$
  4. $n^3<2^n<\frac{(n-1)!}{2}<B(n)$
Explanation. For $n=20$: $n^3=8000$, $2^n\approx 1.05\cdot10^6$, $B(n)\approx 5.17\cdot 10^{13}$ and $\frac{(n-1)!}{2}\approx 6.08\cdot10^{16}$. For small $n$ the order may differ (with $n=5$: $12<32<52$).
oc-f-153 · level facile · notes
Brute force for an IN/OUT problem evaluates all $2^n$ subsets of the $n$ elements. A computer evaluates $10^9$ of them per second. About how long does it take with $n=60$?
  1. About $36$ centuries
  2. About $36$ years
  3. About $18$ minutes
  4. About $13$ days
Explanation. $2^{60}\approx 1.15\cdot10^{18}$, hence about $1.15\cdot10^{9}$ seconds are needed, that is, about $36$ years. $18$ minutes and $13$ days are the times for $n=40$ and $n=50$: every $10$ more elements multiply the time by about one thousand.
oc-f-154 · level facile · notes
A combinatorial optimization problem is given by a ground set $\mathscr{U}=\{1,\dots,n\}$, a family $\mathcal{F}\subseteq 2^{\mathscr{U}}$ of feasible solutions and an objective function $f:\mathcal{F}\to\R$. Which property distinguishes it from a generic optimization problem?
  1. $\mathscr{U}$ is finite, hence the feasible solutions are finitely many
  2. The objective function $f$ is linear in the decision variables
  3. The family $\mathcal{F}$ contains all the subsets of $\mathscr{U}$
  4. The feasible solutions are vectors of real numbers
Explanation. Solutions are subsets of a finite set: there are at most $2^n$ of them, and an optimum always exists if $\mathcal{F}\ne\emptyset$. The objective may be any function and $\mathcal{F}$ describes the constraints.
oc-f-155 · level facile · notes
The 0-1 knapsack problem (items $\mathscr{U}=\{1,\dots,n\}$ with profits $p_j$, weights $w_j$, capacity $c$) is written as a combinatorial optimization problem with $f(S)=\sum_{j\in S}p_j$. What is the family $\mathcal{F}$ of feasible solutions?
  1. The subsets $S\subseteq\mathscr{U}$ with $\sum_{j\in S}w_j=c$
  2. All the $2^n$ subsets of $\mathscr{U}$
  3. The subsets $S\subseteq\mathscr{U}$ with $\sum_{j\in S}p_j\le c$
  4. The subsets $S\subseteq\mathscr{U}$ with $\sum_{j\in S}w_j\le c$
Explanation. The capacity constraint bounds the total weight, it does not fix it: $\mathcal{F}$ also contains the empty set. The equality describes subset sum.
oc-f-156 · level facile · notes
A set has $n=6$ elements. How many of its subsets have exactly $3$ elements, and how many subsets does it have in total?
  1. $20$ and $720$
  2. $18$ and $64$
  3. $20$ and $64$
  4. $120$ and $64$
Explanation. The subsets with $3$ elements are $\binom{6}{3}=20$; in total there are $\sum_k\binom{6}{k}=2^6=64$. $120=6\cdot5\cdot4$ counts the ordered triples, $720=6!$ the permutations.
oc-f-566 · level facile · notes
The decisions of combinatorial optimization problems fall into five categories (IN/OUT, counting, assignment, sequencing, configuration). One must decide how many operators to assign to each of $n$ shifts. To which category does the decision belong and what are its natural variables?
  1. Counting, with integer variables $x_j\in\Z_{\ge 0}$
  2. IN/OUT, with binary variables $x_j\in\{0,1\}$
  3. Sequencing, with a permutation $\sigma$ of the shifts
  4. Configuration, with a partition of the shifts into groups
Explanation. The decision is a discrete quantity for every shift: a vector of non-negative integers. A binary variable would only say whether the shift has operators or not.
oc-f-567 · level facile · notes
Among the decision categories of combinatorial optimization problems, assignment and configuration (partitioning) both have solutions that split the elements into classes. What distinguishes them?
  1. In assignment every element may stay unassigned, in partitioning it may not
  2. In assignment the classes all have the same cardinality, in partitioning they do not
  3. No difference: they are two names for the same category
  4. In assignment the resources are distinct (labelled classes), in partitioning the groups are interchangeable
Explanation. Distinct resources give a function from the elements to the resources ($m^n$ solutions); identical resources give partitions, counted by the Bell numbers.
oc-f-568 · level facile · notes
A facility location problem decides which facilities to open and to which open facility each customer is assigned. With respect to the five decision categories (IN/OUT, counting, assignment, sequencing, configuration), what does it combine?
  1. A counting decision (how many customers) and a sequencing decision (in which order to serve them)
  2. Only a configuration decision, because the facilities are identical
  3. An IN/OUT decision (which facilities to open) and an assignment decision (customers to facilities)
  4. Only a sequencing decision on the customers
Explanation. A real problem often combines several categories: opening is a yes/no choice per facility, then every customer goes to exactly one open facility.
oc-f-569 · level facile · notes
In the multiple knapsack problem (MKP) there are $m$ knapsacks of capacity $c_k$ and $n$ items of profit $p_j$ and weight $w_j$; every item goes into one knapsack or into none. To which decision category does the problem belong?
  1. Sequencing
  2. Assignment
  3. IN/OUT
  4. Partitioning
Explanation. The knapsacks are distinct resources (different capacities) and every item gets at most one knapsack: it is an assignment. It is not a partitioning because the knapsacks are not interchangeable.
oc-f-570 · level facile · notes
The bin packing problem (BPP) packs $n$ items of weight $w_j$ into the minimum number of identical bins of capacity $c$. To which decision category does it belong, and why?
  1. Partitioning: the bins are identical, so a solution is a partition of the items
  2. Assignment: every item gets a labelled bin
  3. IN/OUT: every item is selected or not
  4. Counting: one decides how many copies of each item to use
Explanation. Swapping the names of two identical bins does not change the solution: the distinct solutions are partitions. In the MKP, instead, the knapsacks are distinct.
oc-f-571 · level facile · notes
Before solving a combinatorial optimization problem one counts its candidate solutions. What does this number depend on?
  1. On the numerical values of the data, e.g., weights and capacities
  2. On the number of feasible solutions
  3. On the algorithm used to solve the problem
  4. Only on the combinatorial object of the solutions (subsets, orderings, partitions) and on $n$
Explanation. The candidates are all objects of the right type ($2^n$ subsets, $n!$ permutations, $B(n)$ partitions); the data only decide which ones are feasible.
oc-f-572 · level facile · notes
The Bell numbers count partitions: $B(0)=1$ and $B(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}{k}B(k)$. Knowing that $B(0),\dots,B(4)=1,1,2,5,15$, what is $B(5)$?
  1. $24$
  2. $60$
  3. $52$
  4. $31$
Explanation. $B(5)=\binom40\cdot1+\binom41\cdot1+\binom42\cdot2+\binom43\cdot5+\binom44\cdot15=1+4+12+20+15=52$. $31=2^5-1$ counts the non-empty subsets.
oc-f-573 · level teorema · notes
$n=4$ jobs are assigned to $m=2$ machines. If the machines are distinct there are $m^n=16$ assignments. If the machines are identical (swapping them does not change the solution), how many distinct solutions are there?
  1. $6$: the subsets of $2$ jobs
  2. $8$: the partitions of the $4$ jobs into at most $2$ blocks
  3. $16$: the number of assignments does not change
  4. $15$: all partitions, $B(4)$
Explanation. With interchangeable labels the solutions are the partitions into at most $m$ blocks: $1$ with one block and $7$ with two blocks ($16$ assignments, minus the $2$ with an empty machine, divided by $2$). $B(4)=15$ would also count partitions into $3$ or $4$ blocks.
oc-f-574 · level facile · notes
For $n=10$ elements four counts are compared: $n^3$, the subsets $2^n$, the partitions $B(n)$ (Bell number, $B(10)=115\,975$) and the cyclic orderings $(n-1)!/2$. Which is the largest?
  1. The cyclic orderings, $181\,440$
  2. The partitions, $115\,975$
  3. The subsets, $1\,024$
  4. $n^3=1\,000$
Explanation. $9!/2=181\,440>B(10)>2^{10}=1\,024>10^3$. For $n=5$, instead, the cyclic orderings are only $12$: they grow more slowly at first, then overtake all the others.
oc-f-575 · level facile · notes
For $n=5$ elements one compares $n^2$, the subsets $2^n$, the cyclic orderings $(n-1)!/2$ and the partitions $B(n)$, with $B(5)=52$. Which is the smallest?
  1. $n^2=25$
  2. The subsets, $32$
  3. The partitions, $52$
  4. The cyclic orderings, $12$
Explanation. $4!/2=12$. For small $n$ the factorial growth is not yet visible: already for $n=10$ the cyclic orderings are the most numerous.
oc-f-576 · level facile · notes
Brute force for an IN/OUT problem evaluates all $2^n$ subsets. A computer $1000$ times faster, in the same time, can handle about how many more elements?
  1. Twice as many elements
  2. About $3$, because $\log_{10}1000=3$
  3. About $10$, because $2^{10}=1024\approx 1000$
  4. $1000$ times more elements
Explanation. Multiplying the speed by $1000$ only compensates a factor $2^{10}$ in the number of candidates: $n$ grows by about $10$. A constant speed-up does not beat exponential growth.
oc-f-577 · level facile · notes
A computer evaluates $10^9$ candidate solutions per second and brute force enumerates the $2^n$ subsets of $n=50$ elements ($2^{50}\approx 1.13\cdot 10^{15}$). About how long does the enumeration take?
  1. About $36$ years
  2. About $13$ days
  3. About $1$ second
  4. About $18$ minutes
Explanation. $1.13\cdot10^{15}/10^9\approx1.13\cdot10^6$ seconds, i.e., about $13$ days. $1$ second corresponds to $n=30$, $18$ minutes to $n=40$, $36$ years to $n=60$.
oc-f-578 · level facile · notes
The size of an instance is the number of bits needed to write it. An instance contains $n$ integers, the largest of which is $M$. What is the order of its size?
  1. $n\log_2 M$
  2. $nM$
  3. $n+M$
  4. $n$, independently of $M$
Explanation. An integer $M$ is written with about $\log_2 M$ bits, not with $M$ symbols. This is why an $O(nM)$ algorithm is not polynomial in the size.
oc-f-579 · level teorema · notes
The class NP contains the decision problems whose «yes» instances have a certificate that can be verified in polynomial time. Why is the decision version of the 0-1 knapsack («is there a subset of weight at most $c$ and profit at least $k$?») in NP?
  1. Because a polynomial algorithm solves it
  2. Because the number of subsets is $2^n$, finite
  3. Because every «no» instance has a short certificate
  4. A subset satisfying both conditions is a certificate: weight and profit are summed in polynomial time
Explanation. Membership in NP only asks to verify a certificate of the «yes» instances quickly, not to find it. A polynomial algorithm would put it in P.
oc-f-809 · level ipotesi · notes
In a maximization problem the LP relaxation gives the dual bound $\beta=17.6$, and one wants to round it to $\lfloor\beta\rfloor=17$. Which assumption makes the rounding valid?
  1. That the gap is smaller than $1$
  2. That every feasible solution has an integer objective value (e.g., integer coefficients and integer variables)
  3. That the relaxation has a unique solution
  4. That $\beta$ is positive
Explanation. If $z(I)$ is integer and $z(I)\le17.6$, then $z(I)\le17$. With fractional objective values (e.g., profits $0.5$) the rounding might cut off the optimum.
oc-f-810 · level ipotesi · notes
The 0/1 knapsack is NP-hard but has a pseudo-polynomial algorithm $\Theta(nc)$; the TSP is strongly NP-hard. What can be said about a pseudo-polynomial algorithm for the TSP?
  1. It does not exist, unless P = NP: the problem stays hard even with small numbers, where pseudo-polynomial means polynomial
  2. It always exists, as for the knapsack
  3. It exists only for symmetric distances
  4. It would make the TSP polynomial without consequences on P and NP
Explanation. If the numbers are bounded by a polynomial in the size, a time polynomial in the numbers is polynomial in the size: for a strongly NP-hard problem this would give P = NP.
oc-f-900 · level facile · notes
In Definition 1.1 the family $\mathcal{F}\subseteq 2^{\mathscr{U}}$ of feasible solutions of a combinatorial optimization problem may be given by listing its elements. In the problems of the course (knapsack, bin packing, TSP, …) how is $\mathcal{F}$ given?
  1. By the objective function: the subsets of positive value are feasible
  2. By a polyhedron in continuous variables, whose vertices are taken
  3. By a rule, e.g., a capacity constraint: listing it would be impossible
  4. By an explicit list of the feasible subsets, read as input
Explanation. $\mathcal{F}$ usually has an exponential number of elements: it is described by the constraints of the problem, never by a list. Only in small teaching instances is it listed.
oc-f-901 · level facile · notes
In combinatorial optimization one distinguishes between a problem and an instance $I$ of it, and writes $z(I)$. Which statement is correct?
  1. The instance fixes only $n$ and leaves the other data symbolic; $z(I)$ counts the feasible solutions
  2. The problem has symbolic data, the instance fixes the numbers; $z(I)$ is the optimal value of the instance
  3. The instance is a feasible solution of the problem; $z(I)$ is the value of that solution
  4. The problem is the decision version, the instance the optimization one; $z(I)$ is the threshold
Explanation. An instance is obtained by fixing all the numbers of the problem (e.g., weights and capacities); $z(I)$ is the value of an optimal solution of it.
oc-f-902 · level facile · notes
In a sequencing decision one chooses the order in which $n$ elements are processed (every order is allowed). Which combinatorial object is a candidate solution and how many candidates are there?
  1. A permutation of the $n$ elements: $n!$ candidates
  2. A subset of the $n$ elements: $2^n$ candidates
  3. A partition of the $n$ elements: $B(n)$ candidates
  4. An ordered pair of elements: $n^2$ candidates
Explanation. A processing order is a sequence containing every element once: a permutation $\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$, and there are $n!$ permutations.
oc-f-903 · level facile · notes
Definition 1.1 describes a combinatorial optimization problem as the choice of a subset of a ground set $\mathscr{U}$. To fit a sequencing decision (a tour or a sequence) into this form, which ground set is used?
  1. The set of elements to be ordered
  2. The set of all permutations of the elements
  3. The set of positions $1,\dots,n$ of the sequence
  4. The set of pairs of consecutive elements
Explanation. A sequence is identified by the pairs (element, successor) it uses: the solution is the subset of these pairs. For an assignment, instead, the ground set is the set of pairs (element, resource).
oc-f-904 · level facile · notes
Among the application areas of combinatorial optimization, production planning includes for instance lot sizing. What are its typical decisions?
  1. How to place a set of items into containers
  2. Where to open facilities and which customers each one serves
  3. What, when and how much to produce, with which resources
  4. The order and timing of the operations on single resources
Explanation. The other three options are the typical decisions of other areas: scheduling, packing and facility location.
oc-f-905 · level facile · notes
In the application area of scheduling (order and timing of operations on resources, e.g., jobs on machines), which decision category always appears?
  1. None: scheduling is a continuous problem
  2. Sequencing: the order of the operations on every resource
  3. Counting: how many copies of every operation to run
  4. IN/OUT: which operations to run and which to discard
Explanation. Deciding the order of the operations is a sequencing decision; it is often combined with an assignment of the operations to the resources.
oc-f-906 · level facile · notes
The capacitated lot sizing problem (CLS) decides in which periods to activate production (setup) and how many units to produce in each period. Which decision categories does it involve?
  1. IN/OUT (the setup periods) and counting (the quantities)
  2. Only sequencing (the order of the periods)
  3. Assignment and partitioning of the periods
  4. Only IN/OUT (the periods in which one produces)
Explanation. The setup is a yes/no choice per period; the produced quantities are non-negative integers. The order of the periods is given, not decided.
oc-f-907 · level facile · notes
In an IN/OUT problem on $n$ elements the candidate solutions are the $2^n$ subsets. What is the relation between $2^n$ and the number $|\mathcal{F}|$ of feasible solutions?
  1. $|\mathcal{F}|\ge 2^n$: the constraints add new solutions
  2. $|\mathcal{F}|=2^n$: every subset is always feasible
  3. None: the two numbers can never be compared
  4. $|\mathcal{F}|\le 2^n$: the feasible ones are part of the candidates
Explanation. The constraints discard candidates without creating new ones: e.g., in an instance with $4$ elements only $11$ of the $16$ subsets may be feasible.
oc-f-908 · level facile · notes
For a set of $n=3$ elements, how many subsets, permutations and partitions (Bell number $B(3)$) are there, respectively?
  1. $6$, $6$ and $5$
  2. $8$, $3$ and $5$
  3. $8$, $6$ and $5$
  4. $8$, $6$ and $6$
Explanation. $2^3=8$, $3!=6$; the partitions of $\{1,2,3\}$ are $\{123\}$, $\{1|23\}$, $\{2|13\}$, $\{3|12\}$, $\{1|2|3\}$: $B(3)=5$.
oc-f-909 · level facile · notes
The $2^n$ subsets of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ correspond to the binary vectors $\vet{x}\in\{0,1\}^n$ ($x_j=1$ if and only if $j$ is in the subset). Geometrically, what are these vectors?
  1. The edges of the unit hypercube $[0,1]^n$
  2. The vertices of the unit hypercube $[0,1]^n$
  3. The vertices of the simplex $\{\vet{x}\ge\vet{0}:\sum_j x_j\le 1\}$
  4. The integer points of the sphere of radius $\sqrt n$
Explanation. For $n=2$ they are the $4$ vertices of the square, for $n=3$ the $8$ vertices of the cube. The simplex has only $n+1$ vertices.
oc-f-910 · level teorema · notes
Proposition 1.2 (a set of $n$ elements has $2^n$ subsets) is also proved via the identity $\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}=2^n$. What does the term $\binom{n}{k}$ count in this proof?
  1. The subsets with exactly $k$ elements
  2. The subsets with at most $k$ elements
  3. The partitions of the $n$ elements into $k$ blocks
  4. The ordered sequences of $k$ distinct elements
Explanation. The subsets are grouped by cardinality $k=0,\dots,n$; those of cardinality $k$ are $\binom nk$. The ordered sequences of $k$ elements are $n!/(n-k)!$.
oc-f-911 · level facile · notes
A cyclic ordering places the elements on a circle: a sequence, its rotations and its reverse are the same ordering. For $n=4$ the distinct cyclic orderings are $(1,2,3,4)$, $(1,2,4,3)$ and $(1,3,2,4)$. Which of them coincides with the sequence $(2,1,4,3)$?
  1. $(1,2,4,3)$: it has the pair $4,3$ in the same order
  2. $(1,3,2,4)$: it is one of its rotations
  3. None: it is a fourth cyclic ordering
  4. $(1,2,3,4)$: it is its reverse started from $2$
Explanation. The adjacent elements in $(2,1,4,3)$, closing the circle, are $\{2,1\},\{1,4\},\{4,3\},\{3,2\}$: the same pairs as $(1,2,3,4)$, read backwards.
oc-f-912 · level teorema · notes
Proposition 1.3 says that $n\ge3$ elements have $(n-1)!/2$ distinct cyclic orderings (rotations and reverse do not count). Where do the factor $(n-1)!$ and the division by $2$ come from in the proof?
  1. $(n-1)!$ counts the inversions of the sequence; one divides by $2$ for the rotations
  2. The last element is fixed; every cycle has two ends, the first and the last
  3. The first element is fixed, the other $n-1$ are ordered; every cycle appears once per direction
  4. A random element is excluded; half of the remaining sequences are not cyclic
Explanation. Always starting from element $1$ removes the rotations: $(n-1)!$ sequences remain; each of them and its reverse, e.g., $(1,3,5,2,4)$ and $(1,4,2,5,3)$, give the same cycle.
oc-f-913 · level facile · notes
A partition of a finite set $A$ is a collection of non-empty, pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is $A$. Which collection is a partition of $A=\{1,2,3,4\}$?
  1. $\{\{1,2,3,4\},\emptyset\}$
  2. $\{\{1,4\},\{2\},\{3\}\}$
  3. $\{\{1,2\},\{2,3\},\{4\}\}$
  4. $\{\{1,2\},\{3\}\}$
Explanation. The second has non-disjoint blocks (element $2$ is in two blocks), the third does not cover element $4$, the fourth has an empty block.
oc-f-914 · level facile · notes
Brute force (maximization form) enumerates the candidates and updates the best solution $\bar S$ and its value $\LB$ only if $S$ is feasible and $f(S)>\LB$. If two feasible solutions have the same maximum value, which one does it return?
  1. The first one met in the enumeration order
  2. The last one met in the enumeration order
  3. Both, as the set of optimal solutions
  4. Neither: the tie makes it stop with an error
Explanation. With the strict inequality the second solution of equal value does not replace the first one. The returned value $z(I)=\LB$ is optimal anyway.
oc-f-915 · level facile · notes
Going from $n$ to $n+1$ elements, by which factor are the number $2^n$ of subsets and the number $(n-1)!/2$ of cyclic orderings multiplied?
  1. By $2$ the subsets, by $n+1$ the cyclic orderings
  2. By $n$ the subsets, by $2$ the cyclic orderings
  3. By $2$ both
  4. By $2$ the subsets, by $n$ the cyclic orderings
Explanation. $2^{n+1}/2^n=2$ and $\frac{n!/2}{(n-1)!/2}=n$: the factor of the cyclic orderings grows with $n$, which is why they soon overtake every exponential.
oc-f-916 · level facile · notes
Brute force enumerates the $(n-1)!/2$ cyclic orderings of $n=20$ elements. With a computer $1000$ times faster, in the same time, up to how many elements can one go?
  1. $21$: one extra element multiplies the work by $1000$
  2. $20$: no gain, the work is factorial
  3. $22$: the work grows by $20\cdot21=420<1000$
  4. $30$: about $10$ more elements, as for subsets
Explanation. From $n$ to $n+1$ the number is multiplied by $n$: $20\cdot21=420\le1000$, but $20\cdot21\cdot22=9240>1000$. The gain is only $2$ elements.

2. Knapsack problems (61)

oc-f-006 · level facile · notes
The subset sum problem (SSP) asks whether, given integers $w_1,\dots,w_n$ and $c$, some subset sums to exactly $c$. How is it obtained as a special case of the knapsack problem (KP: profits $p_j$, weights $w_j$, capacity $c$)?
  1. With $w_j=1$ for every $j$: the answer is yes if and only if the optimal value is $c$
  2. With $c=\sum_j w_j$: the answer is yes if and only if the optimal value is $\sum_j p_j$
  3. With $p_j=w_j$ for every $j$: the answer is yes if and only if the optimal value is $c$
  4. With $p_j=1$ for every $j$: the answer is yes if and only if the optimal value is $n$
Explanation. With $p_j=w_j$ the KP looks for the largest total weight not exceeding $c$; the subset sum problem asks whether the total weight $c$ can be reached exactly, i.e., whether the optimal value is $c$.
oc-f-007 · level facile · notes
In the multiple-choice knapsack problem (MCKP) the items, each with a profit and a weight, are partitioned into $q$ classes, and the knapsack has capacity $c$. Which constraint concerns the classes?
  1. All the items of a single class are chosen, without exceeding the capacity
  2. Exactly one item is chosen from every class, without exceeding the capacity
  3. At most one item is chosen from every class, without exceeding the capacity
  4. At least one item is chosen from every class, without exceeding the capacity
Explanation. In the MCKP exactly one item is selected from each class: confusing it with «at most one» is a typical mistake of the chapter.
oc-f-008 · level teorema · notes
In the knapsack problem (KP: profits $p_j$, weights $w_j$, capacity $c$, optimal value $z(I)$), let $\bar k$ be the largest integer such that the $\bar k$ lightest items weigh at most $c$ in total. Which statement is correct?
  1. Every feasible solution has at most $\bar k$ items, hence $z(I)$ is at most the sum of the $\bar k$ largest profits
  2. Every feasible solution has at most $\bar k$ items, hence $z(I)$ is at most the sum of the profits of the $\bar k$ lightest items
  3. Every optimal solution has exactly $\bar k$ items, hence $z(I)$ is the sum of the $\bar k$ largest profits
  4. Every feasible solution has at most $\bar k$ items, hence $z(I)$ is at least the sum of the $\bar k$ largest profits
Explanation. This is the cardinality bound: a feasible subset has at most $\bar k$ items, and any $\bar k$ items have total profit at most the $\bar k$ largest profits. It is a dual bound.
oc-f-009 · level facile · notes
Knapsack problem (KP) with capacity $c=9$, profits $p=(6,5,8,9,6,7)$ and weights $w=(2,3,6,7,5,9)$. The cardinality bound is the sum of the $\bar k$ largest profits, where $\bar k$ is the largest number of lightest items that fit together in the knapsack. What is its value?
  1. $11$
  2. $24$
  3. $15$
  4. $17$
Explanation. The two lightest items weigh $2+3=5\le 9$, the three lightest $2+3+5=10>9$: $\bar k=2$. The two largest profits are $9+8=17$. $15$ is the optimal value, not a bound; $11$ uses the profits of the lightest items.
oc-f-157 · level facile · notes
In the bounded knapsack problem (BKP) there are $n$ item types: type $j$ has profit $p_j$, weight $w_j$ and $b_j$ available copies; the capacity is $c$. What is the domain of the variable $x_j$, the number of chosen copies of type $j$?
  1. $x_j\in\{0,1\}$
  2. $x_j\in\Z_{\ge0}$, without upper bound
  3. $x_j\in\{0,1,\dots,b_j\,w_j\}$
  4. $x_j\in\{0,1,\dots,b_j\}$
Explanation. From $0$ to $b_j$ copies of type $j$ can be taken. With $b_j=1$ it is the 0/1 KP, without upper bound the unbounded knapsack.
oc-f-158 · level facile · notes
In the bounded knapsack problem (BKP) type $j$ has profit $p_j$, weight $w_j$ and $b_j$ available copies. How is a BKP instance transformed into an equivalent 0-1 knapsack (KP) instance?
  1. Type $j$ is replaced by $b_j$ items of profit $p_j/b_j$ and weight $w_j/b_j$
  2. One item per type is kept and the capacity is multiplied by $\max_j b_j$
  3. Type $j$ is replaced by $b_j$ identical items of profit $p_j$ and weight $w_j$
  4. Type $j$ is replaced by one item of profit $b_jp_j$ and weight $b_jw_j$
Explanation. Every copy becomes a 0/1 item: choosing $d$ copies is choosing $d$ of the $b_j$ identical items. A single aggregated item would only allow $0$ or $b_j$ copies.
oc-f-159 · level facile · notes
In the knapsack problem with setups (KPS) the items are partitioned into classes; an item of class $h$ can be chosen only if the class is activated ($y_h=1$), and the activation costs a profit $f_h$ and a weight $s_h$. Which objective is maximized?
  1. $\sum_j p_jx_j-\sum_h s_hy_h$
  2. $\sum_j p_jx_j-\sum_h f_hy_h$
  3. $\sum_j p_jx_j+\sum_h f_hy_h$
  4. $\sum_j p_jx_j-\sum_h f_h\sum_{j\in\mathscr{J}_h}x_j$
Explanation. The setup cost $f_h$ is paid once per activated class, not per item; the setup weight $s_h$ enters the capacity constraint $\sum_j w_jx_j+\sum_h s_hy_h\le c$.
oc-f-160 · level facile · notes
Knapsack with setups (KPS) with capacity $c=10$ and a single class, with setup cost $f=4$ and setup weight $s=3$; the class contains the items $(p_j,w_j)=(6,4)$ and $(5,3)$. What is the optimal value (profit minus setup cost)?
  1. $7$
  2. $11$
  3. $2$
  4. $1$
Explanation. Activating the class leaves $10-3=7$ units of capacity: both items fit, $6+5-4=7$. Without activating it the value is $0$. $11$ forgets the setup cost.
oc-f-161 · level facile · notes
Multidimensional knapsack (MDKP) with $2$ dimensions and capacities $\vet c=(5,4)$; the items have profit and weights $(p_j;w_{1j},w_{2j})$: $A=(4;3,1)$, $B=(3;2,3)$, $C=(3;2,1)$. A subset is feasible if in every dimension the total weight does not exceed the capacity. What is the optimal value?
  1. $10$
  2. $6$
  3. $4$
  4. $7$
Explanation. $\{A,B\}$ weighs $(5,4)$ and $\{A,C\}$ weighs $(5,2)$: both are worth $7$. $\{A,B,C\}$ weighs $(7,5)$ and is infeasible; $10$ ignores the capacities.
oc-f-162 · level facile · notes
In the multidimensional knapsack problem (MDKP) every item $j$ has a weight $w_{dj}$ in each of the $m$ dimensions and the knapsack a capacity $c_d$ per dimension; a chosen item consumes capacity in all dimensions. What is obtained with $m=1$?
  1. The bounded knapsack (BKP)
  2. Subset sum (SSP)
  3. The 0-1 knapsack (KP)
  4. The multiple knapsack (MKP)
Explanation. With a single dimension only one capacity constraint is left: it is the KP. In the multiple knapsack, instead, an item consumes the capacity of a single knapsack.
oc-f-163 · level facile · notes
Multiple-choice knapsack (MCKP: exactly one item per class is chosen, without exceeding the capacity) with $c=7$ and classes $\mathscr{J}_1=\{(3,2),(5,4)\}$, $\mathscr{J}_2=\{(4,3),(6,5)\}$, where every pair is $(p_j,w_j)$. What is the optimal value?
  1. $10$
  2. $9$
  3. $11$
  4. $7$
Explanation. The feasible pairs are $(3,2)+(4,3)$ ($7$, weight $5$), $(3,2)+(6,5)$ ($9$, weight $7$) and $(5,4)+(4,3)$ ($9$, weight $7$); $(5,4)+(6,5)$ weighs $9>7$. $11$ ignores the capacity.
oc-f-164 · level facile · notes
In the multiple knapsack problem (MKP) there are $m$ knapsacks of capacities $c_1,\dots,c_m$ and $n$ items with profit $p_j$ and weight $w_j$. Which statement describes the problem?
  1. The profit of the inserted items is maximized, and every item goes into at most one knapsack
  2. All items are inserted, minimizing the number of knapsacks used
  3. The profit is maximized, and every item can be split among several knapsacks
  4. The profit is maximized, and every item goes into exactly one knapsack
Explanation. In the MKP items may stay out; each one lies entirely in a single knapsack. Inserting all items minimizing the bins is bin packing.
oc-f-165 · level facile · notes
Multiple knapsack (MKP) with $2$ knapsacks of capacity $5$ and $5$ and items $(p_j,w_j)=(6,4),(5,3),(4,3),(3,2)$; every item goes into at most one knapsack. What are the optimal value and the value of the KP with a single knapsack of capacity $10$?
  1. $15$ and $15$
  2. $14$ and $14$
  3. $13$ and $15$
  4. $14$ and $15$
Explanation. With two knapsacks: $\{(6,4)\}$ and $\{(5,3),(3,2)\}$ give $14$; the three most profitable items weigh $4,3,3$ and cannot be split into two groups of weight at most $5$. With capacity $10$ the items $(6,4),(5,3),(4,3)$ fit: $15$, only an upper bound for the MKP.
oc-f-166 · level facile · notes
Subset sum (SSP): given the integers $w=(3,5,7,11)$ and $c=15$, is there a subset summing to exactly $15$?
  1. Yes: $\{3,11\}$
  2. No: the sum closest to $15$ is $14$
  3. Yes: $\{3,5,7\}$
  4. Yes: $\{5,11\}$
Explanation. $3+5+7=15$. Instead $5+11=16$ and $3+11=14$.
oc-f-167 · level facile · notes
Unbounded knapsack (UKP: unlimited copies of every type) with capacity $c=10$ and two types $(p_j,w_j)=(7,4)$ and $(5,3)$. What is the optimal value?
  1. $15$
  2. $17$
  3. $14$
  4. $12$
Explanation. One copy of $(7,4)$ and two of $(5,3)$ weigh $10$ and are worth $17$. Two copies of the most efficient type give $14$ (greedy), three of the second $15$; $12$ is the 0/1 KP.
oc-f-168 · level facile · notes
In the unbounded knapsack problem (UKP) the variable $x_j\in\Z_{\ge0}$ is the number of copies of type $j$ (integer weight $w_j\ge1$), with capacity $c$. Which upper bound holds anyway for $x_j$?
  1. $x_j\le\lfloor c/w_j\rfloor$, because every copy weighs $w_j$
  2. $x_j\le 1$, because every type is chosen once
  3. $x_j\le n$, the number of types
  4. $x_j\le\lfloor c/p_j\rfloor$, because every copy is worth $p_j$
Explanation. $x_j$ copies weigh $w_jx_j\le c$. This is why the UKP is a special case of the BKP with $b_j=\lfloor c/w_j\rfloor$.
oc-f-564 · level ipotesi · notes
In the 0-1 knapsack (capacity $c$), let $\bar k$ be the largest integer such that the $\bar k$ lightest items weigh in total at most $c$. Why does every feasible solution contain at most $\bar k$ items?
  1. Any $\bar k+1$ items weigh at least as much as the $\bar k+1$ lightest ones, which already exceed $c$
  2. Because the lightest items are also the most efficient
  3. Because the greedy by weight always finds the optimal solution
  4. Because every item weighs at most $c/\bar k$
Explanation. The sum of the weights of $\bar k+1$ items is minimum when they are the lightest, and by definition of $\bar k$ this sum exceeds $c$. Hence the cardinality bound: the sum of the $\bar k$ largest profits.
oc-f-580 · level facile · notes
Knapsack problems have items with weight $w_j$ and profit $p_j$ and maximize the total profit while respecting the capacities. In which member of the family are there $k$ capacities $c_d$ and does every item have a weight $w_{dj}$ for each of them?
  1. In the multidimensional knapsack (MDKP)
  2. In the multiple knapsack (MKP)
  3. In the bounded knapsack (BKP)
  4. In the multiple-choice knapsack (MCKP)
Explanation. The MDKP has one knapsack with several resources (e.g., weight and volume). The MKP has several knapsacks, each with a single capacity.
oc-f-581 · level facile · notes
In the knapsack family, the knapsack problem with setups (KPS) groups the items into classes $\mathscr{J}_h$. What distinguishes it from the 0/1 knapsack?
  1. Exactly one item per class must be chosen
  2. Every class has a knapsack with its own capacity
  3. Several copies of the items of the same class may be taken
  4. Every class used pays a setup cost $f_h$ and consumes a setup weight $s_h$
Explanation. In the KPS an item of class $h$ can be taken only if the class is activated, paying $f_h$ in the profit and $s_h$ in the capacity. «Exactly one per class» is the MCKP.
oc-f-582 · level facile · notes
In the bounded knapsack (BKP: at most $b_j$ identical copies of item $j$) the candidate solutions are counted as vectors $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ of numbers of copies, with $0\le x_j\le b_j$. With $n=2$, $b_1=2$ and $b_2=3$, how many candidates are there?
  1. $6$
  2. $5$
  3. $12$
  4. $32$
Explanation. $(b_1+1)(b_2+1)=3\cdot4=12$. Treating the $5$ copies as distinct items would give $2^5=32$ subsets, counting the same solution several times.
oc-f-583 · level facile · notes
In the multiple-choice knapsack (MCKP) exactly one item is chosen from each of $q$ classes without exceeding the capacity $c$. With $q=3$ classes of $2$ items each, how many candidate solutions are there?
  1. $9$
  2. $8$
  3. $64$
  4. $6$
Explanation. One choice per class: $2\cdot2\cdot2=8$. The $2^6=64$ subsets of the $6$ items include choices with zero or two items of the same class.
oc-f-584 · level facile · notes
In the 0/1 knapsack (KP: items of profit $p_j$ and weight $w_j$, capacity $c$, at most one copy per item) one has $p=(10,7,6)$, $w=(5,4,3)$ and $c=8$. What is the optimal value?
  1. $16$
  2. $17$
  3. $13$
  4. $23$
Explanation. $\{1,3\}$ weighs $8\le c$ and is worth $16$; $\{1,2\}$ would be worth $17$ but weighs $9>8$; $\{2,3\}$ is worth $13$. Taking everything ($23$) violates the capacity.
oc-f-585 · level facile · notes
The 0/1 knapsack (KP) has $n$ items of profit $p_j$ and weight $w_j$ and capacity $c$. Which description corresponds to a feasible solution?
  1. A subset $S$ with $\sum_{j\in S}w_j=c$
  2. A vector of copies $x_j\in\Z_{\ge0}$ with $\sum_j w_jx_j\le c$
  3. A subset $S$ with $\sum_{j\in S}p_j\ge c$
  4. A subset $S$ of the items with $\sum_{j\in S}w_j\le c$
Explanation. Every item is taken at most once and only the capacity matters; weight equal to $c$ is the subset sum, integer copies are the unbounded knapsack.
oc-f-586 · level ipotesi · notes
In the 0/1 knapsack (KP: profits $p_j$, weights $w_j$, capacity $c$) one assumes $w_j\le c$ for every item. If the assumption is dropped and an item has $w_j>c$, what happens?
  1. The item must be split into parts of weight at most $c$
  2. The optimal value becomes the sum of all profits
  3. The item is in no feasible solution and can be removed without changing the optimal value
  4. The instance becomes infeasible
Explanation. With $w_j>c$ one has $x_j=0$ in every feasible solution: removing the item changes nothing, so the assumption is not restrictive. The instance stays feasible (the empty set always is).
oc-f-587 · level ipotesi · notes
In the 0/1 knapsack (KP: profits $p_j>0$, weights $w_j$, capacity $c$) one assumes $\sum_j w_j>c$. What would happen with $\sum_j w_j\le c$?
  1. The optimal value would be $0$
  2. Taking all items would be feasible and optimal: the instance is trivial
  3. No subset would be feasible
  4. The continuous relaxation would have a fractional item
Explanation. With positive profits, adding items always improves a solution; if all of them fit, the set of all items is optimal. The assumption only excludes these trivial cases.
oc-f-588 · level ipotesi · notes
In the subset sum (SSP: given integer weights $w_j$ and a target value $c$, one looks for a subset of weight exactly $c$) one assumes $\sum_j w_j\ge c$. What happens if the assumption is dropped?
  1. No subset can weigh $c$: the answer is «no» without computation
  2. The subset of all items is the solution
  3. It is enough to remove the heaviest item
  4. The problem becomes an unbounded knapsack
Explanation. Every subset weighs at most $\sum_j w_j<c$, so it cannot reach $c$. In the 0/1 knapsack the analogous assumption excluded instead the case in which everything fits.
oc-f-589 · level ipotesi · notes
In the bounded knapsack (BKP: at most $b_j$ copies of item $j$, capacity $c$) one assumes $b_j\,w_j\le c$. An item has $w_j=4$, $b_j=5$ and $c=13$. How is the instance brought back to the assumption without changing the optimal value?
  1. Remove the item
  2. Set $b_j=1$
  3. It cannot: the instance is infeasible
  4. Set $b_j=\lfloor c/w_j\rfloor=3$: more than $3$ copies do not fit anyway
Explanation. At most $\lfloor 13/4\rfloor=3$ copies fit in the knapsack, so the bound $b_j=5$ is never active and can be reduced to $3$.
oc-f-590 · level ipotesi · notes
In the unbounded knapsack (UKP: unlimited copies of every item, capacity $c$) let $\hat b_j=\lfloor c/w_j\rfloor$ and assume $\sum_j\hat b_j\,w_j>c$. Why does an instance with a single item always violate the assumption?
  1. Because with a single item the problem is infeasible
  2. Because $\hat b_1=1$ for every $c$
  3. Because $\hat b_1w_1=\lfloor c/w_1\rfloor w_1\le c$: the $\hat b_1$ copies all fit, and they are optimal
  4. Because a single item always has $w_1>c$
Explanation. With a single item the optimal solution takes $\lfloor c/w_1\rfloor$ copies: it is the trivial case that the assumption excludes.
oc-f-591 · level ipotesi · notes
In the multidimensional knapsack (MDKP: capacities $c_d$ and weights $w_{dj}$ for every dimension $d\in\mathscr{D}$) one wants to exclude the trivial case in which all items fit. Which assumption is the right one?
  1. $\sum_d\sum_j w_{dj}>\sum_d c_d$
  2. There is a dimension $d$ with $\sum_j w_{dj}>c_d$
  3. For every dimension $d$, $\sum_j w_{dj}>c_d$
  4. For every item $j$ there is $d$ with $w_{dj}>c_d$
Explanation. All items fit if and only if every dimension is respected; one violated dimension is therefore enough to exclude the trivial case. Asking it for every $d$ would exclude non-trivial instances.
oc-f-592 · level ipotesi · notes
In the multiple knapsack (MKP: knapsacks $k\in\mathscr{K}$ of capacity $c_k$, items of weight $w_j$) one assumes that every item, alone, fits in at least one knapsack. Which condition expresses it?
  1. $w_j\le\max_{k}c_k$ for every item $j$
  2. $w_j\le\min_{k}c_k$ for every item $j$
  3. $w_j\le\sum_k c_k$ for every item $j$
  4. $\sum_j w_j\le\max_k c_k$
Explanation. «There is $k$ with $w_j\le c_k$» is equivalent to $w_j\le\max_k c_k$. Asking for the minimum would exclude items fitting only in the large knapsacks; the sum of the capacities is not enough, because an item cannot be split among knapsacks.
oc-f-593 · level ipotesi · notes
In the multiple-choice knapsack (MCKP: exactly one item per class, capacity $c$) the instance is feasible if and only if $\sum_h\min_{j\in\mathscr{J}_h}w_j\le c$. With classes of weights $\{3,5\}$, $\{2,6\}$, $\{4\}$ and $c=8$, what can be concluded?
  1. The instance is feasible with the items of weight $3$, $2$ and $4$
  2. It is enough to choose two classes out of three
  3. The instance is feasible because every item has $w_j\le c$
  4. The instance is infeasible: even the lightest items weigh $3+2+4=9>8$
Explanation. The lightest choice takes the minimum of every class: if even this one exceeds $c$, no choice of one item per class fits. That every item fits alone is not enough.
oc-f-594 · level ipotesi · notes
In the knapsack with setups (KPS: an item of class $h$ can be taken only by activating the class, which consumes the setup weight $s_h$; capacity $c$) one assumes $w_j+s_h\le c$. A class has $s_h=4$, $c=10$ and contains an item with $w_j=7$. What can be concluded?
  1. The class must always be activated
  2. The instance is infeasible
  3. The item can never be selected and can be removed
  4. The item fits, because $w_j=7\le c$
Explanation. Taking the item requires activating the class: $7+4=11>10$. The right comparison is with $w_j+s_h$, not with $w_j$ alone.
oc-f-595 · level teorema · notes
Karp (1972) included the subset sum (SSP: is there a subset of weights $w_j$ summing exactly to $c$?) among the first $21$ NP-complete problems. What follows for the 0/1 knapsack (KP)?
  1. The KP is strongly NP-hard
  2. The KP is NP-hard, because it contains the SSP as the special case $p_j=w_j$
  3. The KP is in P, because its capacity is an inequality
  4. Nothing: KP and SSP are independent problems
Explanation. With $p_j=w_j$ and capacity $c$ the KP has optimal value $c$ if and only if the SSP answer is «yes»: a polynomial algorithm for the KP would solve the SSP. The KP has however a pseudo-polynomial algorithm, so it is not strongly NP-hard.
oc-f-596 · level facile · notes
Dantzig (1957) solved the continuous version of the 0/1 knapsack (variables $x_j\in[0,1]$) by sorting the items in an order that comes back in many bounds of the course. Which order?
  1. By non-increasing efficiency $p_j/w_j$
  2. By non-decreasing weight $w_j$
  3. By non-increasing profit $p_j$
  4. By increasing index $j$
Explanation. The knapsack is filled with the most efficient items, and the first one that does not fit is taken as a fraction: it is the optimal solution of the continuous relaxation.
oc-f-917 · level facile · notes
In the family of knapsack problems (KP, SSP, BKP, UKP, MDKP, MKP, MCKP, KPS) every item has a profit and a weight. In which member does the profit of every item coincide with its weight?
  1. In the unbounded knapsack problem (UKP)
  2. In the multidimensional knapsack problem (MDKP)
  3. In the multiple-choice knapsack problem (MCKP)
  4. In the subset sum problem (SSP)
Explanation. The SSP looks for a subset of weight exactly $c$: it is the case $p_j=w_j$ of the 0/1 knapsack, where maximizing the profit means filling the knapsack as much as possible.
oc-f-918 · level facile · notes
In the multiple knapsack problem (MKP) there are $m$ distinct knapsacks and $n$ items; every item goes into one knapsack or into none. How many candidate solutions are there, ignoring the capacities?
  1. $2^n\cdot m$
  2. $2^{nm}$
  3. $(m+1)^n$
  4. $m^n$
Explanation. Every item has $m+1$ choices: one of the $m$ knapsacks or none. $m^n$ forgets the choice «none»; $2^{nm}$ also counts the solutions with an item in several knapsacks.
oc-f-919 · level facile · notes
In the 0/1 knapsack problem (KP: items of profit $p_j$ and weight $w_j$, capacity $c$, the total profit is maximized) all profits are multiplied by $2$, leaving weights and capacity unchanged. What happens?
  1. Some optimal solutions become infeasible
  2. The optimal solutions stay the same, the optimal value doubles
  3. The optimal solutions change, the optimal value doubles
  4. The optimal solutions stay the same, the optimal value does not change
Explanation. Feasibility depends only on weights and capacity; the objective $\sum_{j\in S}2p_j$ is twice the original one for every $S$, so the order among the solutions does not change.
oc-f-920 · level ipotesi · notes
In the 0/1 knapsack problem (KP) one assumes (1) $\sum_j w_j>c$ and (2) $w_j\le c$ for every item. An instance has $c=10$ and weights $w=(4,7,12,3)$. How is it brought back to the assumptions?
  1. The item of weight $12$ is removed; the remaining weights sum to $14>c$: both hold
  2. The item of weight $12$ is removed; the optimum is then to take all the others
  3. The weight $12$ is reduced to the value $c=10$ and the item is kept
  4. It cannot: the instance is infeasible
Explanation. An item with $w_j>c$ belongs to no feasible solution, so it is removed without changing $z(I)$. Afterwards, $4+7+3=14>10$: assumption (1) still holds.
oc-f-921 · level facile · notes
The subset sum problem (SSP) asks whether there is a subset of integers $w_j$ summing to exactly $c$. With $w=(4,6,9,13)$, for which value of $c$ is the answer «no»?
  1. $c=10$
  2. $c=19$
  3. $c=17$
  4. $c=12$
Explanation. The reachable sums include $4+6=10$, $6+13=19$, $4+13=17$; for $12$ one would need $4+$an $8$ or $6+6$, and no subset sums to $12$.
oc-f-922 · level ipotesi · notes
In the subset sum problem (SSP: is there a subset of integer weights $w_j$ summing to exactly $c$?) one assumes $w_j\le c$ for every $j$. If an item has $w_j>c$, what happens?
  1. The answer is certainly «yes», since weight can be removed
  2. $w_j$ is replaced by $w_j-c$ and the item is kept
  3. It belongs to no subset of sum $c$: it is removed without changing the answer
  4. The answer is certainly «no», because a weight exceeds $c$
Explanation. With positive weights a subset containing $j$ sums to at least $w_j>c$. The item is useless, but the others may still sum to $c$.
oc-f-923 · level ipotesi · notes
In the subset sum problem (SSP) one assumes (1) $\sum_j w_j\ge c$ and (2) $w_j\le c$ for every $j$. An instance has $w=(4,6,9)$ and $c=20$. What can be said?
  1. It satisfies both assumptions and the answer is «no»
  2. It violates assumption (1): $\sum_j w_j=19<20$, so the answer is «no»
  3. It violates assumption (2), because $9+6+4$ exceeds $c$
  4. It satisfies both assumptions and the answer is «yes»
Explanation. Even taking all items one reaches $19$: no subset reaches $20$. Assumption (2) concerns single weights, and $9\le20$.
oc-f-924 · level facile · notes
In the bounded knapsack problem (BKP: $b_j$ copies of item $j$) the extended set is $\hat{\mathscr{I}}=\{(j,k):j\in\mathscr{I},\ k=1,\dots,b_j\}$ and a solution is an $S\subseteq\hat{\mathscr{I}}$. With $b=(3,2,2)$, how many elements does $\hat{\mathscr{I}}$ have and how is $S$ read?
  1. $7$; the copies of item $j$ taken are the pairs $(j,k)$ in $S$
  2. $12$; the copies of item $j$ taken are the pairs $(j,k)$ in $S$
  3. $7$; every pair $(j,k)$ in $S$ gives $k$ copies of item $j$
  4. $3$; $S$ says which items to take at least once
Explanation. $|\hat{\mathscr{I}}|=\sum_j b_j=3+2+2=7$ (not the product $12$). The pair $(j,k)$ is the $k$-th copy of item $j$: it is worth one copy, not $k$.
oc-f-925 · level ipotesi · notes
In the bounded knapsack problem (BKP: $b_j$ copies of item $j$, capacity $c$) one assumes $\sum_j b_j\,w_j>c$. If the assumption fails, what happens?
  1. The instance has no feasible solutions
  2. Every $b_j$ must be reduced to $\lfloor c/w_j\rfloor$
  3. The optimum takes a single copy of every item
  4. Taking all copies of all items is feasible and optimal
Explanation. If all the copies together weigh at most $c$, the solution «everything» is feasible and, with positive profits, no other solution beats it: the instance is trivial.
oc-f-926 · level teorema · notes
In the bounded knapsack problem (BKP, $b_j\ge1$ copies of item $j$) one makes the assumptions (1) $\sum_j b_jw_j>c$, (2) $w_j\le c$ for every $j$, (3) $b_jw_j\le c$ for every $j$. What logical relation is there among them?
  1. (1) implies (3)
  2. They are independent: none implies another
  3. (3) implies (2), because $w_j\le b_jw_j$
  4. (2) implies (3), because $b_j\ge1$
Explanation. With $b_j\ge1$ one has $w_j\le b_jw_j\le c$. The converse is false: $w_j=4$, $b_j=5$, $c=13$ satisfies (2) but not (3).
oc-f-927 · level facile · notes
In the unbounded knapsack problem (UKP) at most $\lfloor c/w_j\rfloor$ copies of item $j$ can be taken. With $c=10$ and weights $w=(3,4,5)$, how many vectors of copy numbers $(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ respect these single bounds?
  1. $1000$
  2. $36$
  3. $12$
  4. $8$
Explanation. $x_1\in\{0,\dots,3\}$, $x_2\in\{0,1,2\}$, $x_3\in\{0,1,2\}$: $4\cdot3\cdot3=36$. $12=3\cdot2\cdot2$ forgets the value $0$.
oc-f-928 · level ipotesi · notes
In the unbounded knapsack problem (UKP) let $\hat b_j=\lfloor c/w_j\rfloor$ be the maximum number of copies of item $j$ fitting in the knapsack; one assumes $w_j\le c$. If an item has $w_j>c$, what is $\hat b_j$ and what is done?
  1. $\hat b_j=0$: the item can never be taken and is removed
  2. $\hat b_j=1$: one copy of it is taken
  3. $\hat b_j=\infty$: the copies are unlimited
  4. $\hat b_j=0$: the instance is infeasible
Explanation. Not even one copy fits; the empty solution is still feasible, so the instance does not become infeasible: it suffices to remove the item.
oc-f-929 · level ipotesi · notes
In the unbounded knapsack problem (UKP) one assumes $\sum_j\hat b_j\,w_j>c$, with $\hat b_j=\lfloor c/w_j\rfloor$. Why does an instance with a single item ($n=1$) always violate this assumption, and what is its optimum?
  1. $\lfloor c/w_1\rfloor\,w_1>c$ always; the optimum takes a single copy
  2. It violates it only if $w_1$ divides $c$; the optimum takes $c/w_1$ copies
  3. It never violates it; the optimum is found by dynamic programming
  4. $\lfloor c/w_1\rfloor\,w_1\le c$ always; the optimum takes $\lfloor c/w_1\rfloor$ copies
Explanation. By definition of the floor $\lfloor c/w_1\rfloor\,w_1\le c$: all the possible copies fit together, so the instance is trivial.
oc-f-930 · level facile · notes
The multidimensional knapsack problem (MDKP) has $n$ items, $m$ dimensions with capacities $c_d$ and weights $w_{dj}$; every item is taken or not. In the natural model, how many binary variables and how many capacity constraints are there?
  1. $n$ binary variables and a single capacity constraint
  2. $n\cdot m$ binary variables and $n$ assignment constraints
  3. $n$ binary variables and $m$ capacity constraints
  4. $n\cdot m$ binary variables and $m$ capacity constraints
Explanation. One variable $x_j$ per item (the same item consumes capacity in all dimensions) and one constraint $\sum_j w_{dj}x_j\le c_d$ per dimension. The variables $x_{kj}$ and the assignment constraints belong to the MKP.
oc-f-931 · level ipotesi · notes
In the multidimensional knapsack problem (MDKP: capacity $c_d$ and weights $w_{dj}$ per dimension $d$) one assumes $w_{dj}\le c_d$ for every $d$ and every $j$. An item has $w_{1j}\le c_1$ but $w_{2j}>c_2$. What is done?
  1. The instance is declared infeasible
  2. It is removed: it never fits in the knapsack
  3. It is kept: fitting in one dimension is enough
  4. It is kept if $w_{1j}+w_{2j}\le c_1+c_2$
Explanation. A selected item consumes capacity in all dimensions: if it exceeds $c_2$ on its own, no solution containing it is feasible.
oc-f-932 · level ipotesi · notes
In the multidimensional knapsack problem (MDKP) one assumes that there is a dimension $d$ with $\sum_j w_{dj}>c_d$. An instance has $\vet c=(10,8)$, $\sum_j w_{1j}=9$ and $\sum_j w_{2j}=12$. Does the assumption hold?
  1. Yes: in dimension $2$ the total weight exceeds the capacity
  2. No: it should be exceeded in all dimensions
  3. No: one needs $\sum_d\sum_j w_{dj}>\sum_d c_d$ and $21>18$ is not enough
  4. Yes: in dimension $1$ the total weight does not exceed the capacity
Explanation. One dimension in which the items do not all fit is enough to make «take everything» infeasible; here it is dimension $2$ ($12>8$).
oc-f-933 · level facile · notes
In the multiple knapsack problem (MKP: $m$ knapsacks of capacity $c_k$, items of profit $p_j$ and weight $w_j$) and in bin packing (BPP: identical bins of capacity $c$) the items go into containers. What distinguishes them?
  1. MKP: all items must be packed; BPP: an item may stay out
  2. In both the number of containers used is minimized
  3. None, if the capacities of the MKP knapsacks are equal
  4. MKP: an item may stay out; BPP: all items must be packed
Explanation. The MKP chooses which items to load and where (maximum profit, given number of knapsacks); the BPP must pack every item and minimizes the bins.
oc-f-934 · level ipotesi · notes
In the multiple knapsack problem (MKP) one assumes that every item, on its own, fits in at least one knapsack: for every $j$ there is $k$ with $w_j\le c_k$. With capacities $(8,5)$, does an item of weight $6$ satisfy the assumption?
  1. No: it should be split between the two knapsacks
  2. Yes, and it can go into either of the two knapsacks
  3. Yes: it fits in knapsack $1$, and can go only there
  4. No: it should fit in all knapsacks
Explanation. The assumption asks for a single knapsack large enough ($6\le8$); $w_j\le\min_k c_k$ is not needed. The item does not fit in knapsack $2$.
oc-f-935 · level ipotesi · notes
In the multiple knapsack problem (MKP) one assumes (1) $\sum_j w_j>\sum_k c_k$ and (2) every item fits on its own in at least one knapsack. An instance has two knapsacks of capacity $5$ and three items of weight $4$. What holds?
  1. Both fail
  2. Both hold: $12>10$ and $4\le5$
  3. (1) fails, because every item fits in a knapsack
  4. (2) fails, because $4+4>5$
Explanation. (1) compares the total weight with the total capacity ($12>10$); (2) concerns one item at a time ($4\le5$). That two items together do not fit in a knapsack violates nothing.
oc-f-936 · level facile · notes
In the multiple-choice knapsack problem (MCKP) the items are divided into $q$ classes $\mathscr{J}_1,\dots,\mathscr{J}_q$ and the knapsack has capacity $c$. How many items does a feasible solution contain?
  1. Exactly $q$, one per class
  2. At most $q$, at most one per class
  3. At least $q$, at least one per class
  4. Any number, as long as they fit in the knapsack
Explanation. The multiple-choice constraint is an equality: $\sum_{j\in\mathscr{J}_h}x_j=1$ for every class. «At most one» would be a different constraint, allowing a class to be skipped.
oc-f-937 · level teorema · notes
In the multiple-choice knapsack problem (MCKP: exactly one item from each class $\mathscr{J}_h$, capacity $c$) the instance is feasible if and only if $\sum_h\min_{j\in\mathscr{J}_h}w_j\le c$. Why is the condition sufficient?
  1. Every choice of one item per class weighs at least $\sum_h\min_{j}w_j$
  2. The optimal solution always uses the lightest item of every class
  3. Dynamic programming always finds a choice of weight at most $c$
  4. Choosing the lightest item in every class gives a choice that fits in the knapsack
Explanation. The choice of the lightest items weighs exactly $\sum_h\min_j w_j\le c$. The second option is the reason why the condition is necessary.
oc-f-938 · level ipotesi · notes
In the multiple-choice knapsack problem (MCKP) exactly one item must be taken from each class $\mathscr{J}_h$, and one assumes $\mathscr{J}_h\neq\emptyset$ for every $h$. What happens if a class is empty?
  1. An item of profit and weight $0$ is added and the value does not change
  2. The optimal value is $0$, as for the empty knapsack
  3. The instance is infeasible: nothing can be taken from that class
  4. The empty class is ignored and the rest is solved
Explanation. The constraint «exactly one item from class $h$» cannot be satisfied with $\mathscr{J}_h=\emptyset$: no choice is feasible.
oc-f-939 · level facile · notes
Knapsack with setups (KPS): capacity $c=10$; class $1=\{1,2\}$ with setup cost $f_1=3$ and setup weight $s_1=2$; class $2=\{3\}$ with $f_2=4$, $s_2=1$; revenues $p=(5,4,6)$ and weights $w=(3,2,4)$. The setup of every class from which at least one item is taken is paid. Optimal value?
  1. $11$
  2. $6$
  3. $9$
  4. $4$
Explanation. $\{1,2\}$: weight $5+2=7$, value $9-3=6$. $\{1,3\}$: weight $7+3=10$, value $11-7=4$. $\{1,2,3\}$ weighs $9+3=12>10$. $9$ forgets the setup cost.
oc-f-940 · level ipotesi · notes
In the knapsack problem with setups (KPS) one assumes $w_j+s_h\le c$ for every item $j$ of class $h$ ($s_h$ = setup weight of the class). With $c=12$ and a class with $s_h=4$ and items of weight $9$, $7$, $8$, which items violate the assumption?
  1. Only the item of weight $9$
  2. None, because all have weight at most $c$
  3. The items of weight $9$ and $8$
  4. All three
Explanation. $9+4=13>12$, while $7+4=11$ and $8+4=12$ fit. $w_j\le c$ is not enough: taking $j$ activates the class and also consumes $s_h$.
oc-f-941 · level ipotesi · notes
Both in the KPS (knapsack with setups: a class is activated by taking at least one of its items) and in the MCKP (exactly one item per class) one assumes every class is non-empty. What would change with an empty class?
  1. KPS: infeasible instance; MCKP: the class is ignored
  2. In both problems the instance would become infeasible
  3. In both problems the class could be ignored
  4. KPS: the class is never activated; MCKP: infeasible instance
Explanation. The KPS does not force using every class: an empty class is never activated and can be removed. The MCKP forces one item per class, impossible if the class is empty.
oc-f-942 · level facile · notes
Ibarra and Kim (1975) gave the first fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) for the 0/1 knapsack. What does an FPTAS guarantee?
  1. The optimal solution in pseudo-polynomial time, i.e., polynomial in $n$ and $c$
  2. Value $\ge z(I)/2$ in linear time, for every instance
  3. For every $\varepsilon>0$, value $\ge(1-\varepsilon)z(I)$ in time polynomial in $n$ and $1/\varepsilon$
  4. For every $\varepsilon>0$, value $\ge(1-\varepsilon)z(I)$ in time polynomial in $n$ and exponential in $1/\varepsilon$
Explanation. The second option describes a PTAS that is not fully polynomial; the third is dynamic programming; the fourth a fixed-ratio approximation algorithm.
oc-f-943 · level facile · notes
Dantzig (1957) solved the continuous version of the 0/1 knapsack ($x_j\in[0,1]$) by sorting the items by non-increasing efficiency $p_j/w_j$ and filling the knapsack, with a fraction of the first item that does not fit. With $p=(10,9,4)$, $w=(5,6,4)$ and $c=8$, which value is obtained?
  1. $13$
  2. $14.5$
  3. $14$
  4. $19$
Explanation. Efficiencies $2$, $1.5$, $1$: item $1$ whole (weight $5$), then $3/6$ of item $2$: $10+4.5=14.5$. $14=10+4$ skips item $2$ instead of taking a fraction of it.

3. Packing problems (30)

oc-f-010 · level facile · notes
Bin packing (BPP): three items of weight $6$ must be packed into the minimum number of bins of capacity $c=10$. What are the weight bound $\left\lceil\sum_j w_j/c\right\rceil$ and the optimal value $z(I)$?
  1. Weight bound $1$, $z(I)=2$
  2. Weight bound $2$, $z(I)=3$
  3. Weight bound $2$, $z(I)=2$
  4. Weight bound $3$, $z(I)=3$
Explanation. $\lceil 18/10\rceil=2$, but two items of weight $6$ do not fit together: $3$ bins are needed. The weight bound is not always attained.
oc-f-011 · level facile · notes
In bin packing (BPP) $n$ items of weight $w_j$ must be packed into the minimum number of bins of capacity $c$. In cutting stock (CSP) item $j$ also has a demand $d_j\in\Z_{\ge1}$. How are the two problems related?
  1. The CSP asks to pack $d_j$ identical copies of item $j$; the BPP is the case $d_j=1$ for every $j$
  2. The CSP has bins of different capacities $d_j$; the BPP is the case with all capacities equal
  3. The CSP allows splitting an item into $d_j$ parts; the BPP is the case without splitting
  4. The CSP asks to fill $d_j$ bins with item $j$; the BPP is the case with a single bin
Explanation. The CSP asks to pack $d_j$ copies of every item $j$ into the minimum number of bins of capacity $c$; with $d_j=1$ for every $j$ it is the BPP. Items are not split and the capacity is unique.
oc-f-012 · level facile · notes
In bin packing (BPP) a solution is a partition of the $n$ items into bins, and the order of the bins does not matter. How many candidate partitions of $n$ items are there, before checking the capacities ($B(n)$ is the $n$-th Bell number)?
  1. $2^n$
  2. $n!$
  3. $\frac{(n-1)!}{2}$
  4. $B(n)$
Explanation. The partitions of a set of $n$ elements are $B(n)$ (Bell numbers); the order of the bins does not matter. $2^n$ counts the subsets, $n!$ the orderings.
oc-f-169 · level facile · notes
In bin packing (BPP) $n$ items of weight $w_j$ must be packed into the minimum number of bins of capacity $c$. Why is $w_j\le c$ assumed for every item?
  1. Otherwise two items could share the same bin
  2. Otherwise the number of bins could exceed $n$
  3. Otherwise the item fits in no bin and there are no feasible solutions
  4. Otherwise the weight bound $\lceil\sum_j w_j/c\rceil$ would not be an integer
Explanation. An item heavier than the capacity cannot be packed: the instance would have no solution. With $w_j\le c$ putting every item in its own bin is always feasible.
oc-f-170 · level facile · notes
Bin packing (BPP: minimum number of bins of capacity $c$) with $c=10$ and weights $w=(7,6,5,4,3,2)$. What is the optimal value $z(I)$?
  1. $6$
  2. $3$
  3. $4$
  4. $2$
Explanation. $\sum_j w_j=27$, hence at least $\lceil 2.7\rceil=3$ bins are needed; $\{7,3\}$, $\{6,4\}$, $\{5,2\}$ is a solution with $3$ bins, hence optimal.
oc-f-171 · level teorema · notes
In bin packing (weights $w_j$, capacity $c$, optimal value $z(I)$) the weight bound is $L_1=\left\lceil\sum_j w_j/c\right\rceil$. Which statement is correct?
  1. $L_1\le z(I)$ for every instance, and $L_1<z(I)$ is possible
  2. $L_1=z(I)$ for every instance
  3. $L_1\ge z(I)$ for every instance, because it is rounded up
  4. $L_1\le z(I)$ only if all weights are smaller than $c/2$
Explanation. $z(I)$ bins contain at most $z(I)\,c$ units of weight, hence $z(I)\ge\sum_jw_j/c$, rounded up because $z(I)$ is an integer. With three items of weight $6$ and $c=10$: $L_1=2<3=z(I)$.
oc-f-172 · level facile · notes
In bin packing with capacity $c$, two items of weight larger than $c/2$ never share a bin. With $c=10$ and weights $w=(6,6,7,2,2,2)$, which lower bound on the number of bins does this observation give, and which the weight bound $\lceil\sum_j w_j/c\rceil$?
  1. $3$ and $2$
  2. $2$ and $3$
  3. $6$ and $3$
  4. $3$ and $3$
Explanation. The three items of weight $6,6,7$ exceed $c/2=5$: $3$ different bins are needed. $\sum_jw_j=25$ and $\lceil 25/10\rceil=3$. Here the two bounds coincide, and $\{6,2,2\},\{6,2\},\{7\}$ is optimal.
oc-f-173 · level facile · notes
In bin packing a solution with $k$ bins can be written by giving every item the number $1,\dots,k$ of its bin. How many assignment vectors describe the same partition of the items, if all $k$ bins are non-empty?
  1. $k$, one for every starting bin
  2. $k^n$, one for every assignment of the $n$ items
  3. $k!$, one for every way of numbering the bins
  4. $2^k$, one for every subset of bins
Explanation. Renumbering the bins does not change the solution: every partition corresponds to $k!$ vectors. This is the symmetry that weakens the models with numbered bins.
oc-f-174 · level facile · notes
Bin packing (BPP: items of weight $w_j$ into the minimum number of bins of capacity $c$) is strongly NP-hard. What does this imply, if $P\neq NP$?
  1. Every instance with more than $50$ items is intractable
  2. There is no pseudo-polynomial algorithm, for example of time $O(nc)$
  3. There is no exact algorithm at all for the BPP
  4. There is an $O(nc)$ algorithm by DP, as for the knapsack
Explanation. Strongly NP-hard means it stays hard even with small numbers: an algorithm polynomial in $n$ and in the value of $c$ is not expected. Exponential exact algorithms exist, and many large instances are solved in practice.
oc-f-175 · level facile · notes
Cutting stock (CSP): rolls of length $c=10$; $d_1=5$ pieces of length $4$ and $d_2=4$ pieces of length $3$ are needed, and the number of cut rolls is minimized. What is the weight bound $\left\lceil\sum_j d_jw_j/c\right\rceil$?
  1. $4$
  2. $3$
  3. $5$
  4. $9$
Explanation. $\sum_j d_jw_j=5\cdot4+4\cdot3=32$ and $\lceil 3.2\rceil=4$. The bound is attained: two rolls $4+3+3$, one $4+4$ and one $4$. $9$ is the number of pieces.
oc-f-176 · level facile · notes
In cutting stock (CSP) $d_j$ identical copies of piece $j$ are needed, cut from rolls of length $c$. Why is a solution described by cutting patterns (how many copies of each type are cut from a roll)?
  1. Cutting patterns allow cutting one piece from two rolls
  2. Cutting patterns make every roll different from the others
  3. Cutting patterns remove the length constraint $c$
  4. Copies of the same piece are identical: only how many each roll contains matters
Explanation. Treating every copy as a distinct item multiplies the equivalent solutions; a pattern only states how many copies of each type the roll contains and satisfies $\sum_j a_jw_j\le c$.
oc-f-177 · level facile · notes
A cutting stock instance (pieces $j=1,\dots,n$ with demand $d_j$ and length $w_j$, rolls of length $c$) can be seen as bin packing with $\sum_j d_j$ items. What is the drawback of this transformation?
  1. The resulting bin packing has bins of different capacities
  2. The transformation works only if all $d_j$ equal $1$
  3. The number of items grows with the values $d_j$, and identical copies create many symmetric solutions
  4. The resulting bin packing has an optimal value different from the CSP one
Explanation. The transformation is correct (same optimal value), but the instance becomes large when the demands are large, and exchanging identical copies gives equivalent solutions.
oc-f-563 · level ipotesi · notes
In bin packing ($n$ items of weight $w_j$, bins of capacity $c$) every feasible solution uses at least $\lceil\sum_j w_j/c\rceil$ bins. Which facts are needed to prove it?
  1. A solution with $k$ bins has $\sum_j w_j\le kc$, since every bin carries at most $c$; and $k$ is integer
  2. Every item weighs at most $c/2$; and $k$ is integer
  3. The items are sorted by non-increasing weight; and every bin is full
  4. At most one bin is less than half full; and $k$ is integer
Explanation. Adding up the loads, $\sum_j w_j\le kc$, i.e., $k\ge\sum_j w_j/c$; since $k$ is integer it is rounded up. No assumption on the weights or on the order is needed.
oc-f-597 · level facile · notes
Packing problems put items of weight $w_j$ into identical bins of capacity $c$. What distinguishes the cutting stock (CSP) from bin packing (BPP)?
  1. In the CSP the packed weight is maximized
  2. In the CSP every bin receives at most one item
  3. In the CSP $d_j$ copies of item $j$ must be packed, in the BPP only one
  4. In the CSP the bins have different capacities
Explanation. The two problems have the same bins and the same objective (minimum number of bins); the CSP groups identical copies with a demand $d_j$.
oc-f-598 · level facile · notes
In packing problems ($n$ items of weight $w_j$, identical bins of capacity $c$, unlimited in number) what is the objective?
  1. Maximize the number of items packed with $m$ given bins
  2. Pack all items in the minimum number of bins
  3. Pack the largest weight into a single bin
  4. Minimize the free space of the last bin
Explanation. All items must be packed, no bin exceeds $c$, and the number of bins used is minimized. Maximizing the weight in one bin is a knapsack.
oc-f-599 · level ipotesi · notes
In bin packing (BPP: items of weight $w_j$, bins of capacity $c$) one assumes $w_j\le c$. In the 0/1 knapsack an item with $w_j>c$ can be removed. What happens instead in the BPP if an item has $w_j>c$?
  1. The instance is infeasible: all items must be packed and that item fits in no bin
  2. The item is removed without changing the optimal value
  3. The item occupies two bins
  4. The bound $\lceil\sum_j w_j/c\rceil$ becomes exact
Explanation. In the BPP every item must go into a bin, so a too heavy item makes the feasible set empty. In the knapsack, instead, an item may simply not be taken.
oc-f-600 · level ipotesi · notes
In bin packing (BPP: items of weight $w_j\le c$, bins of capacity $c$) one assumes $\sum_j w_j>c$. What happens if the assumption is dropped?
  1. The instance is infeasible
  2. The optimal value is $n$
  3. The bound $\lceil\sum_j w_j/c\rceil$ equals $0$
  4. All items fit in a single bin and the optimal value is $1$
Explanation. With $\sum_j w_j\le c$ one bin is enough, and it is the minimum possible with at least one item: the instance is trivial.
oc-f-601 · level facile · notes
In cutting stock (CSP: $d_j$ copies of item $j$ of weight $w_j$, bins of capacity $c$) one assumes $\sum_j d_jw_j>c$. With $c=10$, $w=(3,4)$ and $d=(2,1)$, does the assumption hold?
  1. Yes: $2+1=3$ copies are more than one
  2. No: because $w_2>c/3$
  3. No: $2\cdot3+1\cdot4=10\le c$, all copies fit in one bin
  4. Yes: $3+4=7$ and the copies do not count
Explanation. In the CSP the assumption concerns the weight of all required copies: $\sum_j d_jw_j=10$, so one bin is enough and the instance is trivial.
oc-f-602 · level facile · notes
Cutting stock (CSP) with bins of capacity $c=10$, weights $w=(4,5,3,6)$ and required copies $d=(2,1,3,1)$. What is the weight bound $\mathrm{LB}=\lceil\sum_j d_jw_j/c\rceil$?
  1. $7$
  2. $3$
  3. $2$
  4. $4$
Explanation. $\sum_j d_jw_j=8+5+9+6=28$, hence $\lceil 2.8\rceil=3$. Forgetting the copies gives $\lceil18/10\rceil=2$; $7$ is the number of copies.
oc-f-603 · level facile · notes
A cutting stock (CSP) instance requires $7$ copies overall, of $4$ different items. Counting identical copies as different items, the candidate solutions are the partitions of the $7$ copies. How many are there?
  1. $B(7)=877$
  2. $B(4)=15$
  3. $2^7=128$
  4. $7!=5040$
Explanation. The partitions of a set of $7$ elements are counted by the Bell number $B(7)=877$; this count is an overestimate, since swapping two identical copies does not change the solution.
oc-f-604 · level facile · notes
Johnson and coauthors (1974) analysed in the worst case the First Fit rule for bin packing (every item, in the given order, goes into the first bin where it fits). Which guarantee did they prove, with $z(I)$ the optimal number of bins?
  1. First Fit uses at most $z(I)+1$ bins
  2. First Fit is always optimal
  3. First Fit uses at most $\frac32 z(I)$ bins
  4. First Fit uses at most $\frac{17}{10}z(I)+2$ bins
Explanation. It is the classical result $\frac{17}{10}z(I)+2$; no polynomial heuristic can have absolute ratio better than $\frac32$, unless P = NP.
oc-f-944 · level facile · notes
In packing problems the $n$ items of weight $w_j\le c$ must all be packed into identical bins of capacity $c$, available in unlimited number. Why are $n$ bins always enough?
  1. Because any two items always fit together in a bin
  2. Because the optimal number of bins is always $\lceil n/2\rceil$
  3. They are not: sometimes more than $n$ bins are needed
  4. Because every item, on its own, fits in a bin
Explanation. With $w_j\le c$ the solution «one item per bin» is feasible, so $z(I)\le n$. Two items may not fit together (e.g., two weights larger than $c/2$).
oc-f-945 · level facile · notes
In a packing problem with bins of capacity $c$, all $n$ items have weight strictly larger than $c/2$. What is the minimum number of bins?
  1. $\lceil\sum_j w_j/c\rceil$
  2. $n-1$
  3. $n$
  4. $\lceil n/2\rceil$
Explanation. Two items of weight $>c/2$ together exceed the capacity: every bin holds only one of them. The weight bound $\lceil\sum_j w_j/c\rceil$ can be much lower, about $n/2$.
oc-f-946 · level ipotesi · notes
In bin packing (BPP: items of integer weight $w_j\ge1$, bins of capacity $c$) one assumes $w_j\le c$ for every item. Does an item with $w_j=c$ satisfy the assumption? What does it imply?
  1. No; the instance becomes infeasible
  2. Yes; in every solution it occupies a bin on its own
  3. No; the assumption requires $w_j<c$ and the item is removed
  4. Yes; it can share its bin with another item
Explanation. The assumption allows equality. Since the other weights are at least $1$, no other item fits in its bin.
oc-f-947 · level ipotesi · notes
In cutting stock (CSP: $d_j$ pieces of length $w_j$ are needed, cut from rolls of length $c$) one assumes $w_j\le c$. If a required piece is longer than a roll, what happens?
  1. The instance is infeasible: all required pieces must be cut
  2. The piece is removed, like a too heavy item in the knapsack
  3. The piece is cut from two rolls placed side by side
  4. Its length is reduced to $c$
Explanation. In packing problems every required copy must be packed: a piece with $w_j>c$ fits in no roll. In the knapsack, instead, an item can be left out.
