Lot sizing over $3$ periods with demands $d=(2,2,2)$, setup cost $sc_t=10$, variable cost $vc_t=1$ per unit produced and holding cost $hc_t=2$ per unit of stock at the end of a period. What is the cost of the plan $x=(4,0,2)$?
  1. $26$
  2. $34$
  3. $36$
  4. $30$
Explanation. Setups in periods $1$ and $3$: $20$; production of $6$ units: $6$; stocks $(2,0,0)$: $4$. Total $30$. Forgetting the stock gives $26$, charging a setup also in period $2$ gives $40$.
oc-f-200 · level facile · notes
In lot sizing with unsatisfied demand (LS-UD), part of the demand $d_{pt}$ of product $p$ in period $t$ may be left unsatisfied, at a penalty $cu_{pt}$ per unit. When is it convenient to leave a unit unsatisfied?
  1. When the penalty $cu_{pt}$ is higher than the cost of producing and holding that unit
  2. Only in the last period, because its demand creates no stock
  3. When the penalty $cu_{pt}$ is lower than the cost of producing and holding that unit
  4. Never: the demand must always be met, the penalty only measures the service level
Explanation. The model compares the penalty with the cost of serving the unit: if serving it costs more (setup, production, stock), paying $cu_{pt}$ is cheaper.
oc-f-201 · level facile · notes
In lot sizing with several products and setup times (MLS), the products $p\in P$ share the time $cap_t$ available in period $t$; a unit of $p$ takes $vt_{pt}$ units of time, and the setup of $p$ has a cost and a setup time. What changes with respect to the single-product CLS?
  1. The demands of the products add up and the problem becomes a single-product CLS
  2. Setups consume capacity: more setups in a period leave less time for production
  3. Setups have no cost: only the production time $vt_{pt}$ is paid
  4. Every product has its own capacity, so the products are independent problems
Explanation. With setup times the capacity of a period is shared by production and setups of the products: the products are not independent, and opening a setup also costs time.
oc-f-202 · level facile · notes
In lot sizing with overtime (LS-OT) normal working time costs $cw_t$ per unit up to $cap^{N}_t$ and overtime costs $co_t$ per unit up to $cap^{O}_t$, with $co_t>cw_t$. How much can be produced at most in period $t$, and when is overtime used?
  1. Up to $cap^{N}_t+cap^{O}_t$; overtime only after normal time is used up
  2. Up to $cap^{N}_t$; overtime replaces normal time when it is cheaper
  3. Up to $\max\{cap^{N}_t,cap^{O}_t\}$; only one of the two modes is chosen
  4. Without limit; overtime is paid only above the demand of the period
Explanation. The capacity is not fixed: it reaches $cap^{N}_t+cap^{O}_t$. Since overtime is more expensive, an optimal plan uses it only when normal time is exhausted.
oc-f-630 · level facile · notes
In lot sizing problems every period $t$ has demand $d_t$, setup cost $sc_t$, variable cost $vc_t$ and holding cost $hc_t$. Which trade-off must a production plan balance?
  1. Few setups (producing in advance) against little inventory (producing close to the demand)
  2. Maximum production against maximum demand
  3. Number of products against number of periods
  4. Capacity against variable cost, independently of the inventory
Explanation. Producing for several periods in a single setup saves $sc_t$ but keeps goods in stock paying $hc_t$; producing in every period does the opposite.
oc-f-631 · level facile · notes
In the lot sizing family, what do the variants LS-OT (overtime) and LS-UD (unmet demand) add to capacitated lot sizing (CLS)?
  1. LS-OT: several products; LS-UD: initial inventory
  2. LS-OT: no capacity; LS-UD: setup times
  3. LS-OT: backlogged demand at no cost; LS-UD: infinite capacity
  4. LS-OT: extra capacity at a higher cost; LS-UD: part of the demand lost with a penalty
Explanation. Both relax a constraint by paying a cost: overtime increases the capacity, unmet demand gives up part of the demand.
oc-f-632 · level ipotesi · notes
In capacitated lot sizing (CLS: demands $d_t$, capacities $cap_t$, zero initial inventory) one assumes $\sum_{u=1}^{t}cap_u\ge\sum_{u=1}^{t}d_u$ for every $t$. Why is the condition cumulative and not $cap_t\ge d_t$ period by period?
  1. Because unmet demand is recovered later
  2. Because the condition $cap_t\ge d_t$ always holds
  3. Because the demand of a period can also be covered by the production of earlier periods, kept in stock
  4. Because capacities can be moved to later periods
Explanation. With $d=(0,10)$ and $cap=(10,5)$ one has $cap_2<d_2$, but producing $10$ in period $1$ the plan is feasible. Production cannot come after the demand, however, so the sums up to every $t$ are needed.
oc-f-633 · level ipotesi · notes
In capacitated lot sizing (CLS) one assumes that the produced quantities are integer. With integer data, why does this assumption not change the optimal cost?
  1. Because the demands are all equal
  2. Once the setup periods are fixed, a min-cost flow problem remains, which has an integer optimal solution
  3. Because fractional quantities always cost more
  4. Because the setup cost is paid only for integer quantities
Explanation. With the setups fixed the residual problem has a network flow matrix, totally unimodular: with integer data an integer optimum exists.
oc-f-634 · level facile · notes
How are the variants of capacitated lot sizing (ULS, MLS, LS-SI, LS-OT, LS-UD) built with respect to the CLS?
  1. They keep the CLS data (periods, demands, costs) and change a single feature
  2. They are problems with completely different data
  3. They remove the setup costs
  4. They all add a second product
Explanation. Every definition reports only what changes: for instance the ULS removes the capacities, the MLS adds products sharing the time.
oc-f-635 · level facile · notes
In lot sizing with initial inventory (LS-SI) the quantity $si_p$ of product $p$ available at the start of the horizon is a decision, at cost $fc_p$ per unit. How does it differ from the CLS?
  1. In the LS-SI the final inventory must be positive
  2. In the LS-SI there are no setup costs
  3. In the LS-SI the initial inventory is a fixed datum
  4. In the CLS the initial inventory is fixed to zero; in the LS-SI it can be bought and pays $fc_p$ per unit
Explanation. The CLS assumes empty inventory at the start and at the end; the LS-SI turns the initial inventory into a variable with a unit cost.
oc-f-636 · level ipotesi · notes
Wagner and Whitin (1958) used a property of the optimal plans of uncapacitated lot sizing (ULS): one produces only when the inventory is empty. Why does the property fail in capacitated lot sizing (CLS)?
  1. Because in the CLS the final inventory is positive
  2. The property also holds in the CLS
  3. A low capacity may force production in advance, while there is still inventory
  4. Because in the CLS the setup costs are zero
Explanation. With $cap_t<d_t$ part of the demand of period $t$ must be produced earlier, even if the warehouse is not empty. Without the property the CLS is NP-hard.
oc-f-999 · level facile · notes
In lot sizing problems ($m$ periods, demand $d_t$, zero initial stock) a solution is a production plan $\vet{x}=(x_1,\dots,x_m)$. Once the quantities $x_t$ are fixed, what is determined?
  1. Only the periods with a setup; the stocks are free
  2. Only the stocks; the setups are chosen separately
  3. Nothing: demands and capacities must still be chosen
  4. The end-of-period stocks $s_t$ and the periods with a setup
Explanation. $s_t=\sum_{u\le t}(x_u-d_u)$ and there is a setup in $t$ if and only if $x_t>0$: the plan $\vet{x}$ determines the whole cost.
oc-f-1000 · level facile · notes
In lot sizing problems every period $t$ has a holding cost $hc_t$. To which quantity does it apply?
  1. To the demand of period $t$
  2. To the average stock between the start and the end of period $t$
  3. To the units in stock at the end of period $t$
  4. To the units produced in period $t$
Explanation. The cost of a plan contains $\sum_t hc_t\,s_t(\vet{x})$, with $s_t$ the end-of-period stock; it is paid also in periods without production.
oc-f-1001 · level facile · notes
Capacitated lot sizing over $4$ periods: demands $d=(2,3,1,2)$, capacity $5$ per period, zero initial stock. A plan $\vet{x}$ is feasible if $x_t\le 5$, the stocks $s_t=\sum_{u\le t}(x_u-d_u)$ are non-negative and $s_4=0$. Which plan is feasible?
  1. $(3,3,1,2)$
  2. $(2,4,0,2)$
  3. $(4,0,4,0)$
  4. $(2,0,6,0)$
Explanation. $(2,4,0,2)$ has stocks $(0,1,0,0)$. $(4,0,4,0)$ has $s_2=-1$ (it produces late); $(2,0,6,0)$ exceeds the capacity; $(3,3,1,2)$ leaves $s_4=1$.
oc-f-1002 · level ipotesi · notes
In capacitated lot sizing (CLS) the stock at the end of the horizon is assumed to be zero, $s_m=0$. Why does the assumption not exclude optimal plans, with non-negative costs?
  1. Removing the leftover units at the end never increases the cost
  2. Because the demand of the last period is always the largest
  3. Because a positive final stock violates the capacities
  4. Because the final stock is sold back at production cost
Explanation. Producing units that nobody asks for adds variable and holding cost (and possibly setups): reducing them gives a plan that is not more expensive.
oc-f-1003 · level facile · notes
In a capacitated lot sizing instance with $5$ periods, $8$ of the $32$ subsets of setup periods are feasible, but there are $94$ feasible plans. Why are the plans more than the setup choices?
  1. Because some plans have setups in periods without production
  2. Because the plans also count the infeasible setup choices
  3. Because every plan is counted once per ordering of the periods
  4. For a setup choice the quantities can be distributed in several ways
Explanation. Once the setup periods are fixed, how much to produce in each of them (respecting capacities and non-negative stocks) often leaves several choices.
oc-f-1004 · level teorema · notes
In uncapacitated lot sizing ($m$ periods, zero initial stock, $d_t\ge1$) the plans that produce only when the stock is empty are $2^{m-1}$. Why $2^{m-1}$ and not $2^m$?
  1. Half of the subsets of periods are infeasible because of the capacities
  2. Every plan is counted twice, once per direction
  3. Period $1$ must have a setup; the other $m-1$ are free
  4. The last period can never have a setup
Explanation. With zero initial stock and $d_1\ge1$ one must produce in period $1$. Once the other setup periods are chosen, each one produces the demand up to the next setup.
oc-f-1005 · level facile · notes
Capacitated lot sizing with capacity $4$ in every period and cumulative demands $D_t=\sum_{u\le t}d_u=(2,3,6,10,11)$. How many setups are needed at least in the first $4$ periods?
  1. $1$
  2. $3$
  3. $2$
  4. $4$
Explanation. In the first $4$ periods at least $10$ units must be produced, and every setup gives at most $4$: $\lceil10/4\rceil=3$ setups are needed.
oc-f-1006 · level facile · notes
In lot sizing a plan is improved by merging: the demand $d_t$ of period $t$ is produced in period $t-1$ (which already has a setup), removing the setup of period $t$. With constant variable cost, when does it pay off?
  1. When the setup cost $sc_t$ exceeds the holding cost $hc_{t-1}\,d_t$
  2. When the demand $d_t$ exceeds the demand $d_{t-1}$
  3. Always, because setups cost more than stocks
  4. When the holding cost $hc_{t-1}\,d_t$ exceeds the setup $sc_t$
Explanation. One saves $sc_t$ and pays the stock of the $d_t$ anticipated units for one period; enough capacity in period $t-1$ is also needed.
oc-f-1007 · level teorema · notes
In capacitated lot sizing the lower bound sums the $k$ smallest setup costs. If there are also variable costs $vc_t\ge0$, which term can be added keeping a valid bound ($D=\sum_t d_t$, zero initial and final stock)?
  1. $D\cdot\max_t vc_t$
  2. $\sum_t vc_t\,d_t$
  3. $\sum_t vc_t\,cap_t$
  4. $D\cdot\min_t vc_t$
Explanation. Every plan produces exactly $D$ units, each at a cost of at least $\min_t vc_t$. $\sum_t vc_t d_t$ is the variable cost of lot-for-lot: a plan anticipating production into cheaper periods spends less.
oc-f-1008 · level facile · notes
Among the variants of capacitated lot sizing (ULS uncapacitated, MLS multi-product, LS-SI with initial stock, LS-OT with overtime, LS-UD with unmet demand), which one is solved in polynomial time?
  1. LS-OT
  2. LS-UD
  3. ULS
  4. MLS
Explanation. Without capacities the Wagner-Whitin property holds and dynamic programming solves the problem in polynomial time; with capacities the problem is NP-hard.
oc-f-1009 · level facile · notes
The variants of capacitated lot sizing change one feature of the problem. Which variant removes a constraint instead of adding decisions?
  1. Lot sizing with unmet demand (LS-UD)
  2. Uncapacitated lot sizing (ULS)
  3. Lot sizing with initial stock (LS-SI)
  4. Lot sizing with overtime (LS-OT)
Explanation. The ULS makes the capacities non-binding. LS-SI decides the initial stock, LS-OT the overtime hours, LS-UD the demand not to serve.
oc-f-1010 · level teorema · notes
Uncapacitated lot sizing (ULS) is the CLS with, for instance, $cap_t\ge\sum_{u\in T}d_u$ for every period. Why does this condition make the capacities non-binding (zero initial and final stock)?
  1. No feasible plan produces in a period more than the total demand
  2. Because every period must produce at least the total demand
  3. Because the stock can never exceed the capacity
  4. Because the setup costs become zero
Explanation. With $s_m=0$ the total production is $\sum_u d_u$, so $x_t\le\sum_u d_u\le cap_t$ in every plan: the constraint $x_t\le cap_t$ cuts nothing.
oc-f-1011 · level facile · notes
In uncapacitated lot sizing there are optimal plans producing only when the stock is empty (Wagner-Whitin property). With demands $d=(2,3,1,2)$ and zero initial stock, which plan has this property?
  1. $(4,1,3,0)$
  2. $(5,0,2,1)$
  3. $(3,2,1,2)$
  4. $(5,0,3,0)$
Explanation. In $(5,0,3,0)$ production happens in $1$ and $3$, with stock $0$ at the start of both. In $(4,1,3,0)$ one produces in $2$ with stock $2$; in $(5,0,2,1)$ in $4$ with stock $1$; in $(3,2,1,2)$ in $2$ with stock $1$.
oc-f-1012 · level facile · notes
In multi-product lot sizing with setup times (MLS) the products share the time $cap_t$ of the period, and every setup of product $p$ consumes $st_{pt}$ time units. What effect do the setup times have on the decisions?
  1. They reduce the variable cost of every unit produced
  2. They force producing every product in every period
  3. Every setup takes time: fewer setups and larger lots pay off
  4. None: the setup time just adds to the setup cost
Explanation. Besides costing $sc_{pt}$, a setup consumes capacity; fewer setups leave more time for production, at the price of more stock.
oc-f-1013 · level facile · notes
Multi-product lot sizing with setup times (MLS): in a period with available time $cap_t=20$ one produces $5$ units of product $A$ ($1$ time unit each, setup of $3$) and $2$ units of product $B$ ($2$ time units each, setup of $4$). How much time is used?
  1. $12$
  2. $16$
  3. $9$
  4. $7$
Explanation. $A$: $5\cdot1+3=8$; $B$: $2\cdot2+4=8$; total $16\le20$. $9$ counts only production, $7$ only setups.
oc-f-1014 · level facile · notes
In lot sizing with initial stock (LS-SI) the quantity $si_p$ of product $p$ available at the start is a decision, at cost $fc_p$ per unit. What does the stock at the end of period $t$ become ($x_{pu}$ production, $d_{pu}$ demand)?
  1. $s_{pt}=si_p+\sum_{u\le t}(x_{pu}-d_{pu})$
  2. $s_{pt}=\sum_{u\le t}(x_{pu}-d_{pu})-si_p$
  3. $s_{pt}=si_p\cdot\sum_{u\le t}(x_{pu}-d_{pu})$
  4. $s_{pt}=\sum_{u\le t}(x_{pu}-d_{pu})$, with $si_p$ only in the cost
Explanation. The initial stock adds to what is produced: the cumulative balance starts from $si_p$ instead of $0$.
oc-f-1015 · level facile · notes
In lot sizing with initial stock (LS-SI) the initial stock $si_p$ is bought at cost $fc_p$ per unit. If $fc_p$ is enormously larger than every setup, production and holding cost, what does an optimal plan do?
  1. It buys the whole demand of the horizon as initial stock
  2. It buys only the demand of period $1$ as initial stock
  3. No feasible plan exists for that product
  4. It sets $si_p=0$, as in the problem without initial stock
Explanation. Every bought unit costs more than any way of producing it, and producing is always possible under the capacity assumptions: it pays not to buy.
oc-f-1016 · level teorema · notes
In lot sizing with overtime (LS-OT) regular time costs $cw_t$ per unit up to $cap^N_t$ and overtime $co_t>cw_t$ per unit up to $cap^O_t$. Why does an optimal plan use overtime in period $t$ only if the regular time of $t$ is exhausted?
  1. Because the overtime capacity is always $cap^O_t\le cap^N_t$
  2. It is not true: overtime is used to anticipate production
  3. Otherwise moving time from overtime to regular time would cost less
  4. Because overtime is available only in the last period
Explanation. With free regular time, every unit of overtime can be replaced by a regular unit costing $cw_t<co_t$.
oc-f-1017 · level facile · notes
Lot sizing with overtime (LS-OT): in a period regular time costs $2$ per unit up to $cap^N_t=8$, overtime $5$ per unit up to $cap^O_t=4$. $11$ time units are needed. What is the minimum cost of the working time?
  1. $40$
  2. $31$
  3. $22$
  4. $55$
Explanation. $8$ regular units ($16$) and $3$ of overtime ($15$): $31$. $22$ ignores the limit $cap^N_t=8$; $55$ pays everything as overtime.
oc-f-1018 · level facile · notes
In lot sizing with unmet demand (LS-UD) part of the demand may stay unserved, with penalty $cu_{pt}$ per unit. If all penalties are enormously larger than the other costs, what does an optimal plan do?
  1. It serves all the demand, as in the base problem
  2. It leaves all the demand of the horizon unmet
  3. It leaves the demand of the last period unmet
  4. There is no optimal plan, the cost is unbounded
Explanation. Leaving a unit unserved costs more than producing it, and producing everything is possible under the capacity assumptions: the variant reduces to the base problem.
oc-f-1019 · level facile · notes
Lot sizing with unmet demand (LS-UD): in the last period $3$ units of demand remain and there is no stock. The alternatives are a setup (cost $50$, zero variable cost, everything served) or leaving the $3$ units unserved (penalty $10$ per unit). Minimum cost?
  1. $50$
  2. $80$
  3. $0$
  4. $30$
Explanation. Serving costs $50$, not serving $3\cdot10=30$: the penalty pays off. $80$ adds the two alternatives.
oc-f-1020 · level facile · notes
Capacitated lot sizing is NP-hard, while the uncapacitated case is solved by the Wagner-Whitin algorithm. What does the NP-hardness of the capacitated case imply, if $P\neq NP$?
  1. The uncapacitated case is NP-hard too
  2. The Wagner-Whitin algorithm also solves the capacitated case
  3. There is no polynomial algorithm for the capacitated case
  4. The capacitated case has no integer optimal solutions
Explanation. NP-hard means that a polynomial algorithm would give $P=NP$. The uncapacitated case stays polynomial: the capacities are the source of the difficulty.
oc-f-1021 · level ipotesi · notes
The Wagner-Whitin property («produce only when the stock is empty») holds without capacities. Why can it fail with capacities?
  1. It does not fail: the property holds with capacities too
  2. Scarce capacity forces producing in advance with positive stock
  3. Because with capacities the setup costs become zero
  4. Because with capacities the final stock must be positive
Explanation. For instance with capacity $4$ the optimal plan $(3,0,4,4,0)$ produces in period $4$ with $1$ unit in stock, to cover a demand that period $4$ alone could not serve.
oc-f-1022 · level facile · notes
In lot sizing ($x_t$ production in period $t$, $s_t$ end-of-period stock, $s_0=0$), how is the Wagner-Whitin property «produce only when the stock is empty» written?
  1. $x_t\,s_{t-1}=0$ for every $t$
  2. $x_t\,s_t=0$ for every $t$
  3. $s_t=0$ for every $t$
  4. $x_t\le d_t$ for every $t$
Explanation. If $x_t>0$ the incoming stock $s_{t-1}$ must be zero. $x_ts_t=0$ would forbid producing for future periods; $s_t=0$ everywhere is lot-for-lot.

Part: Formulations and their properties (241)

9. Formulations of knapsack problems (56)

oc-f-031 · level teorema · notes
In the knapsack problem (KP, weights $w_j\le c$) let $z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{KP}})$ be the optimal value and $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}})$ that of the LP relaxation (with $0\le x_j\le 1$). Which statement on their ratio is correct?
  1. $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}})/z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{KP}})\le \frac{3}{2}$ for every instance, and the value $\frac32$ is reached asymptotically
  2. $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}})/z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{KP}})$ is unbounded: it grows with the number $n$ of items
  3. $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}})/z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{KP}})\le 2$ for every instance, and the value $2$ is reached asymptotically for $c\to+\infty$
  4. $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}})/z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{KP}})\le 2$ for every instance, and some instance has ratio exactly $2$
Explanation. Propositions 9.7 and 9.8: the ratio is at most $2$, and the family with $c=2\vartheta$ and two items of weight $\vartheta+1$ has ratio $\frac{2\vartheta}{\vartheta+1}\to 2$, without attaining it.
oc-f-032 · level ipotesi · notes
In the KP (weights $w_j\le c$), with the items sorted by non-increasing efficiency $p_j/w_j$, let $s$ be the split item (the first one that does not fit entirely) and $\mathit{rc}=c-\sum_{j<s}w_j$. Which facts are needed to prove $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}})\le 2\,z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{KP}})$?
  1. Weak duality between $\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}}$ and its dual; items sorted by non-decreasing weight; $w_s\le c$
  2. Items $1,\dots,s-1$ form a feasible solution; item $s$ alone is feasible ($w_s\le c$); $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}})\le\sum_{j<s}p_j+p_s$
  3. Items $1,\dots,s-1$ form an optimal solution; $\mathit{rc}<w_s$; $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}})\le\sum_{j<s}p_j+p_s$
  4. Profits are integer, hence $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}})$ is rounded down; item $s$ alone is feasible; $\mathit{rc}<w_s$
Explanation. The two lower bounds $\sum_{j<s}p_j\le z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{KP}})$ and $p_s\le z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{KP}})$, added, exceed $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}})=\sum_{j<s}p_j+p_s\,\mathit{rc}/w_s$. The integrality of the profits is needed for the Dantzig bound, not here.
oc-f-033 · level ipotesi · notes
In the KP (profits $p_j$, weights $w_j$, capacity $c$), with the items sorted by efficiency, let $s$ be the split item and $\mathit{rc}=c-\sum_{j<s}w_j$ the residual capacity. What is needed to prove that $\mathrm{UB}_{\mathrm{D}}=\sum_{j<s}p_j+\left\lfloor p_s\,\mathit{rc}/w_s\right\rfloor$ is an upper bound on the optimal value?
  1. The order by non-increasing efficiency, the formula of $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}})$ and integer profits
  2. The order by non-increasing efficiency, the formula of $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}})$ and integer weights
  3. The order by non-increasing profit, strong duality and integer profits
  4. The greedy solution, the item of maximum profit and integer profits
Explanation. $\mathrm{UB}_{\mathrm{D}}=\lfloor z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}})\rfloor$: the formula of $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}})$ holds with the items sorted by efficiency, and rounding is allowed because $z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{KP}})$ is an integer ($p_j\in\Z_{\ge1}$).
oc-f-034 · level facile · notes
Knapsack problem (KP) with capacity $c=9$; the item of maximum efficiency $p_j/w_j$ has $p_1=6$ and $w_1=2$. What is the relaxation $z(\mathrm{LP}\text{-}0_{\mathrm{KP}})$, which keeps the capacity constraint and only the constraints $x_j\ge 0$ (without $x_j\le 1$)?
  1. $6$
  2. $\frac{49}{3}$
  3. $54$
  4. $27$
Explanation. Without the constraints $x_j\le 1$ all the capacity goes to the most efficient item: $z=p_1\,c/w_1=6\cdot 9/2=27$. It is a much weaker bound than $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}})$.
oc-f-035 · level teorema · notes
In the KP let $D(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}})$ be the dual of the LP relaxation, with variable $\pi$ for the capacity constraint and $\mu_j$ for $x_j\le 1$. With the items sorted by non-increasing efficiency $p_j/w_j$ and $s$ the split item (the first one that does not fit entirely), which dual solution is optimal?
  1. $\tilde\pi=\frac{p_1}{w_1}$, $\tilde\mu_j=p_j-w_j\frac{p_1}{w_1}$ for $j<s$ and $\tilde\mu_j=0$ for $j\ge s$
  2. $\tilde\pi=0$, $\tilde\mu_j=p_j$ for $j<s$ and $\tilde\mu_j=0$ for $j\ge s$
  3. $\tilde\pi=\frac{p_s}{w_s}$, $\tilde\mu_j=p_j-w_j\frac{p_s}{w_s}$ for $j<s$ and $\tilde\mu_j=0$ for $j\ge s$
  4. $\tilde\pi=\frac{p_s}{w_s}$, $\tilde\mu_j=0$ for $j<s$ and $\tilde\mu_j=p_j-w_j\frac{p_s}{w_s}$ for $j\ge s$
Explanation. The capacity multiplier is the efficiency of the split item, and the items taken entirely have $\tilde\mu_j=p_j-w_j\,p_s/w_s\ge 0$ (Proposition 9.5). With $\tilde\pi=p_1/w_1$ the $\tilde\mu_j$ would be negative; with $\tilde\pi=0$ the dual constraints of items $j\ge s$ are violated.
oc-f-220 · level facile · notes
The $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{SSP}}$ model of subset sum maximizes $\sum_j w_jx_j$ subject to $\sum_j w_jx_j\le c$ and $x_j\in\{0,1\}$; the answer is yes if and only if the optimal value is $c$. With weights $w=(2,3,6,7,5,9)$ and $c=9$, what is $z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{SSP}})$?
  1. $7$, the largest weight fitting alone
  2. $9$, hence the answer is yes
  3. $8$, hence the answer is no
  4. $32$, the sum of all the weights
Explanation. For example $\{2,7\}$, $\{3,6\}$ or $\{9\}$ sum to $9=c$, hence $z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{SSP}})=9$ and the answer is yes.
oc-f-221 · level facile · notes
In the $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{SSP}}$ model of subset sum (the KP with profits $p_j=w_j$, capacity $c$, and $\sum_j w_j>c$), why does the LP relaxation, with $0\le x_j\le 1$, not help to answer?
  1. All items have efficiency $1$, so the relaxation always equals $c$
  2. The relaxation is unbounded, because profits equal weights
  3. The relaxation always equals $0$, because the split item is the first one
  4. The relaxation always equals $\sum_j w_j$, because no constraint is active
Explanation. With $p_j/w_j=1$ for every item, the relaxation fills the knapsack fractionally and equals $c$: the bound $c$ does not distinguish yes-instances from no-instances.
oc-f-222 · level facile · notes
Bounded knapsack (BKP): the model has integer variables $x_j\in\{0,\dots,b_j\}$ (copies of item $j$). Capacity $c=9$, profits $p=(6,5,8,9,6,7)$, weights $w=(2,3,6,7,5,9)$, copies $b=(2,2,1,1,1,1)$. What is the optimal value?
  1. $15$
  2. $24$
  3. $17$
  4. $18$
Explanation. Two copies of item $1$ and item $5$ weigh $9$ and are worth $12+6=18$. With one copy per item (KP) one gets $15$, with unlimited copies (UKP) $24$ (four copies of item $1$).
oc-f-223 · level facile · notes
A bounded knapsack (BKP) with available copies $b=(2,2,1,1,1,1)$ can be rewritten as a 0-1 knapsack (KP) by replacing every item $j$ with $b_j$ identical items. How many binary variables does the resulting model have?
  1. $12$
  2. $64$
  3. $8$
  4. $6$
Explanation. The copies are $\sum_j b_j=2+2+1+1+1+1=8$. The $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{BKP}}$ model uses $6$ integer variables instead, one per item type.
oc-f-224 · level facile · notes
Unbounded knapsack (UKP): variables $x_j\in\Z_{\ge0}$, capacity $c=9$, profits $p=(6,5,8,9,6,7)$, weights $w=(2,3,6,7,5,9)$; item $1$ has the largest efficiency $p_j/w_j$, namely $3$. What are the optimal value and the LP relaxation $c\,p_1/w_1$?
  1. $18$ and $27$
  2. $24$ and $27$
  3. $27$ and $27$
  4. $24$ and $24$
Explanation. Four copies of item $1$ weigh $8$ and are worth $24$, and no combination does better; the relaxation uses $4.5$ copies and is worth $27$. $18$ is the value of the BKP with $b_1=2$.
oc-f-225 · level facile · notes
In the $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{UKP}}$ model of the unbounded knapsack ($x_j\in\Z_{\ge0}$ copies of item $j$, weights $w_j$, capacity $c$) there is no explicit upper bound on the variables. Which bound is implied anyway by the capacity constraint?
  1. $x_j\le\lfloor c/w_j\rfloor$
  2. $x_j\le 1$
  3. $x_j\le\lceil c/w_j\rceil$
  4. $x_j\le c$
Explanation. From $w_jx_j\le\sum_i w_ix_i\le c$ and the integrality of $x_j$ we get $x_j\le\lfloor c/w_j\rfloor$: the UKP is a BKP with $b_j=\lfloor c/w_j\rfloor$.
oc-f-226 · level facile · notes
Multidimensional knapsack (MDKP) with capacities $c_1=10$, $c_2=12$: profits $p=(6,7,5,9)$, weights in dimension 1 $w_{1\cdot}=(4,5,3,7)$ and in dimension 2 $w_{2\cdot}=(6,4,5,3)$; every item is taken at most once. What is the optimal value?
  1. $13$
  2. $16$
  3. $21$
  4. $14$
Explanation. $\{3,4\}$ weighs $(10,8)$ and is worth $14$. $\{2,4\}$ would be worth $16$ but weighs $12>10$ in dimension 1; $21$ is obtained looking at dimension 2 only.
oc-f-227 · level facile · notes
In the multidimensional knapsack (MDKP) model, with one constraint $\sum_j w_{dj}x_j\le c_d$ per dimension $d$, all the constraints are added into a single one, $\sum_j(\sum_d w_{dj})x_j\le\sum_d c_d$. What does the optimal value of the resulting 0-1 knapsack give?
  1. The MDKP optimal value, because the sum of the constraints is equivalent to them
  2. A feasible MDKP solution, because it respects the total capacity
  3. An upper bound on the MDKP optimal value, because the new problem is a relaxation
  4. A lower bound on the MDKP optimal value, because the new problem is more constrained
Explanation. Every MDKP solution satisfies the sum of the constraints, so the new problem has more feasible solutions: its optimum is an upper bound. Its optimal solution may violate a single dimension.
oc-f-228 · level facile · notes
The $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{MKP}}$ model of the multiple knapsack has a binary variable $x_{jk}$ for every item $j$ and knapsack $k$, one capacity constraint per knapsack and one constraint $\sum_k x_{jk}\le 1$ per item. With $n=5$ items and $m=2$ knapsacks, how many variables and linear constraints does it have?
  1. $5$ variables and $2$ constraints
  2. $10$ variables and $7$ constraints
  3. $10$ variables and $10$ constraints
  4. $7$ variables and $10$ constraints
Explanation. The variables are $nm=10$; the constraints are $m=2$ capacity constraints plus $n=5$ assignment constraints, i.e., $7$ (not counting the variable domains).
oc-f-229 · level facile · notes
In the $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{MKP}}$ model of the multiple knapsack ($x_{jk}=1$ if item $j$ goes into knapsack $k$), why is the constraint of every item $\sum_k x_{jk}\le 1$ and not $\sum_k x_{jk}=1$?
  1. An item may stay out of all the knapsacks
  2. An item may be split among several knapsacks
  3. The equality constraint would make the model non-linear
  4. The constraint is needed only for empty knapsacks
Explanation. As in the KP, we choose the items to insert: with the equality every item would have to be inserted, and the instance might have no feasible solution.
oc-f-230 · level facile · notes
Multiple-choice knapsack (MCKP): capacity $c=15$, classes $\mathscr{J}_1=\{1,2\}$, $\mathscr{J}_2=\{3,4\}$, $\mathscr{J}_3=\{5,6\}$, profits $p=(6,8,5,7,4,9)$, weights $w=(4,6,5,8,3,7)$; exactly one item per class is chosen. What is the optimal value?
  1. $15$
  2. $24$
  3. $20$
  4. $17$
Explanation. $\{1,4,5\}$ weighs $15$ and is worth $17$, as $\{2,3,5\}$ (weight $14$). $24=8+7+9$ takes the best item of each class ignoring the capacity; $\{1,3,5\}$ is worth $15$.
oc-f-231 · level facile · notes
In the $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{MCKP}}$ model of the multiple-choice knapsack (classes $\mathscr{J}_1,\dots,\mathscr{J}_q$, $x_j=1$ if item $j$ is chosen) the class constraints are $\sum_{j\in\mathscr{J}_h}x_j=1$. What would change writing $\le 1$?
  1. Two items of the same class could be chosen
  2. The model would become non-linear
  3. A class could contribute nothing: another problem would be solved
  4. Nothing: in an optimum every class gives an item anyway, since profits are positive
Explanation. With $\le 1$ a class may stay empty, and if the knapsack is too small for all the classes the optimum leaves one empty: it is a different problem from the MCKP, which imposes exactly one item per class.
oc-f-232 · level facile · notes
In the $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{KPS}}$ model of the knapsack with setups, $x_j=1$ if item $j$ is chosen and $y_h=1$ if class $h$ is activated (with setup cost $f_h$ and setup weight $s_h$). Which pair (objective, capacity) is correct?
  1. $\max\sum_j (p_j-f_h)x_j$ with $\sum_j (w_j+s_h)x_j\le c$
  2. $\max\sum_j p_jx_j-\sum_h f_hy_h$ with $\sum_j w_jx_j+\sum_h s_hy_h\le c$
  3. $\max\sum_j p_jx_j+\sum_h f_hy_h$ with $\sum_j w_jx_j\le c+\sum_h s_hy_h$
  4. $\max\sum_j p_jx_j-\sum_h f_hy_h$ with $\sum_j w_jx_j\le c$
Explanation. The setup of an activated class is paid once, in the profit ($-f_h$) and in the capacity ($+s_h$). The last option would pay it once for every chosen item.
oc-f-233 · level facile · notes
In the $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{KPS}}$ model of the knapsack with setups ($x_j$ item chosen, $y_h$ class activated, $h(j)$ the class of item $j$), what are the constraints $x_j\le y_{h(j)}$ for?
  1. To forbid choosing an item without paying the setup of its class
  2. To impose that all the items of an activated class are chosen
  3. To impose that at most one class is activated
  4. To forbid activating a class without choosing items from it
Explanation. Without these constraints, since setups cost, the optimum would set $y_h=0$ and choose the items anyway. An activated but empty class is feasible, but not convenient.
oc-f-637 · level facile · notes
The ILP models of knapsack problems have the scheme $\max\{\sum_j p_jx_j:\sum_j w_jx_j\le c,\ x_j\in D_j\}$. In which problem is the domain $D_j=\Z_{\ge0}$?
  1. In the unbounded knapsack (UKP)
  2. In the 0/1 knapsack (KP)
  3. In the bounded knapsack (BKP)
  4. In the subset sum (SSP)
Explanation. $\Z_{\ge0}$ counts copies without limit. The KP and the SSP have $D_j=\{0,1\}$, the BKP $D_j=\{0,1,\dots,b_j\}$.
oc-f-638 · level facile · notes
In the ILP model of the multiple knapsack (MKP: $m$ knapsacks of capacity $c_k$, every item in at most one knapsack), which variables are used?
  1. Binary $x_j$, equal to $1$ if item $j$ is selected
  2. Integer $x_j$, the number of the knapsack of item $j$
  3. Binary $y_k$, equal to $1$ if knapsack $k$ is used
  4. Binary $x_{jk}$, equal to $1$ if item $j$ goes into knapsack $k$
Explanation. One needs to know in which knapsack the item goes, hence an extra index; the constraint $\sum_k x_{jk}\le1$ imposes at most one knapsack per item.
oc-f-639 · level facile · notes
Model $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{KP}}$ of the 0/1 knapsack with $c=9$, $p=(6,5,8,9,6,7)$ and $w=(2,3,6,7,5,9)$. Which vector is feasible and has the highest value among those proposed?
  1. $\vet x=(0,0,0,0,0,1)$, value $7$
  2. $\vet x=(1,1,0,0,0,0)$, value $11$
  3. $\vet x=(1,0,0,1,0,0)$, value $15$
  4. $\vet x=(1,1,1,0,0,0)$, value $19$
Explanation. $(1,0,0,1,0,0)$ weighs $2+7=9\le c$ and is worth $15$ (it is the optimum of the instance); $(1,1,1,0,0,0)$ weighs $11>9$; the others are feasible but worth less.
oc-f-640 · level facile · notes
The model $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{KP}}$ of the 0/1 knapsack with $n$ items has how many variables and how many linear constraints, besides the domain constraints $x_j\in\{0,1\}$?
  1. $2^n$ variables, one per subset
  2. $n$ binary variables and a single capacity constraint
  3. $n$ variables and $n$ capacity constraints
  4. $n^2$ variables and one constraint
Explanation. One variable per item and the constraint $\sum_j w_jx_j\le c$: the model is compact, even though the problem is NP-hard.
oc-f-641 · level teorema · notes
The relaxation $\mathrm{LP}\text{-}0_{\mathrm{KP}}$ of the 0/1 knapsack replaces $x_j\in\{0,1\}$ by $x_j\ge0$ (without $x_j\le1$); item $1$ is the most efficient. With $c=9$ and items $(p_j,w_j)=(6,2),(5,3),(8,6)$, what is $z(\mathrm{LP}\text{-}0_{\mathrm{KP}})$?
  1. $27$
  2. $\frac{49}{3}$
  3. $19$
  4. $11$
Explanation. Without $x_j\le1$ it pays to fill the knapsack with the most efficient item: $x_1=c/w_1=\frac92$ and $z=p_1c/w_1=27$, certified by the dual $\pi=p_1/w_1$. $\frac{49}{3}$ is the relaxation with $x_j\le1$.
oc-f-642 · level ipotesi · notes
The value $z(\mathrm{LP}\text{-}0_{\mathrm{KP}})=p_1c/w_1$ of the 0/1 knapsack relaxation with only the constraints $x_j\ge0$ is proved with the dual $\tilde\pi=p_1/w_1$. Which assumption on item $1$ is needed for $\tilde\pi$ to be dual feasible ($w_j\tilde\pi\ge p_j$ for every $j$)?
  1. That item $1$ has the maximum profit
  2. That item $1$ has the minimum weight
  3. None: it holds for any item
  4. That item $1$ has maximum efficiency: $p_1/w_1\ge p_j/w_j$ for every $j$
Explanation. $w_j\,p_1/w_1\ge p_j$ is equivalent to $p_1/w_1\ge p_j/w_j$. With an item not of maximum efficiency the value $p_1c/w_1$ would only be a feasible primal value, not the optimum.
oc-f-643 · level facile · notes
The LP relaxation $\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}}$ of the 0/1 knapsack uses $0\le x_j\le1$. With $c=9$ and items, already sorted by non-increasing efficiency, $(p_j,w_j)=(6,2),(5,3),(8,6),(9,7)$, what is $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}})$?
  1. $27$
  2. $\frac{50}{3}$
  3. $\frac{49}{3}$
  4. $16$
Explanation. Items $1$ and $2$ fit (weight $5$, profit $11$); item $3$ is the split item with residual capacity $4$: $11+8\cdot\frac46=\frac{49}{3}$. $16$ is its rounding down (Dantzig bound).
oc-f-644 · level facile · notes
The efficiency of a knapsack item is $p_j/w_j$. With items $(p_j,w_j)=(9,7),(8,6),(5,3)$, what is the order by non-increasing efficiency?
  1. $3,1,2$
  2. $3,2,1$
  3. $1,2,3$
  4. $2,1,3$
Explanation. $5/3\approx1.67>8/6\approx1.33>9/7\approx1.29$. Sorting by profit ($1,2,3$) is a typical mistake.
oc-f-645 · level facile · notes
0/1 knapsack with $c=9$ and items sorted by non-increasing efficiency, of weights $w=(2,3,6,7)$. The split item $s$ is the first one not fitting entirely when adding the items in order, and the residual capacity is $\mathit{rc}=c-\sum_{j<s}w_j$. What are they?
  1. $s=3$, $\mathit{rc}=4$
  2. $s=2$, $\mathit{rc}=7$
  3. $s=3$, $\mathit{rc}=-2$
  4. $s=4$, $\mathit{rc}=3$
Explanation. $2+3=5\le9$, but $5+6=11>9$: item $3$ is the split item and $9-5=4$ units remain. The residual capacity is never negative.
oc-f-646 · level teorema · notes
For the 0/1 knapsack the ratio $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}})/z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{KP}})$ is at most $2$. The instance with $c=2\vartheta$ and two items with $p_j=1$, $w_j=\vartheta+1$ shows that the bound is tight. What is the ratio for $\vartheta=4$?
  1. $2$
  2. $\frac45$
  3. $1$
  4. $\frac85$
Explanation. $c=8$: only one item fits, $z(\mathrm{ILP})=1$; the relaxation takes the second one for $\frac{8-5}{5}=\frac35$, hence $z(\mathrm{LP})=\frac85$. In general $\frac{2\vartheta}{\vartheta+1}\to2$.
oc-f-647 · level ipotesi · notes
The Dantzig bound of the 0/1 knapsack is $\UB_{\mathrm{D}}=\lfloor z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}})\rfloor$. On which assumption does the rounding down rely?
  1. That the items are sorted by efficiency
  2. That the residual capacity is positive
  3. That the profits $p_j$ are integer, so every integer solution has integer value
  4. That the weights $w_j$ are integer
Explanation. If $z(\mathrm{ILP})$ is integer and at most $z(\mathrm{LP})$, it is at most $\lfloor z(\mathrm{LP})\rfloor$. With fractional profits the rounding would not be valid.
oc-f-648 · level teorema · notes
The Martello-Toth bound of the 0/1 knapsack is $\max\{\UB_0,\UB_1\}$: $\UB_0$ excludes the split item $s$ and fills $\mathit{rc}$ with the efficiency of item $s+1$, $\UB_1$ includes $s$ removing weight with the efficiency of item $s-1$. Why is it valid?
  1. Because $\UB_1\le\UB_0$ in every instance
  2. Every integer solution has $x_s=0$ or $x_s=1$, and $\UB_0$, $\UB_1$ are upper bounds in the two cases
  3. Because $\UB_0$ and $\UB_1$ are both feasible solutions
  4. Because $\max\{\UB_0,\UB_1\}$ always equals $z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{KP}})$
Explanation. It is a disjunction on the fractional variable: the maximum of the bounds of the two cases bounds every integer solution, and it is at most the Dantzig bound.
oc-f-1023 · level facile · notes
Among the ILP models of the knapsack problems (KP, SSP, BKP, UKP, MDKP, MKP, MCKP, KPS), which one has two families of binary variables, one for the items and one for the classes?
  1. The multiple knapsack problem (MKP)
  2. The multidimensional knapsack problem (MDKP)
  3. The knapsack problem with setups (KPS)
  4. The multiple-choice knapsack problem (MCKP)
Explanation. In the KPS $x_j$ says whether item $j$ is chosen and $y_h$ whether class $h$ is activated. The MCKP has classes but only the variables $x_j$; the MKP has two-index variables $x_{jk}$.
oc-f-1024 · level facile · notes
Among the ILP models of the knapsack problems, which one has several capacity constraints weighing the same vector of variables $\vet{x}\in\{0,1\}^n$, one per dimension?
  1. The knapsack problem with setups (KPS)
  2. The multidimensional knapsack problem (MDKP)
  3. The multiple knapsack problem (MKP)
  4. The bounded knapsack problem (BKP)
Explanation. In the MDKP every dimension $d$ gives $\sum_j w_{dj}x_j\le c_d$ on the same $x_j$. In the MKP every knapsack has its own constraint, but on different variables $x_{jk}$.
oc-f-1025 · level facile · notes
Model $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{KP}}$ of the 0/1 knapsack ($\max\sum_jp_jx_j$, $\sum_jw_jx_j\le c$, $x_j\in\{0,1\}$) with $c=9$ and weights $w=(2,3,6,7,5,9)$. Which vector is NOT feasible?
  1. $(1,1,0,0,1,0)$
  2. $(1,0,0,1,0,0)$
  3. $(0,1,1,0,0,0)$
  4. $(0,0,0,0,0,1)$
Explanation. $(1,1,0,0,1,0)$ weighs $2+3+5=10>9$. The others weigh $9$, $9$ and $9$: they satisfy the capacity constraint with equality.
oc-f-1026 · level facile · notes
In the model $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{KP}}$ of the 0/1 knapsack $x_j\in\{0,1\}$ is replaced by $0\le x_j\le1$. What is obtained?
  1. An equivalent model, because the vertices are integer
  2. A more constrained model, with a smaller optimal value
  3. A model without feasible solutions
  4. A relaxation: the optimum may take a fraction of an item
Explanation. One obtains $\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}}$: its optimal solution takes the critical item in part, so in general it is not integer and $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}})\ge z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{KP}})$.
oc-f-1027 · level facile · notes
The relaxation $\mathrm{LP}\text{-}0_{\mathrm{KP}}$ of the 0/1 knapsack has only $\sum_jw_jx_j\le c$ and $x_j\ge0$ (no bound $x_j\le1$); item $1$ has the largest efficiency $p_j/w_j$. Which solution is optimal?
  1. $x_j=c/\sum_k w_k$ for every $j$
  2. $x_j=1$ for all items that fit
  3. $x_1=c/w_1$ and $x_j=0$ for $j\neq1$
  4. $x_1=1$, then the other items by efficiency until full
Explanation. Without $x_j\le1$ it pays to spend the whole capacity on the most efficient item: value $p_1c/w_1$. Then taking the others by efficiency is the solution of $\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}}$.
oc-f-1028 · level teorema · notes
For the 0/1 knapsack one compares the model $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{KP}}$, the relaxation $\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}}$ ($0\le x_j\le1$) and the relaxation $\mathrm{LP}\text{-}0_{\mathrm{KP}}$ ($x_j\ge0$). Which chain holds for the optimal values?
  1. $z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{KP}})=z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}})\le z(\mathrm{LP}\text{-}0_{\mathrm{KP}})$
  2. $z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{KP}})\le z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}})\le z(\mathrm{LP}\text{-}0_{\mathrm{KP}})$
  3. $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}})\le z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{KP}})\le z(\mathrm{LP}\text{-}0_{\mathrm{KP}})$
  4. $z(\mathrm{LP}\text{-}0_{\mathrm{KP}})\le z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}})\le z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{KP}})$
Explanation. The feasible regions are nested: integers $\subseteq$ $[0,1]^n$ with capacity $\subseteq$ $\R_{\ge0}^n$ with capacity. In a maximization problem, a larger region gives a value that is not smaller.
oc-f-1029 · level facile · notes
In the 0/1 knapsack the optimal solution of $\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}}$ ($0\le x_j\le1$) is found by sorting the items by non-increasing efficiency $p_j/w_j$. Which items have a fractional value in that solution?
  1. At most one: the critical item
  2. All those after the critical item
  3. At most two: the critical item and the next one
  4. None: the solution is always integer
Explanation. The items before the critical item $s$ have $x_j=1$, those after it $x_j=0$, and $x_s=\mathit{rc}/w_s$ may be fractional.
oc-f-1030 · level facile · notes
In the knapsack the efficiency of item $j$ is $p_j/w_j$. With items $(p_j,w_j)=(10,4),(8,3),(9,4),(5,2)$, which item comes last in the order by non-increasing efficiency?
  1. $(5,2)$
  2. $(10,4)$
  3. $(8,3)$
  4. $(9,4)$
Explanation. Efficiencies $2.5$, $2.67$, $2.25$, $2.5$: the last is $(9,4)$. Sorting by profit would put $(5,2)$ last, which has instead efficiency $2.5$.
oc-f-1031 · level facile · notes
In the 0/1 knapsack the relaxation $\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}}$ is solved by sorting the items by efficiency $p_j/w_j$. If two items have the same efficiency, is the optimal solution of $\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}}$ unique?
  1. Yes, if ties are broken by increasing index
  2. No: with equal efficiencies the relaxation is unbounded
  3. Not always: moving weight between them keeps the value
  4. Yes: the optimal solution of an LP is always unique
Explanation. Moving $\delta$ units of weight from one item to the other, with the same efficiency, changes the profit by $0$: there may be other optimal solutions. The sorting rule picks one of them.
oc-f-1032 · level facile · notes
0/1 knapsack with $c=10$ and items already sorted by non-increasing efficiency $(p_j,w_j)=(12,4),(9,3),(10,5),(4,4)$. The critical item $s$ is the first that does not fit entirely; $\mathit{rc}=c-\sum_{j<s}w_j$. What are $s$, $\mathit{rc}$ and $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{KP}})=\sum_{j<s}p_j+\mathit{rc}\,p_s/w_s$?
  1. $s=4$, $\mathit{rc}=3$, $z=24$
  2. $s=3$, $\mathit{rc}=3$, $z=27$
  3. $s=3$, $\mathit{rc}=3$, $z=31$
  4. $s=3$, $\mathit{rc}=5$, $z=31$
Explanation. $4+3=7\le10$ but $7+5=12>10$: $s=3$, $\mathit{rc}=3$, $z=21+3\cdot\frac{10}5=27$. $31$ takes the critical item entirely.
oc-f-1033 · level facile · notes
0/1 knapsack, items sorted by efficiency $(p_j,w_j)=(12,4),(9,3),(10,5),(4,4)$, $c=10$: critical item $s=3$, $\mathit{rc}=3$. Martello-Toth: $\UB_0=\sum_{j<s}p_j+\lfloor\mathit{rc}\,p_{s+1}/w_{s+1}\rfloor$, $\UB_1=\lfloor\sum_{j\le s}p_j-(w_s-\mathit{rc})\,p_{s-1}/w_{s-1}\rfloor$. What is $\UB_{\mathrm{MT}}=\max\{\UB_0,\UB_1\}$?
  1. $25$
  2. $27$
  3. $24$
  4. $31$
Explanation. $\UB_0=21+\lfloor3\cdot\frac44\rfloor=24$; $\UB_1=\lfloor31-2\cdot3\rfloor=25$; the maximum is $25$, better than Dantzig's bound $\lfloor27\rfloor=27$.
oc-f-1034 · level facile · notes
The model $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{SSP}}$ of subset sum maximizes $\sum_jw_jx_j$ with $\sum_jw_jx_j\le c$, $x_j\in\{0,1\}$; the answer is «yes» if and only if the optimum equals $c$. With $w=(4,6,9,13)$ and $c=21$, what is the optimum and what is the answer?
  1. $21$: the answer is «yes»
  2. $22$: the answer is «yes»
  3. $17$: the answer is «no»
  4. $19$: the answer is «no»
Explanation. The sums at most $21$ are at most $4+6+9=19$ (also $6+13=19$); $9+13=22$ exceeds $c$. Since $19<21$, no subset sums to $21$.
oc-f-1035 · level teorema · notes
Subset sum asks whether there is a subset of sum exactly $c$, but the model $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{SSP}}$ uses $\max\sum_jw_jx_j$ with the constraint $\sum_jw_jx_j\le c$ instead of the equality. Why this choice?
  1. Because with the equality the linear relaxation would always be integer
  2. Because the maximum is always $c$, so the answer is always «yes»
  3. The model is always feasible, and the optimum is compared with $c$
  4. Because an equality constraint is not linear
Explanation. With $\le$ the model always has solutions and its optimum says how close one gets to $c$: the answer is «yes» exactly when the optimum equals $c$. The equality is linear, but it would make the model infeasible for «no» answers.
oc-f-1036 · level facile · notes
Bounded knapsack (BKP): $x_j\in\{0,\dots,b_j\}$ copies of item $j$. With $c=9$ and items $(p_j,w_j,b_j)=(6,2,2)$ and $(5,3,2)$, what is the linear relaxation, with $0\le x_j\le b_j$?
  1. $27$
  2. $61/3$
  3. $22$
  4. $17$
Explanation. Efficiencies $3$ and $5/3$: two copies of the first item (weight $4$, profit $12$), then $5/3$ copies of the second: $12+\frac53\cdot5=\frac{61}3$. $22$ would take two whole copies of the second, weighing $6>5$.
oc-f-1037 · level facile · notes
In the model $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{BKP}}$ of the bounded knapsack the domain is $x_j\in\{0,1,\dots,b_j\}$. What is obtained by replacing it with $x_j\in\Z_{\ge0}$?
  1. The unbounded knapsack (UKP): more than $b_j$ copies can be taken
  2. The 0/1 knapsack (KP): every item is taken at most once
  3. The same problem, because the capacity already bounds the copies
  4. Subset sum (SSP), because the profits become the weights
Explanation. Removing the bound $b_j$ allows unlimited copies, bounded only by the capacity ($x_j\le\lfloor c/w_j\rfloor$). It coincides with the BKP only if $b_j\ge\lfloor c/w_j\rfloor$.
oc-f-1038 · level facile · notes
Unbounded knapsack (UKP, $x_j\in\Z_{\ge0}$) with $c=10$ and two items $(p_j,w_j)=(7,4)$ and $(5,3)$. What are the linear relaxation ($x_j\ge0$) and the integer optimum?
  1. $17.5$ and $14$
  2. $17$ and $17$
  3. $16.7$ and $15$
  4. $17.5$ and $17$
Explanation. The relaxation uses only the most efficient item: $10\cdot\frac74=17.5$. Integer: $(7,4)+2\cdot(5,3)$ weighs $10$ and is worth $17$; two copies of $(7,4)$ are worth only $14$.
oc-f-1039 · level teorema · notes
In the linear relaxation of the model $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{UKP}}$ of the unbounded knapsack ($\max\sum_jp_jx_j$, $\sum_jw_jx_j\le c$, $x_j\ge0$) the optimum uses only the item of maximum efficiency $p_j/w_j$. Why?
  1. Because the relaxation of an integer problem always has a single positive variable
  2. Because the most efficient item is also the lightest
  3. Without upper bounds on the $x_j$, every unit of capacity yields more on that item
  4. Because in the unbounded knapsack the other items are infeasible
Explanation. It is the same reasoning as for $\mathrm{LP}\text{-}0_{\mathrm{KP}}$: with only the capacity constraint, the value is $c\cdot\max_jp_j/w_j$.
oc-f-1040 · level teorema · notes
The linear relaxation of the 0/1 knapsack is solved by sorting by efficiency $p_j/w_j$. Why does this method not apply to the linear relaxation of the multidimensional knapsack (MDKP, weights $w_{dj}$ and capacities $c_d$ per dimension)?
  1. Because the relaxation of the MDKP is unbounded
  2. Every item has one weight per dimension: no single efficiency
  3. Because the relaxation of the MDKP is always integer
  4. Because in the MDKP the variables are integer and not binary
Explanation. With $|\mathscr{D}|\ge2$ constraints the LP optimum may have several fractional variables and must be computed as a general LP (e.g., with the simplex method).
oc-f-1041 · level facile · notes
In the model of the multidimensional knapsack (MDKP: one constraint $\sum_jw_{dj}x_j\le c_d$ per dimension $d$, $x_j\in\{0,1\}$) a dimension has $\sum_jw_{dj}\le c_d$. What can be done with its constraint?
  1. Remove it: it cuts no binary vector
  2. Keep it: it is the tightest constraint
  3. Turn it into an equality
  4. Remove it together with all items of that dimension
Explanation. Even taking all items that dimension is not saturated: the constraint is redundant. A single dimension with $\sum_jw_{dj}>c_d$ is enough for the problem not to be trivial.
oc-f-1042 · level teorema · notes
In the model $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{MKP}}$ of the multiple knapsack ($x_{jk}=1$ if item $j$ goes into knapsack $k$) all $m$ knapsacks have the same capacity. A partition of the items into $m$ non-empty groups corresponds to how many solutions of the model?
  1. $1$: the model distinguishes the groups
  2. $m$: one per knapsack
  3. $2^m$: one per subset of knapsacks
  4. $m!$: one per permutation of the knapsacks
Explanation. With equal capacities the knapsacks are interchangeable: permuting the indices $k$ gives $m!$ equivalent solutions (symmetry), which slow down branch-and-bound.
oc-f-1043 · level ipotesi · notes
In the model $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{MKP}}$ of the multiple knapsack the constraint of every item is $\sum_kx_{jk}\le1$. What would change by writing $\sum_kx_{jk}=1$?
  1. An item could be put into two knapsacks
  2. The problem would become a 0/1 knapsack
  3. All items must be loaded: it may have no solution
  4. Nothing, because the optimum loads all items anyway
Explanation. With the equality no item stays out; if the total weight exceeds the total capacity (an assumption of the MKP) the model has no solutions.
oc-f-1044 · level facile · notes
The model $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{MCKP}}$ of the multiple-choice knapsack has $n$ items in $q$ classes. How many variables and how many linear constraints does it have, besides the domain constraints?
  1. $n+q$ binary variables, $n$ constraints
  2. $n$ binary variables, $1+q$ constraints
  3. $n\cdot q$ binary variables, $q$ constraints
  4. $n$ binary variables, $1$ constraint
Explanation. One $x_j$ per item; the capacity constraint and one constraint $\sum_{j\in\mathscr{J}_h}x_j=1$ per class.
oc-f-1045 · level teorema · notes
In the multiple-choice knapsack (MCKP: exactly one item per class, capacity $c$) two items $a$ and $b$ of the same class have $p_a\le p_b$ and $w_a\ge w_b$. Can $a$ be removed without losing the optimum?
  1. Yes: swapping $a$ for $b$ keeps feasibility and profit
  2. No: $a$ might help to fill the knapsack better
  3. Yes, but only when the two weights are equal
  4. No: every class must keep all its items
Explanation. $a$ is dominated by $b$: it weighs at least as much as $b$ and yields at most as much as $b$. Every solution with $a$ has a solution with $b$ that is at least as good.
oc-f-1046 · level teorema · notes
In the model $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{KPS}}$ of the knapsack with setups ($x_j\le y_h$ for every item $j$ of class $h$; setup cost $f_h\ge1$ and weight $s_h\ge1$) there is no constraint forbidding to activate a class without chosen items. Why is it not needed?
  1. Because $y_h\le x_j$ is already implied by $x_j\le y_h$
  2. Because every class must always be activated
  3. It is needed: without it the model is wrong
  4. Activating it empty costs $f_h$ and uses $s_h$: never optimal
Explanation. Setting $y_h=0$ in a class without chosen items improves the objective and frees capacity: no optimal solution has needlessly activated classes.
oc-f-1047 · level teorema · notes
In the knapsack with setups the item-class link can be written with the disaggregated constraints $x_j\le y_h$ (one per item $j$ of class $h$) or the aggregated ones $\sum_{j\in\mathscr{J}_h}x_j\le|\mathscr{J}_h|\,y_h$ (one per class). Which formulation has the stronger linear relaxation?
  1. They have the same relaxation, because they describe the same integer solutions
  2. The aggregated one, because the coefficient $|\mathscr{J}_h|$ is larger
  3. The disaggregated one: its solutions satisfy the aggregated one
  4. The aggregated one, because it has fewer constraints
Explanation. Summing $x_j\le y_h$ over the class gives the aggregated constraint, not vice versa: e.g., $x=(1,0)$, $y_h=\frac12$ satisfies the aggregated one but not $x_1\le y_h$.

10. Formulations of packing problems (26)

oc-f-036 · level teorema · notes
Bin packing ($n$ items of weight $w_j$, bins of capacity $c$): $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{BPP}}$ has variables $y_b$ (bin $b$ used) and $x_{jb}$ (item $j$ in bin $b$), and $\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{BPP}}$ is its LP relaxation. Which statement is correct?
  1. $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{BPP}})=\sum_j w_j/c$ and $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{BPP}})/z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{BPP}})\ge\frac12$, with $\frac12$ reached asymptotically
  2. $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{BPP}})=\sum_j w_j/c$ and $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{BPP}})=z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{BPP}})$ for every instance with integer weights
  3. $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{BPP}})=\sum_j w_j/c$ and $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{BPP}})/z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{BPP}})\ge\frac{10}{17}$, with $\frac{10}{17}$ reached asymptotically
  4. $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{BPP}})=n/2$ and $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{BPP}})/z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{BPP}})\ge\frac12$, with $\frac12$ reached asymptotically
Explanation. Corollary 10.5 and Propositions 10.6–10.7: the value of the relaxation is the total weight divided by the capacity, and it is at least half of the integer optimum; the ratio $\frac12$ is attained as $c\to+\infty$.
oc-f-037 · level ipotesi · notes
In bin packing (capacity $c$), the LP relaxation of the model $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{BPP}}$ has value $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{BPP}})=\sum_j w_j/c$. Which key fact is used to prove $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{BPP}})/z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{BPP}})\ge\frac12$?
  1. In an optimal solution every item has weight not exceeding $c/2$
  2. In an optimal solution the bins are sorted by non-increasing total weight
  3. The dual of the LP relaxation always has an integer optimal solution
  4. In an optimal solution at most one bin has total weight not exceeding $c/2$
Explanation. If two bins weighed at most $c/2$ each, their contents would fit in one bin, against optimality: so almost all the bins are more than half full and $\sum_j w_j/c$ exceeds about $z/2$.
oc-f-038 · level facile · notes
The bin packing model $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{BPP}}$ with $m$ available bins has $y_b=1$ if bin $b$ is used, $x_{jb}=1$ if item $j$ goes into bin $b$, and minimizes $\sum_b y_b$. Which statement is correct?
  1. $m$ must be at least the number of bins of an optimal solution; the constraints force $y_b=0$ for every empty bin
  2. $m$ must be at least $n$; permuting the bins gives solutions with different objective values
  3. $m$ must be at least the number of bins of an optimal solution; an empty bin may have $y_b=1$, but not in an optimum
  4. $m$ may be the weight bound $\lceil\sum_j w_j/c\rceil$; an empty bin may have $y_b=1$, but not in an optimum
Explanation. With $m$ too small the model may have no feasible solution; an empty bin may have $y_b=1$, but not in an optimal solution. Permuting the bins gives equivalent solutions (symmetry).
oc-f-234 · level facile · notes
The $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{BPP}}$ model of bin packing with $n$ items and $m$ available bins has binary variables $y_b$ (bin used) and $x_{jb}$ (item $j$ in bin $b$), constraints $\sum_b x_{jb}=1$ and $\sum_j w_jx_{jb}\le c\,y_b$. With $n=5$ and $m=3$, how many variables and linear constraints does it have?
  1. $18$ variables and $15$ constraints
  2. $8$ variables and $18$ constraints
  3. $18$ variables and $8$ constraints
  4. $15$ variables and $8$ constraints
Explanation. The variables are $m+nm=3+15=18$; the constraints are $n=5$ assignment and $m=3$ capacity constraints, i.e., $8$.
oc-f-235 · level facile · notes
Bin packing with capacity $c=10$ and three items of weight $6$. The LP relaxation of the $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{BPP}}$ model equals $\sum_j w_j/c$. What are $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{BPP}})$, its round-up and the optimal value?
  1. $\frac{18}{5}$, $4$ and $3$
  2. $\frac95$, $2$ and $3$
  3. $\frac95$, $2$ and $2$
  4. $3$, $3$ and $3$
Explanation. $\sum_j w_j/c=18/10=9/5$ and $\lceil 9/5\rceil=2$; but two items of weight $6$ do not fit together, so $3$ bins are needed.
oc-f-236 · level teorema · notes
In bin packing ($n$ items of weight $w_j$, capacity $c$, $m$ available bins), which solution is optimal for the LP relaxation of the $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{BPP}}$ model (assignment variables $x_{jb}$, usage variables $y_b$, objective $\min\sum_b y_b$)?
  1. $\tilde x_{jb}=\frac1m$ for all $j,b$ and $\tilde y_b=\frac{\sum_j w_j}{mc}$ for all $b$
  2. $\tilde x_{jb}=\frac1m$ for all $j,b$ and $\tilde y_b=1$ for all $b$
  3. $\tilde x_{jb}=\frac1n$ for all $j,b$ and $\tilde y_b=\frac{\sum_j w_j}{nc}$ for all $b$
  4. $\tilde x_{j1}=1$ for all $j$ and $\tilde y_1=\frac{\sum_j w_j}{c}$, the other $\tilde y_b=0$
Explanation. Every item is split equally among the $m$ bins, and every $y_b$ equals the fractional load divided by $c$; the sum is $\sum_j w_j/c$. The last option has $\tilde y_1>1$ if the total weight exceeds $c$, so it violates $y_b\le 1$.
oc-f-237 · level teorema · notes
In bin packing the LP relaxation of the $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{BPP}}$ model equals $\sum_j w_j/c$. Which family of instances shows that the ratio $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{BPP}})/z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{BPP}})$ tends to $\frac12$ as $c\to+\infty$?
  1. Two items of weight $\frac c2$: the relaxation is $1$ and $2$ bins are needed
  2. One item of weight $c$: the relaxation is $1$ and $1$ bin is needed
  3. $c$ items of weight $1$: the relaxation is $1$ and $1$ bin is needed
  4. Two items of weight $\frac c2+1$: the relaxation is $\frac{c+2}{c}\to 1$ and $2$ bins are needed
Explanation. Two items of weight $\frac c2+1$ do not fit together, so $z(\mathrm{ILP})=2$, while $z(\mathrm{LP})=\frac{c+2}{c}$; the ratio $\frac{c+2}{2c}$ tends to $\frac12$. Two items of weight $\frac c2$ fit into one bin.
oc-f-238 · level teorema · notes
In bin packing, also the rounded bound $\lceil z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{BPP}})\rceil=\lceil\sum_j w_j/c\rceil$ has a ratio to the optimum tending to $\frac12$, as $n\to+\infty$. Which family of instances shows it?
  1. $n$ items of weight $1$: the bound is $\lceil n/c\rceil$ and $n$ bins are needed
  2. $n$ items of weight $c$: the bound is $n$ and $n$ bins are needed
  3. $n$ items of weight $\frac c2+1$: the bound is about $\frac n2$ and $n$ bins are needed
  4. $n$ items of weight $\frac c2$: the bound is $\frac n2$ and $\frac n2$ bins are needed
Explanation. Items heavier than $\frac c2$ go one per bin, so the optimum is $n$; their total weight divided by $c$ is a bit more than $\frac n2$, and the ratio tends to $\frac12$.
oc-f-239 · level facile · notes
In the LP relaxation of the $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{BPP}}$ bin packing model (constraints $\sum_b x_{jb}=1$ and $\sum_j w_jx_{jb}\le c\,y_b$, $0\le x,y\le 1$), why is the optimal value only $\sum_j w_j/c$?
  1. The constraint $\sum_b x_{jb}=1$ is relaxed into $\sum_b x_{jb}\ge 0$
  2. Fractional $y_b$ pay only for the occupied part of a bin, as if the items were divisible
  3. The $x_{jb}$ stay binary, but bins can be filled beyond their capacity
  4. The relaxation uses a single bin, of capacity $\sum_j w_j$
Explanation. With $y_b=\sum_j w_jx_{jb}/c$ the cost of a bin is proportional to its load: the relaxation measures only the total weight, and ignores that items cannot be split.
oc-f-240 · level facile · notes
In the $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{CSP}}$ model of cutting stock, item $j$ has demand $d_j$ and the integer variable $x_{jb}$ counts its copies in bin $b$. Which constraint guarantees the demand?
  1. $\sum_b x_{jb}=d_j$ for every item $j$
  2. $\sum_b x_{jb}=1$ for every item $j$
  3. $\sum_j x_{jb}=d_j$ for every bin $b$
  4. $x_{jb}\le d_j\,y_b$ for all $j,b$
Explanation. The copies of item $j$ distributed among the bins must be exactly $d_j$. With $d_j=1$ the constraint becomes the assignment constraint of bin packing.
oc-f-241 · level facile · notes
Cutting stock with $n=4$ items, demands $d=(2,1,3,1)$ and $m=3$ available bins. The $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{CSP}}$ model uses one integer variable $x_{jb}$ per item and bin; the bin packing model on the copies uses one binary variable per copy and bin. How many assignment variables does each have?
  1. $12$ integer and $12$ binary
  2. $7$ integer and $21$ binary
  3. $21$ integer and $12$ binary
  4. $12$ integer and $21$ binary
Explanation. $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{CSP}}$: $nm=12$; bin packing on the $\sum_j d_j=7$ copies: $7\cdot 3=21$. The copies of an item are identical, and a single integer variable counts them.
oc-f-242 · level facile · notes
In the $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{CSP}}$ model of cutting stock (items with demand $d_j$) the number $m$ of available bins must be fixed. Which value of $m$ is always valid?
  1. $m=\lceil\sum_j d_jw_j/c\rceil$, the weight bound
  2. $m=\max_j d_j$, the largest demand
  3. $m=\sum_j d_j$, or the number of bins of any feasible solution
  4. $m=n$, the number of distinct items, whatever the demands
Explanation. With one bin per copy every instance is solved, and the number of bins of a known solution is enough too. The weight bound is a lower bound: with $m$ smaller than the optimum the model has no solution.
oc-f-649 · level facile · notes
The bin packing ILP model uses $m$ potential bins, $x_{jb}=1$ if item $j$ goes into bin $b$ and $y_b=1$ if bin $b$ is used. What must hold for $m$?
  1. $m$ must equal the optimal value
  2. $m$ must be the lower bound $\lceil\sum_jw_j/c\rceil$
  3. $m$ can be anything, even smaller than the optimum
  4. $m$ must be an upper bound on the number of bins, e.g., $m=n$ or the value of a heuristic
Explanation. With $m$ smaller than the optimum the model would be infeasible; with $m$ large the model has more variables and more symmetry. A heuristic solution gives a valid value.
oc-f-650 · level facile · notes
In the bin packing ILP model (items $j$ of weight $w_j$, bins $b$ of capacity $c$) the capacity constraint reads $\sum_jw_jx_{jb}\le c\,y_b$. Why does $y_b$ appear on the right-hand side?
  1. To allow exceeding the capacity when $y_b=1$
  2. It is not needed: one could write $\le c$
  3. It links the use of the bin to the items: if $y_b=0$ no item can go into $b$
  4. To count full bins twice
Explanation. With $\le c$ the used bins would not be linked to the variables $y_b$, and the model would minimize $\sum_by_b$ by setting all $y_b=0$.
oc-f-651 · level teorema · notes
The relaxation $\mathrm{LP}\text{-}0_{\mathrm{BPP}}$ of bin packing (variables $x_{jb},y_b\ge0$) has optimal value $\sum_jw_j/c$. With weights $w=(7,6,5,4,3,3)$ and $c=10$, which integer lower bound on the number of bins follows?
  1. $\frac{14}{5}$
  2. $3$
  3. $2$
  4. $6$
Explanation. $\sum_jw_j=28$, hence $z(\mathrm{LP}\text{-}0)=2.8$ and, since the number of bins is integer, at least $\lceil2.8\rceil=3$. $\frac{14}{5}$ is the unrounded value.
oc-f-652 · level facile · notes
In bin packing, summing the constraints $\sum_jw_jx_{jb}\le c\,y_b$ over all bins and using $\sum_bx_{jb}=1$, one obtains an inequality valid for every solution of the LP relaxation. Which one?
  1. $\sum_by_b\ge\sum_jw_j/c$
  2. $\sum_by_b\le\sum_jw_j/c$
  3. $\sum_by_b\ge n$
  4. $\sum_by_b\ge\max_jw_j/c$
Explanation. $c\sum_by_b\ge\sum_b\sum_jw_jx_{jb}=\sum_jw_j$. It is the weight bound; a solution attaining it, for instance with the $y_b$ concentrated on the first bins, is optimal.
oc-f-653 · level teorema · notes
For bin packing $\lceil z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{BPP}})\rceil/z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{BPP}})\ge\frac12$, with $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{BPP}})=\sum_jw_j/c$. On which fact does the proof rely?
  1. In an optimal solution every bin is full
  2. Every item weighs at least $c/2$
  3. The LP relaxation always has an integer solution
  4. In an optimal solution at most one bin has load at most $c/2$, otherwise two would be merged
Explanation. If two bins had load $\le c/2$, their content would fit into one. Hence almost all loads are $>c/2$ and $\sum_jw_j$ exceeds about $zc/2$.
oc-f-654 · level ipotesi · notes
In the proof of $\lceil z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{BPP}})\rceil\ge\frac12 z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{BPP}})$ for bin packing one uses that at most one bin has load $\le c/2$. Why does the property apply to an optimal solution and not to any solution?
  1. Because only an optimal solution uses bins of capacity $c$
  2. There is no difference: it holds for every solution
  3. Any solution may have many almost empty bins, which an optimal solution would have merged
  4. Because in any solution the loads exceed $c$
Explanation. Putting every item into a different bin is feasible and may have all loads small; the merging argument requires optimality.
oc-f-1048 · level facile · notes
The ILP models of packing problems use a set $\mathscr{B}=\{1,\dots,m\}$ of usable bins. Why is it necessary to fix an upper bound $m$ on the number of bins?
  1. To have finitely many variables; $m\ge z(I)$ keeps an optimum
  2. Because the problem asks to use exactly $m$ bins
  3. Because with more than $m$ bins the relaxation is unbounded
  4. Because $m$ is the optimal value, known in advance
Explanation. The variables are indexed over the bins; $m=n$ always suffices (one item per bin), and a smaller value that is still $\ge z(I)$, e.g., from a heuristic, gives a smaller model.
oc-f-1049 · level facile · notes
In the ILP models of packing problems $x_{jb}=1$ if item $j$ goes into bin $b$. Which constraint guarantees that every item is packed into exactly one bin?
  1. $\sum_{j}x_{jb}=1$ for every bin $b$
  2. $\sum_{b\in\mathscr{B}}x_{jb}\le1$ for every item $j$
  3. $\sum_j w_jx_{jb}\le c$ for every bin $b$
  4. $\sum_{b\in\mathscr{B}}x_{jb}=1$ for every item $j$
Explanation. The assignment constraint is written per item. With $\le1$ an item could stay out, as in the multiple knapsack; the capacity constraint bounds the load, not the assignment.
oc-f-1050 · level teorema · notes
In the ILP model of bin packing the bins are identical, so permuting the indices $b$ gives equivalent solutions. What is the effect of adding the constraints $y_b\ge y_{b+1}$ for $b=1,\dots,m-1$ ($y_b=1$ if bin $b$ is used)?
  1. It makes the linear relaxation integer
  2. None: these constraints are already implied by the model
  3. It removes symmetric solutions, but not the optimal value
  4. It makes the model invalid, because it excludes optimal solutions
Explanation. Every solution can be renumbered so that the used bins are $1,\dots,k$: the value does not change, and branch-and-bound explores fewer equivalent solutions.
oc-f-1051 · level facile · notes
Model $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{BPP}}$ ($\min\sum_by_b$, $\sum_bx_{jb}=1$, $\sum_jw_jx_{jb}\le c\,y_b$): weights $w=(6,5,4)$, $c=10$, $m=3$. Why is the solution $x_{11}=x_{31}=1$, $x_{22}=1$, $y=(1,0,1)$ infeasible?
  1. Bin $3$ is activated but empty
  2. In bin $2$ the load $5$ exceeds $c\,y_2=0$
  3. Bin $1$ exceeds the capacity $c$
  4. Item $2$ is assigned to two bins
Explanation. $y_2=0$ sets the capacity of bin $2$ to zero, but item $2$ is assigned to it. An activated empty bin $3$ is feasible, just not optimal; bin $1$ carries $6+4=10$.
oc-f-1052 · level facile · notes
In the model $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{BPP}}$ of bin packing ($y_b=1$ if bin $b$ is used, $\sum_by_b$ is minimized), can a solution have $y_b=1$ for a bin without items?
  1. Yes, but it is not optimal: set $y_b=0$
  2. No, the capacity constraint forbids it
  3. No, because $\sum_bx_{jb}=1$ forbids it
  4. Yes, and it is optimal if all the other bins are full
Explanation. No constraint forces an activated bin to contain items; but its $y_b$ can be set to zero, reducing the objective by $1$.
oc-f-1053 · level teorema · notes
In the linear relaxation of the bin packing model (constraints $\sum_jw_jx_{jb}\le c\,y_b$, objective $\min\sum_by_b$, continuous variables), why does every capacity constraint hold with equality at an optimal solution?
  1. Because every bin must be full in the integer solution
  2. Because the variables $x_{jb}$ are all equal to $1/m$
  3. It is not true: the capacity constraints are always slack
  4. If it were slack, $y_b$ could be reduced, lowering the objective
Explanation. $y_b$ appears only in its constraint and in the objective with a positive coefficient: at the optimum $y_b=\sum_jw_jx_{jb}/c$, and summing over $b$ gives $\sum_jw_j/c$.
oc-f-1054 · level facile · notes
In bin packing the linear relaxation of the model $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{BPP}}$ is $\sum_jw_j/c$. To which combinatorial bound does $\lceil z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{BPP}})\rceil$ correspond?
  1. To the number of bins of First Fit
  2. To the number of items $n$
  3. To the weight bound $\lceil\sum_jw_j/c\rceil$
  4. To the number of items heavier than $c/2$
Explanation. The relaxation sees nothing but the total weight: rounded up, it is the weight bound of Chapter 3, which does not count, e.g., the items that cannot stay together.
oc-f-1055 · level teorema · notes
Cutting stock (demand $d_j$ of item $j$) can be modelled as bin packing on the extended set of the $\sum_jd_j$ copies, or with integer variables $x_{jb}$ (number of copies of $j$ in bin $b$). What does the second model gain?
  1. A number of available bins that is no longer needed
  2. Fewer variables and no symmetries among identical copies
  3. A linear relaxation that is always integer
  4. The possibility of not cutting all required copies
Explanation. Identical copies, treated as different items, multiply variables and equivalent solutions; counting them with one integer per (item, bin) pair avoids both.

11. Formulations of coloring problems (19)

oc-f-039 · level teorema · notes
The vertex coloring model $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{VCP}}$ has $x_{vc}=1$ if vertex $v$ takes color $c$, $y_c=1$ if color $c$ is used, and the constraints $x_{uc}+x_{vc}\le y_c$ for every edge $\{u,v\}$. What is its LP relaxation value $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{VCP}})$ on a graph with at least one edge (at least $2$ available colors)?
  1. $\omega(G)$, the cardinality of a maximum clique
  2. $\lceil n/\alpha(G)\rceil$, with $\alpha(G)$ the maximum stable set size
  3. $2$, for every graph with at least one edge
  4. $\chi(G)$, the chromatic number of the graph
Explanation. Putting $\frac12$ on two colors for all the vertices is feasible and costs $2$; the dual solution on an edge $\{u,v\}$ certifies optimality. The bound is very weak: on the complete graph $\chi=n$.
oc-f-040 · level facile · notes
The vertex coloring model $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{VCP}}$ with $k$ available colors has the variables $x_{vc}$ (vertex $v$ takes color $c$) and $y_c$ (color $c$ is used). How many variables does it have for a graph with $n=5$ vertices and $k=5$?
  1. $35$
  2. $30$
  3. $25$
  4. $10$
Explanation. There are $k\cdot n=25$ variables $x_{vc}$ and $k=5$ variables $y_c$: $30$ in total. The value $k=n$ is always valid.
oc-f-041 · level facile · notes
In the vertex coloring model $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{VCP}}$ of $G$ (variables $x_{vc}$ and $y_c$ for $k$ available colors), what happens if $k$ is smaller than the chromatic number $\chi(G)$?
  1. The model has no feasible solution
  2. The model still finds a coloring with $\chi(G)$ colors
  3. The LP relaxation of the model becomes unbounded
  4. The optimal value becomes $k$, with two adjacent vertices of the same color
Explanation. With fewer than $\chi(G)$ colors no coloring is feasible: $k$ must be at least $\chi(G)$, and $k=n$ always works.
oc-f-243 · level facile · notes
The $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{VCP}}$ coloring model with $k$ colors has one constraint $\sum_c x_{vc}=1$ per vertex and one constraint $x_{uc}+x_{vc}\le y_c$ per edge and color. How many linear constraints does it have for a graph with $n=5$ vertices, $m=6$ edges and $k=3$?
  1. $18$
  2. $30$
  3. $23$
  4. $11$
Explanation. $n=5$ assignment constraints plus $mk=18$ edge constraints: $23$. The value $11=n+m$ forgets that edge constraints are written for every color.
oc-f-244 · level teorema · notes
In the LP relaxation of the $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{VCP}}$ coloring model (constraints $\sum_c x_{vc}=1$ and $x_{uc}+x_{vc}\le y_c$), why is the solution $x_{v1}=x_{v2}=\frac12$ for every vertex, $y_1=y_2=1$ and the rest zero feasible on every graph?
  1. Because the edge constraints are relaxed into $x_{uc}+x_{vc}\ge 0$
  2. For every edge and color $x_{uc}+x_{vc}\le\frac12+\frac12=1=y_c$, and every vertex has total color $1$
  3. Because the graph is bipartite, and two colors suffice also in the integer model
  4. Because every vertex has degree at most $2$ when the variables are fractional
Explanation. The two halves of color respect every edge constraint, whatever the graph; the value is $y_1+y_2=2$. This is why $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{VCP}})=2$ on every graph with at least one edge.
oc-f-245 · level facile · notes
In vertex coloring, the LP relaxation of the $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{VCP}}$ model equals $2$ on every graph with at least one edge. What is the ratio $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{VCP}})/z(\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{VCP}})$ on the complete graph $K_{10}$?
  1. $\frac15$
  2. $\frac12$
  3. $1$
  4. $\frac1{10}$
Explanation. $\chi(K_{10})=10$ and the relaxation equals $2$: the ratio is $\frac{2}{10}=\frac15$. On large complete graphs the ratio tends to $0$: the bound is arbitrarily weak.
oc-f-246 · level teorema · notes
For the $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{VCP}}$ coloring model two relaxations are compared: $\mathrm{LP}\text{-}0_{\mathrm{VCP}}$, with only $x,y\ge 0$, and $\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{VCP}}$, with also $x_{vc}\le 1$ and $y_c\le 1$. Which statement is correct, for a graph with at least one edge?
  1. $\mathrm{LP}\text{-}0_{\mathrm{VCP}}$ equals $1$ and $\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{VCP}}$ equals $2$
  2. $\mathrm{LP}\text{-}0_{\mathrm{VCP}}$ is unbounded and $\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{VCP}}$ equals $2$
  3. $\mathrm{LP}\text{-}0_{\mathrm{VCP}}$ equals $2$ and $\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{VCP}}$ equals $\omega(G)$
  4. Both equal $2$: the upper bounds do not strengthen the relaxation
Explanation. The same solution with two halves of color is optimal for both, with value $2$ (Corollaries 11.2 and 11.5): adding the upper bounds does not change the bound.
oc-f-247 · level facile · notes
In the $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{VCP}}$ coloring model with $k$ available colors (variables $x_{vc}$ and $y_c$), an optimal coloring with $q$ colors corresponds to how many optimal model solutions, if $k=q$?
  1. $2^q$, one per subset of colors
  2. $q^n$, one per assignment of the colors
  3. $q!$, one per permutation of the colors
  4. $1$, because the colors are numbered
Explanation. Renaming the colors gives another model solution with the same value: $q!$ equivalent solutions. This symmetry, as in bin packing, makes the model hard for branch-and-bound.
oc-f-248 · level facile · notes
In the $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{VCP}}$ coloring model the number $k$ of available colors must be fixed. Which choice is always valid and does not weaken the model needlessly?
  1. Always $k=2$, because the LP relaxation equals $2$
  2. The number of colors of a heuristic coloring, for example of $DSATUR$
  3. The size of a clique found by hand, because it is a lower bound
  4. The stable set bound $\lceil n/\alpha(G)\rceil$
Explanation. We need $k\ge\chi(G)$: the number of colors of a feasible coloring works, and a small $k$ reduces variables and symmetry. A lower bound may be smaller than $\chi(G)$ and make the model infeasible.
oc-f-249 · level facile · notes
The $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{VCP}}$ coloring model and the $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{BPP}}$ bin packing model are assignment models. Which correspondence between the two is correct?
  1. Vertex ↔ item, color ↔ bin, edge constraints ↔ capacity constraints
  2. Vertex ↔ bin, color ↔ item, edge constraints ↔ assignment constraints
  3. Edge ↔ item, color ↔ bin, vertex constraints ↔ capacity constraints
  4. Vertex ↔ item, color ↔ bin, edge constraints ↔ assignment constraints
Explanation. A vertex receives a color as an item goes into a bin, and $y_c$ counts the colors as $y_b$ the bins; what can stay together is decided by the edges instead of the capacity.
oc-f-250 · level facile · notes
In the $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{VCP}}$ coloring model ($x_{vc}=1$ if vertex $v$ has color $c$, $y_c=1$ if color $c$ is used), what do the constraints $x_{uc}+x_{vc}\le y_c$, written for every edge $\{u,v\}$ and color $c$, forbid?
  1. Two non-adjacent vertices with the same color
  2. A vertex with two different colors
  3. A color used by more than two vertices
