  4. Two adjacent vertices with the same color, and using a color with $y_c=0$
Explanation. With $y_c=1$ at most one endpoint of the edge has color $c$; with $y_c=0$ neither does. One color per vertex is imposed by the constraints $\sum_c x_{vc}=1$.
oc-f-286 · level facile · notes
In vertex coloring the LP relaxation of the $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{VCP}}$ model equals $2$ on every graph with at least one edge. On which graphs does this bound equal the chromatic number $\chi(G)$?
  1. On complete graphs, where $\chi(G)=n$
  2. On odd cycles, where $\chi(G)=3$
  3. On all planar graphs, where $\chi(G)\le 4$
  4. On bipartite graphs with at least one edge, for example even cycles
Explanation. The bound is exact only when $\chi(G)=2$, i.e., on bipartite graphs with at least one edge. Already on an odd cycle it is $2<3$, and on $K_n$ it is $2<n$.
oc-f-655 · level teorema · notes
The relaxation $\mathrm{LP}\text{-}0_{\mathrm{VCP}}$ of the coloring model ($x_{vc}=1$ if vertex $v$ has color $c$, $y_c=1$ if color $c$ is used, constraints $x_{uc}+x_{vc}\le y_c$ on the edges) has optimal value $2$ for every graph with at least one edge. What does this say about the bound?
  1. It is as strong as the clique bound $\omega(G)$
  2. It holds only for bipartite graphs
  3. It is weak: it gives $\chi(G)\ge2$ even on graphs needing many colors
  4. It is exact: $\chi(G)=2$ for every graph
Explanation. Setting $x_{v1}=x_{v2}=\frac12$ and $y_1=y_2=1$ every constraint is satisfied whatever the graph: the relaxation does not see the structure of the edges.
oc-f-656 · level facile · notes
In the LP relaxation of the coloring model ($x_{vc}$, $y_c$, constraints $x_{uc}+x_{vc}\le y_c$ for every edge $\{u,v\}$ and color $c$, $\sum_cx_{vc}=1$) one sets $x_{v1}=x_{v2}=\frac12$ for every vertex. Which minimum values of $y_1$ and $y_2$ make the edge constraints feasible?
  1. $y_1=1$, $y_2=0$, with value $1$
  2. $y_1=y_2=1$, with value $2$
  3. $y_1=y_2=\frac12$, with value $1$
  4. $y_1=y_2=0$, with value $0$
Explanation. For an edge $\{u,v\}$: $x_{u1}+x_{v1}=\frac12+\frac12=1\le y_1$, and the same for color $2$. The value $y_1+y_2=2$ is the optimum of the relaxation.
oc-f-657 · level facile · notes
In the vertex coloring ILP model one fixes a number $k$ of available colors, with variables $x_{vc}$ and $y_c$ for $c=1,\dots,k$. Which value of $k$ guarantees that the model is feasible?
  1. An upper bound on $\chi(G)$, e.g., the number of colors of a heuristic or $n$
  2. The clique number $\omega(G)$
  3. The stability number $\alpha(G)$
  4. $k=2$
Explanation. With $k<\chi(G)$ there is no coloring with $k$ colors. $\omega(G)$ is a lower bound, not an upper bound.
oc-f-811 · level ipotesi · notes
In the coloring ILP model ($x_{vc}=1$ if vertex $v$ has color $c$, $y_c=1$ if color $c$ is used, $\sum_cy_c$ is minimized) the edge constraint is $x_{uc}+x_{vc}\le y_c$. What would happen writing $x_{uc}+x_{vc}\le1$ instead?
  1. The model would become infeasible
  2. Two adjacent vertices could have the same color
  3. The $y_c$ would no longer be linked to the colors used: the model would set all $y_c=0$ and the optimal value would be $0$
  4. Nothing: the two constraints are equivalent
Explanation. $x_{uc}+x_{vc}\le1$ still forbids conflicts, but does not force paying $y_c$ when the color is used; the constraint with $y_c$ does both (and linking constraints are needed for isolated vertices too).
oc-f-1056 · level facile · notes
The ILP model of vertex colouring with $k$ available colours has one constraint $x_{uc}+x_{vc}\le y_c$ for every edge $\{u,v\}$ and every colour $c$. How many such constraints are there for a graph with $m$ edges?
  1. $n\cdot k$
  2. $m\cdot k$
  3. $m$
  4. $k$
Explanation. One constraint per (edge, colour) pair. The $n$ assignment constraints $\sum_cx_{vc}=1$ are a different family.
oc-f-1057 · level teorema · notes
In the colouring model ($x_{vc}=1$ if vertex $v$ has colour $c$, $y_c=1$ if $c$ is used) the edge constraints are $x_{uc}+x_{vc}\le y_c$. For a triangle $\{u,v,w\}$ of $G$, what is the constraint $x_{uc}+x_{vc}+x_{wc}\le y_c$?
  1. Valid and stronger than the three edge constraints
  2. Invalid: it excludes feasible colourings
  3. Valid but implied by the three edge constraints
  4. Valid only if the triangle is a maximum clique
Explanation. A clique has at most one vertex per colour, so the constraint is valid. The fractional solution $x=\frac12$ with $y_c=1$ satisfies the edge constraints but not this one ($\frac32>1$).
oc-f-1058 · level facile · notes
The linear relaxation of the colouring model is $2$ on every graph with at least one edge. On the complete graph $K_5$, what does the comparison with the clique bound $\omega(G)$ show?
  1. Both give $5$: the relaxation is exact on complete graphs
  2. The relaxation gives $5$ and the clique bound $2$
  3. Both give $2$: $K_5$ needs two colours
  4. Relaxation $2$, clique bound $5=\chi(K_5)$: it is weak
Explanation. The fractional solution with $x_{vc}=\frac12$ on two colours and $y_1=y_2=1$ stays feasible on $K_5$ too; the $5$-vertex clique instead forces $5$ colours.

12. Formulations of clique problems (37)

oc-f-042 · level teorema · notes
In the maximum clique problem (MCP) on $G$ with $n$ vertices, the edge formulation $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{MCP}}$ maximizes $\sum_v x_v$ with $x_u+x_v\le 1$ for the non-adjacent pairs; $\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{MCP}}$ is its LP relaxation and $\omega(G)$ the optimal value. Which statement holds for every graph?
  1. $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{MCP}})\le 2\,\omega(G)$, hence the ratio is at most $2$
  2. $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{MCP}})\ge n/2$, hence the ratio $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{MCP}})/\omega(G)$ is unbounded
  3. $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{MCP}})\le n/2$, hence the ratio $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{MCP}})/\omega(G)$ is at most $n/4$
  4. $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{MCP}})=\omega(G)$, hence the LP relaxation is always exact
Explanation. The point $x_v=\frac12$ satisfies all the constraints $x_u+x_v\le 1$: the bound is at least $n/2$ even when $\omega(G)=2$.
oc-f-043 · level facile · notes
In the maximum clique problem (MCP) on a graph $G$, the edge formulation uses $x_v=1$ if vertex $v$ is in the clique and constraints $x_u+x_v\le 1$. On which pairs of vertices are they written?
  1. On every pair of non-adjacent vertices of $G$, i.e., on every edge of $\overline{G}$
  2. On every pair of adjacent vertices of $G$, i.e., on every edge of $G$
  3. On every pair of distinct vertices, adjacent or not in $G$
  4. On every pair of vertices at distance exactly two in $G$
Explanation. Two non-adjacent vertices cannot belong to the same clique. Written on the edges of $G$, the same constraints would describe the stable sets of $G$.
oc-f-044 · level ipotesi · notes
In the maximum clique problem on $G$, let $\mathrm{LP}^{\mathrm{CL}}_{\mathrm{MCP}}$ be the LP relaxation of the formulation with the clique inequalities ($\sum_{v\in S}x_v\le 1$ for every maximal stable set $S$). What is used to prove $\omega(G)\le z(\mathrm{LP}^{\mathrm{CL}}_{\mathrm{MCP}})\le\chi(G)$?
  1. It is a relaxation of the problem; its dual is the LP relaxation of the edge formulation; strong duality
  2. The point $x_v=\frac12$ is feasible; the graph is perfect; strong duality
  3. The $DSATUR$ algorithm is optimal; $\omega(G)=\alpha(\overline{G})$; weak duality
  4. It is a relaxation of the problem; its dual is the LP relaxation of a coloring model on the stable sets; weak duality
Explanation. The dual has one variable per stable set: an optimal coloring is an integer feasible solution of value $\chi(G)$, and by weak duality $z(\mathrm{LP}^{\mathrm{CL}}_{\mathrm{MCP}})\le\chi(G)$.
oc-f-251 · level facile · notes
In the maximum clique problem, the LP relaxation $\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{MCP}}$ of the edge formulation ($x_u+x_v\le 1$ for every non-adjacent pair, $0\le x_v\le 1$) always admits the point $x_v=\frac12$. On a cycle with $n=10$ vertices (maximum clique $\omega=2$), which bound does this point give?
  1. $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{MCP}})\ge 5$, against $\omega=2$
  2. $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{MCP}})\ge 2$, equal to $\omega$
  3. $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{MCP}})\ge 10$, against $\omega=2$
  4. $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{MCP}})\ge\frac52$, against $\omega=2$
Explanation. The point $x_v=\frac12$ satisfies every constraint and is worth $\frac n2=5$. On large sparse graphs the relaxation stays at least $\frac n2$ while $\omega$ is small: the ratio is unbounded.
oc-f-252 · level teorema · notes
In the maximum clique problem on $G$ ($x_v=1$ if vertex $v$ is in the clique), let $Q$ be a stable set of $G$ (pairwise non-adjacent vertices). Why is the clique inequality $\sum_{v\in Q}x_v\le 1$ valid?
  1. A stable set contains at most one vertex of every maximum clique
  2. It is the sum of the constraints $x_u+x_v\le 1$ on the pairs of $Q$
  3. It holds only for perfect graphs, where $\omega(G)=\chi(G)$
  4. A clique contains at most one vertex of a stable set
Explanation. Two vertices of $Q$ are not adjacent, so they cannot be in the same clique. Adding the pair constraints gives $\sum_{v\in Q}x_v\le\frac{|Q|}2$, weaker for $|Q|\ge 3$.
oc-f-253 · level facile · notes
In the maximum clique problem, the formulation with clique inequalities has $\sum_{v\in S}x_v\le 1$ for every maximal stable set $S$ of $G$. On the cycle $C_5$ (maximum clique $2$, chromatic number $3$) the maximal stable sets are the $5$ pairs of non-adjacent vertices. What is the LP relaxation value?
  1. $3$
  2. $5$
  3. $\frac52$
  4. $2$
Explanation. The point $x_v=\frac12$ satisfies the $5$ inequalities and is worth $\frac52$; adding the $5$ inequalities (every vertex is in two pairs) gives $2\sum_v x_v\le 5$. Hence $2\le\frac52\le 3$.
oc-f-254 · level facile · notes
In the maximum clique problem, why does the formulation with one inequality $\sum_{v\in S}x_v\le 1$ per maximal stable set $S$ not need the constraints $x_u+x_v\le 1$ on non-adjacent pairs?
  1. Because the number of maximal stable sets is always smaller than the number of pairs
  2. Every non-adjacent pair lies in a maximal stable set, whose inequality implies that of the pair
  3. Because the pair constraints are already implied by the bounds $x_v\le 1$
  4. Because non-adjacent pairs are edges of the graph, and edges give no constraint
Explanation. A non-adjacent $\{u,v\}$ is a stable set, so it lies in a maximal one $S$, and $x_u+x_v\le\sum_{w\in S}x_w\le 1$ with $x\ge 0$. Maximal stable sets may instead be exponentially many.
oc-f-255 · level facile · notes
The edge formulation of the maximum clique writes $x_u+x_v\le 1$ for every pair of non-adjacent vertices of $G$. How many such constraints does it have for a graph with $n=6$ vertices and $m=9$ edges?
  1. $6$
  2. $9$
  3. $15$
  4. $36$
Explanation. The non-adjacent pairs are the edges of the complement: $\binom62-m=15-9=6$. The $9$ edges of $G$ give no constraint.
oc-f-256 · level facile · notes
For the maximum stable set problem (MSSP) on $G$, with $x_v=1$ if vertex $v$ is in the set, the same formulation as for the maximum clique is used, written on another graph. What are the constraints?
  1. $x_u+x_v\le 1$ for every non-adjacent pair of $G$
  2. $x_u+x_v\ge 1$ for every edge $\{u,v\}$ of $G$
  3. $x_u+x_v=1$ for every edge $\{u,v\}$ of $G$
  4. $x_u+x_v\le 1$ for every edge $\{u,v\}$ of $G$
Explanation. A stable set of $G$ is a clique of $\overline G$: the clique constraints on $\overline G$ are the non-adjacent pairs of $\overline G$, i.e., the edges of $G$. $x_u+x_v\ge 1$ would describe an edge cover.
oc-f-257 · level facile · notes
In the maximum clique problem, the dual of the LP relaxation with clique inequalities is the LP relaxation of a coloring model with one variable $y_Q$ per stable set $Q$. On a graph with $\omega(G)=4$ and $\chi(G)=5$, in which interval does the relaxation $z(\mathrm{LP}^{\mathrm{CL}}_{\mathrm{MCP}})$ lie?
  1. In $[5,+\infty)$
  2. It equals exactly $4$
  3. In $[4,5]$
  4. In $[\frac52,4]$
Explanation. The relaxation is an upper bound on $\omega(G)=4$, and by weak duality it is at most the value of every dual solution, in particular of a coloring with $\chi(G)=5$ colors.
oc-f-258 · level facile · notes
In the vertex-weighted maximum clique problem (VWMCP: weight $w_v>0$ for every vertex) the $\mathrm{ILP}^{\mathrm{VW}}_{\mathrm{MCP}}$ model is obtained from the edge formulation of the maximum clique. What changes?
  1. The constraints are written on the edges of $G$ instead of the non-adjacent pairs
  2. Only the objective function, which becomes $\max\sum_v w_vx_v$
  3. Only the constraints, which become $w_ux_u+w_vx_v\le 1$
  4. One variable per edge is added, with weight $w_u+w_v$
Explanation. The feasible solutions are still the cliques of $G$: only the weight of a vertex in the objective changes. With $w_v=1$ we get back the maximum clique model.
oc-f-259 · level facile · notes
In the $\mathrm{ILP}^{\mathrm{EW}}_{\mathrm{MCP}}$ model of the edge-weighted maximum clique (weights $r_{uv}>0$), the binary variable $y_{uv}$ is $1$ if both endpoints of the edge are in the clique, and $\sum r_{uv}y_{uv}$ is maximized. Why are the constraints $y_{uv}\le x_u$ and $y_{uv}\le x_v$ enough?
  1. With positive weights, in an optimum $y_{uv}$ takes the largest allowed value, $\min\{x_u,x_v\}$
  2. Because $y_{uv}=x_ux_v$ is already linear when the variables are binary
  3. Because the constraint $y_{uv}\ge x_u+x_v-1$ would make the model infeasible
  4. Because every edge already has a constraint $x_u+x_v\le 1$ in the model
Explanation. The two constraints impose $y_{uv}=1\Rightarrow x_u=x_v=1$; the opposite implication is not needed, since leaving $y_{uv}=0$ with both endpoints chosen is never optimal with $r_{uv}>0$.
oc-f-658 · level facile · notes
In the maximum clique ILP models, with $x_v=1$ if vertex $v$ is in the clique, on which pairs of vertices are the conflict constraints $x_u+x_v\le1$ written?
  1. Only on the pairs of vertices of maximum degree
  2. On the non-edges of $G$, i.e., on the edges of the complement $\overline G$
  3. On the edges of $G$
  4. On all pairs of vertices
Explanation. Two non-adjacent vertices cannot both be in the clique. Written on the edges of $G$, the same constraints select stable sets.
oc-f-659 · level ipotesi · notes
The relaxation $\mathrm{LP}\text{-}0_{\mathrm{MCP}}$ of maximum clique replaces $x_v\in\{0,1\}$ by $x_v\ge0$ and keeps $x_u+x_v\le1$ on the non-edges. If a vertex is adjacent to all others, what happens without the bounds $x_v\le1$?
  1. The vertex appears in no constraint and the relaxation is unbounded
  2. The vertex is always worth $\frac12$
  3. The relaxation becomes infeasible
  4. Nothing: the bounds $x_v\le1$ are always implied
Explanation. A universal vertex has no non-edges, so $x_v$ can grow without limit. In the other cases $x_u+x_v\le1$ already implies $x_v\le1$.
oc-f-660 · level facile · notes
In the LP relaxation of the non-edge formulation of maximum clique ($x_u+x_v\le1$ for every non-edge, $x_v\ge0$), the vector $x_v=\frac12$ for every vertex is always feasible. On a graph with $7$ vertices, with no vertex adjacent to all others, which upper bound does this vector give at least?
  1. $1$
  2. $7$
  3. $\omega(G)$ exactly
  4. $\frac72$: the relaxation is worth at least $n/2$, a weak bound
Explanation. $\frac12+\frac12=1$ satisfies every conflict constraint, so $z(\mathrm{LP})\ge n/2$ even when $\omega(G)$ is small: the bound grows with $n$, not with the clique.
oc-f-661 · level facile · notes
In the edge-weighted maximum clique (EWMCP) one maximizes the sum of the weights $w_{uv}$ of the edges with both endpoints in the clique. How is the product $x_ux_v$ linearized in the ILP model?
  1. With an integer variable $y_{uv}=x_u+x_v$
  2. No linearization is needed: one uses $\sum w_{uv}x_ux_v$
  3. With a variable $y_{uv}\in\{0,1\}$ per edge and the constraints $y_{uv}\le x_u$, $y_{uv}\le x_v$
  4. With the constraint $x_u+x_v\le1$ on every edge
Explanation. With positive weights the maximization pushes $y_{uv}$ to $1$, and the two constraints allow it only if both endpoints are in the clique.
oc-f-662 · level facile · notes
How does the ILP model of the vertex-weighted maximum clique (VWMCP, weights $w_v>0$) differ from that of maximum clique?
  1. The constraints are written on the edges instead of the non-edges
  2. Only the objective changes, $\max\sum_vw_vx_v$; the non-edge constraints stay
  3. Variables for every edge are needed
  4. The constraints become $x_u+x_v\le w_u+w_v$
Explanation. The set of cliques does not depend on the weights: only what is maximized changes.
oc-f-1059 · level facile · notes
ILP formulation of maximum clique: $\max\sum_vx_v$ with $x_u+x_v\le1$ for every pair of non-adjacent vertices. With $V=\{1,2,3,4\}$ and $E=\{\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{2,3\},\{3,4\}\}$, which vector is feasible?
  1. $(1,1,1,0)$
  2. $(0,1,1,1)$
  3. $(1,0,1,1)$
  4. $(1,1,0,1)$
Explanation. The non-edges are $\{1,4\}$ and $\{2,4\}$. $(1,1,1,0)$ does not violate them; $(0,1,1,1)$ violates $\{2,4\}$, $(1,0,1,1)$ violates $\{1,4\}$, $(1,1,0,1)$ violates both.
oc-f-1060 · level facile · notes
In the ILP formulation of maximum clique the conflict constraints $x_u+x_v\le1$ are written on the non-edges of $G$. If $G$ is complete, how many conflict constraints are there and what is the optimum?
  1. $\binom n2$ constraints; the optimum is $1$
  2. $n$ constraints; the optimum is $n-1$
  3. No constraints; the model is unbounded
  4. No constraints; the optimum takes all $n$ vertices
Explanation. A complete graph has no non-edges; with $x_v\in\{0,1\}$ the optimum is $\vet x=\vet 1$, $\omega(G)=n$. The model is not unbounded because the variables are binary.
oc-f-1061 · level facile · notes
In the maximum clique models the constraints can be written on the cliques of the complement $\overline{G}$: $\sum_{v\in Q}x_v\le1$. Read on the graph $G$, what is the set $Q$?
  1. A cycle of $G$
  2. The neighbourhood of a vertex of $G$
  3. A stable set of $G$
  4. A clique of $G$
Explanation. Vertices pairwise adjacent in $\overline{G}$ are pairwise non-adjacent in $G$: a clique of $G$ contains at most one of them.
oc-f-1062 · level facile · notes
In the edge formulation of maximum clique, for a non-edge $\{u,v\}$ the constraint is $x_u+x_v\le1$. Which implication does it model, for binary variables?
  1. $x_u=x_v$ for every non-edge
  2. $x_u=1\Rightarrow x_v=0$ (not the converse)
  3. $x_u=0\Rightarrow x_v=1$ (and the converse)
  4. $x_u=1$ if and only if $x_v=0$
Explanation. At most one of the two endpoints is chosen; $x_u=x_v=0$ stays feasible, so $x_u=0$ does not force $x_v=1$.
oc-f-1063 · level teorema · notes
The edge formulation $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{MCP}}$ of maximum clique has $x_v\in\{0,1\}$ and $x_u+x_v\le1$ for every non-edge. Why does every feasible solution correspond to a clique?
  1. Two chosen vertices are never a non-edge
  2. Because the objective maximizes the number of vertices
  3. Because every chosen vertex has maximum degree
  4. Because the constraint imposes $x_u+x_v=1$ on the edges
Explanation. If $x_u=x_v=1$ then $\{u,v\}$ is not a non-edge, i.e., it is an edge: the chosen vertices are pairwise adjacent, regardless of the objective.
oc-f-1064 · level facile · notes
The relaxation $\mathrm{LP}\text{-}0_{\mathrm{MCP}}$ of maximum clique has $x_u+x_v\le1$ on the non-edges and only $x_v\ge0$. On a star (centre $1$ adjacent to $2,3,4$, which are not adjacent to each other), what is its value?
  1. $2$: the centre together with a leaf
  2. $3/2$: half of the three leaves
  3. $3$: the three non-adjacent leaves
  4. $+\infty$: the centre is in no constraint
Explanation. Vertex $1$ is adjacent to all others, so $x_1$ is bounded by no conflict constraint: without $x_v\le1$ the relaxation is unbounded.
oc-f-1065 · level teorema · notes
The dual of $\mathrm{LP}\text{-}0_{\mathrm{MCP}}$ ($\max\sum_vx_v$, $x_u+x_v\le1$ on the non-edges, $x\ge0$) has a variable $\pi_{uv}\ge0$ for every non-edge and the constraints $\sum_{u:\{u,v\}\in\overline{E}}\pi_{uv}\ge1$. Which problem is it?
  1. A fractional stable set of $\overline{G}$
  2. A shortest path between two vertices of $\overline{G}$
  3. A fractional cover of the vertices by edges of $\overline{G}$
  4. A fractional colouring of the vertices of $G$
Explanation. Every vertex must receive weight at least $1$ from the edges of $\overline{G}$ touching it, and the total weight is minimized: it is a fractional edge cover.
oc-f-1066 · level teorema · notes
In the linear relaxation $\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{MCP}}$ of the edge formulation ($x_u+x_v\le1$ on the non-edges, $0\le x_v\le1$), why is $z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{MCP}})\ge n/2$ on every graph with $n$ vertices?
  1. Because the dual has value $n/2$
  2. The vector $x_v=\frac12$ is always feasible
  3. Because every graph has a clique of $n/2$ vertices
  4. Because half of the vertices have degree at least $n/2$
Explanation. Every constraint gives $\frac12+\frac12=1$: the point is feasible and worth $n/2$. That is why the bound can be arbitrarily weak, while $\omega(G)$ may be $2$.
oc-f-1067 · level facile · notes
On the cycle $C_5$ ($\omega(C_5)=2$) the linear relaxation of the edge formulation of maximum clique is $\frac52$. Which integer dual bound follows, and why is it allowed?
  1. $\lfloor\frac52\rfloor=2$: the ILP optimum is integer
  2. $\lceil\frac52\rceil=3$: one always rounds up
  3. $\frac52$: a bound cannot be rounded
  4. $2$: because the relaxation is always integer
Explanation. In a maximization problem with integer optimum, $\omega(G)\le z(\mathrm{LP})$ implies $\omega(G)\le\lfloor z(\mathrm{LP})\rfloor$. Here the rounded bound coincides with $\omega(C_5)$.
oc-f-1068 · level facile · notes
The maximum clique formulation with clique inequalities has one constraint $\sum_{v\in Q}x_v\le1$ for every maximal clique $Q$ of the complement $\overline{G}$. Why, in practice, are these inequalities added only when violated?
  1. Because almost all of them are redundant
  2. Because they make the relaxation unbounded
  3. Because they are not valid for all cliques
  4. They can be up to $3^{n/3}$
Explanation. Moon and Moser showed graphs with $3^{n/3}$ maximal cliques: writing them all is impossible, so the ones violated by the current fractional solution are separated.
oc-f-1069 · level teorema · notes
In maximum clique, the relaxation $\mathrm{LP}^{\mathrm{CL}}_{\mathrm{MCP}}$ has $\sum_{v\in Q}x_v\le1$ for every maximal stable set $Q$ of $G$. Given a colouring of $G$ with $k$ colours, why is $z(\mathrm{LP}^{\mathrm{CL}}_{\mathrm{MCP}})\le k$?
  1. Because the colouring has $k$ classes of equal cardinality
  2. Because the relaxation is always integer
  3. One sums the $k$ constraints of the colour classes
  4. Because every clique has at most $k$ vertices
Explanation. Every class lies in a maximal stable set, and the classes cover all vertices once: the sum of the constraints bounds $\sum_vx_v$. It is the duality with fractional colouring.
oc-f-1070 · level teorema · notes
In maximum clique one compares the relaxation $\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{MCP}}$ (constraints $x_u+x_v\le1$ on the non-edges) and $\mathrm{LP}^{\mathrm{CL}}_{\mathrm{MCP}}$ (constraints $\sum_{v\in Q}x_v\le1$ on the maximal stable sets $Q$ of $G$), both with $0\le x_v\le1$. Why is $z(\mathrm{LP}^{\mathrm{CL}}_{\mathrm{MCP}})\le z(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{MCP}})$?
  1. Because $\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{MCP}}$ has integer variables
  2. Every non-edge lies in a maximal stable set
  3. Because $\mathrm{LP}^{\mathrm{CL}}_{\mathrm{MCP}}$ has fewer constraints
  4. Because the two relaxations always have the same value
Explanation. If $\{u,v\}\subseteq Q$, from $\sum_{w\in Q}x_w\le1$ and $x\ge0$ one gets $x_u+x_v\le1$: the region of $\mathrm{LP}^{\mathrm{CL}}_{\mathrm{MCP}}$ is contained in the other, and in a maximization the value does not grow.
oc-f-1071 · level facile · notes
Maximum stable set (MSSP) with $x_v=1$ if vertex $v$ is chosen and $x_u+x_v\le1$ for every edge $\{u,v\}$ of $G$. The graph is a triangle $\{1,2,3\}$ plus an isolated vertex $4$. Which vector is optimal?
  1. $(1,0,0,1)$
  2. $(1,1,0,1)$
  3. $(0,0,0,1)$
  4. $(1,1,1,1)$
Explanation. At most one vertex of the triangle is taken; the isolated vertex has no constraints: $\alpha(G)=2$. $(1,1,0,1)$ violates the edge $\{1,2\}$; $(0,0,0,1)$ is feasible but worth $1$.
oc-f-1072 · level teorema · notes
For maximum stable set on $G$ ($x_v=1$ if $v$ is chosen) one adds the inequalities $\sum_{v\in K}x_v\le1$ for every clique $K$ of $G$. Why are they valid?
  1. Because every clique is also a stable set
  2. Because every vertex belongs to a single clique
  3. They are not valid: they exclude feasible stable sets
  4. A stable set contains at most one vertex of every clique
Explanation. Two vertices of a clique are adjacent, so they cannot be together in a stable set. They are the clique inequalities of maximum clique, read on the complement.
oc-f-1073 · level facile · notes
On the complete graph $K_4$ two linear relaxations of maximum stable set are compared: with only the edge constraints $x_u+x_v\le1$, or with the clique inequality $\sum_{v}x_v\le1$. What are their values ($0\le x_v\le1$)?
  1. $2$ in both cases, with $x=\frac12$
  2. $4$ with the edges, $1$ with the clique
  3. $2$ with the edges, $1$ with the clique
  4. $1$ in both cases, as $\alpha(K_4)$
Explanation. With only the edges $x_v=\frac12$ is feasible and worth $2$; the clique inequality immediately gives $\sum_vx_v\le1=\alpha(K_4)$.
oc-f-1074 · level facile · notes
The model $\mathrm{ILP}^{\mathrm{EW}}_{\mathrm{MCP}}$ of edge-weighted maximum clique has one variable $x_v$ per vertex and one variable $y_{uv}$ per edge. How many binary variables does it have on a graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges?
  1. $n+\binom n2$
  2. $n+m$
  3. $n$
  4. $n\cdot m$
Explanation. The $y_{uv}$ are needed only on the edges of $G$, where a weight is collected; on the non-edges the conflict constraints on the $x$ suffice.
oc-f-1075 · level facile · notes
Vertex-weighted maximum clique ($\max\sum_vw_vx_v$, $x_u+x_v\le1$ on the non-edges). With $E=\{\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{2,3\},\{3,4\}\}$ and weights $w=(1,2,2,4)$, what is the optimum?
  1. $6$
  2. $5$
  3. $8$
  4. $9$
Explanation. The maximal cliques are $\{1,2,3\}$ (weight $5$) and $\{3,4\}$ (weight $6$). $\{2,3,4\}$, of weight $8$, is not a clique: $2$ and $4$ are not adjacent.
oc-f-1076 · level teorema · notes
The clique inequalities $\sum_{v\in Q}x_v\le1$ ($Q$ a stable set of $G$) strengthen the maximum clique formulation. Do they remain valid in the vertex-weighted model ($\max\sum_vw_vx_v$)?
  1. No: with weights a clique may contain two vertices of a stable set
  2. Yes, but only if all weights are equal
  3. No: they must be multiplied by the weights $w_v$
  4. Yes: the solutions are still the cliques of $G$
Explanation. The weighted model changes only the objective; a constraint valid for all cliques of $G$ stays valid whatever the weights.
oc-f-1077 · level teorema · notes
In the edge-weighted clique model ($\max\sum r_{uv}y_{uv}$, $y_{uv}\le x_u$, $y_{uv}\le x_v$, weights $r_{uv}>0$) the constraint $y_{uv}\ge x_u+x_v-1$ is missing. Why is it not needed?
  1. Because $y_{uv}$ always equals $x_ux_v$ in the relaxation
  2. It is needed: without it the model overestimates the weight
  3. With $r_{uv}>0$ the optimum sets $y_{uv}=1$ whenever $x_u=x_v=1$
  4. Because it is implied by $y_{uv}\le x_u$ and $y_{uv}\le x_v$
Explanation. The present constraints prevent counting a weight without both endpoints; counting it when both are there always pays, since $r_{uv}>0$. Without the constraint the model can only underestimate, and never at the optimum.
oc-f-1078 · level facile · notes
Edge-weighted maximum clique: one maximizes the sum of the weights $r_{uv}$ of the edges with both endpoints in the clique. With edges $r_{12}=3$, $r_{13}=4$, $r_{23}=5$, $r_{34}=10$ (no other edge), what is the optimum?
  1. $15$
  2. $12$
  3. $10$
  4. $22$
Explanation. $\{1,2,3\}$ collects $3+4+5=12$; $\{3,4\}$ only $10$. $15=r_{23}+r_{34}$ would require $\{2,3,4\}$, which is not a clique.

13. Formulations of routing problems (33)

oc-f-045 · level facile · notes
In the MTZ (Miller-Tucker-Zemlin) model of the TSP with $n=6$ cities ($x_{ij}=1$ if arc $(i,j)$ is in the tour), city $1$ is the start and every other city $i$ has a position variable $u_i$. How many MTZ constraints link the $u_i$ to the arcs?
  1. $30$
  2. $26$
  3. $36$
  4. $20$
Explanation. The MTZ constraints are written for the ordered pairs of cities different from city $1$: $(n-1)(n-2)=5\cdot 4=20$. The DFJ model would have $2^{n-1}-n=26$ subtour elimination constraints.
oc-f-046 · level teorema · notes
For the TSP ($x_{ij}=1$ if arc $(i,j)$ is in the tour), the MTZ model eliminates subtours with position variables and $O(n^2)$ constraints, the DFJ model with one constraint for every proper subset of cities. Which statement is correct?
  1. Both are correct, and the two LP relaxations always have the same value
  2. Only DFJ is correct: MTZ admits integer solutions containing subtours
  3. Both are correct, and the LP relaxation of DFJ is stronger than that of MTZ
  4. Both are correct, and the LP relaxation of MTZ is stronger than that of DFJ
Explanation. Propositions 13.1 and 13.2: both models exclude the subtours. MTZ has few constraints but a weak relaxation (Proposition 13.3); DFJ has exponentially many constraints, generated when needed, and a stronger relaxation.
oc-f-047 · level facile · notes
In the DFJ model of the TSP ($x_{ij}=1$ if arc $(i,j)$ is in the tour, $\mathscr{V}$ set of cities) the subtour elimination constraints are $\sum_{i,j\in S}x_{ij}\le |S|-1$. Why are they not written for $S=\mathscr{V}$?
  1. City $1$ has no position variable and must be excluded from $S$
  2. A tour uses $|\mathscr{V}|$ arcs with endpoints in $\mathscr{V}$: the constraint would exclude every tour
  3. The constraint would be redundant: it is already implied by the degree constraints
  4. The constraint is already guaranteed by the MTZ constraints on the positions $u_i$
Explanation. The sets $S$ are proper subsets with at least two cities: for $S=\mathscr{V}$ the constraint would cut off all the feasible solutions.
oc-f-260 · level facile · notes
In the DFJ model of the TSP with $n$ cities, the subtour elimination constraints $\sum_{i,j\in S}x_{ij}\le|S|-1$ are written for the subsets $S$ excluding city $1$, with $|S|\ge 2$. How many are there for $n=5$?
  1. $11$
  2. $16$
  3. $26$
  4. $12$
Explanation. The subsets of $\{2,\dots,5\}$ with at least two cities are $2^{4}-1-4=11=2^{n-1}-n$. $16=2^4$ also counts the empty set and the singletons.
oc-f-261 · level facile · notes
In the MTZ model of the TSP, $u_i$ is the position of city $i\ne 1$ after leaving city $1$, and the constraint $u_i-u_j+(n-1)x_{ij}\le n-2$ is written for every pair of cities different from $1$. What does it impose when arc $(i,j)$ is in the tour ($x_{ij}=1$)?
  1. $u_j\le u_i-1$: city $j$ comes before city $i$
  2. $u_j=n-1$: city $j$ is the last one
  3. Nothing: the constraint is always satisfied
  4. $u_j\ge u_i+1$: city $j$ comes after city $i$
Explanation. With $x_{ij}=1$ the constraint becomes $u_i-u_j\le -1$. A subtour not through city $1$ would need strictly increasing positions along a cycle, which is impossible.
oc-f-262 · level facile · notes
In the MTZ model of the TSP ($1\le u_i\le n-1$ positions of the cities $i\ne 1$), why does the constraint $u_i-u_j+(n-1)x_{ij}\le n-2$ exclude nothing when $x_{ij}=0$?
  1. It becomes $u_i=u_j$, true because unvisited cities share a position
  2. It becomes $(n-1)\le n-2$, true for every $n$
  3. It becomes $u_i-u_j\le n-2$, always true because positions lie in $[1,n-1]$
  4. It becomes $u_i-u_j\le 0$, true because positions are increasing
Explanation. The difference of two positions in $[1,n-1]$ is at most $n-2$: the coefficient $n-1$ is the smallest big-M that excludes no tour.
oc-f-263 · level teorema · notes
In the LP relaxation of the MTZ model of the TSP, setting $u_i=1$ for every city $i\ne1$, the MTZ constraints become $(n-1)x_{ij}\le n-2$. What follows?
  1. The relaxation coincides with that of the DFJ model
  2. Every $x$ satisfying the degree constraints with $x_{ij}\le\frac{n-2}{n-1}$ is feasible: the relaxation is weak
  3. Every feasible $x$ has $x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}$: the relaxation is exact
  4. The relaxation becomes infeasible for $n\ge 4$
Explanation. With all positions equal the MTZ constraints only bound the $x_{ij}$ by $\frac{n-2}{n-1}$, a value close to $1$: almost all the solutions of the assignment relaxation remain feasible.
oc-f-264 · level facile · notes
In the TSP ($x_{ij}=1$ if arc $(i,j)$ is in the tour), the assignment relaxation keeps only the degree constraints (one arc leaves and one enters every city) with $x_{ij}\ge 0$. What can an integer solution of it contain?
  1. Several disjoint subtours covering all the cities
  2. Only one tour through all the cities
  3. Cities with two outgoing arcs
  4. Arcs from a city to itself
Explanation. The degree constraints describe an assignment: every city has a successor, and the integer solutions are sets of disjoint cycles. The MTZ or DFJ constraints are needed to remove subtours.
oc-f-265 · level facile · notes
For the TSP the MTZ model has $O(n^2)$ constraints and the DFJ model an exponential number, with a stronger LP relaxation. How is the DFJ model used in practice?
  1. All the constraints are written at the start, since the solver handles them in polynomial time
  2. The constraints are replaced by the MTZ constraints, which have the same relaxation
  3. Only the constraints of the subsets with two cities are written
  4. Subtour elimination constraints are added only when the current relaxation solution violates them
Explanation. With $2^{n-1}-n$ constraints the model cannot be written in full: the relaxation is solved, violated subtours are searched and their constraints added.
oc-f-266 · level facile · notes
In the $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}$ model of the asymmetric TSP ($x_{ij}=1$ if arc $(i,j)$ is in the tour, distances $d_{ij}$ and $d_{ji}$ different) with $n=4$ cities, two subtours $1\to2\to1$ and $3\to4\to3$ satisfy the degree constraints. Which constraint excludes them?
  1. $x_{34}+x_{43}=2$
  2. $u_3-u_4+3x_{34}\le 2$ without position variables
  3. $x_{34}+x_{43}\le 1$, the elimination constraint of $S=\{3,4\}$
  4. $x_{12}+x_{21}\ge 1$
Explanation. The subtour $3\to4\to3$ uses $2=|S|$ arcs inside $S=\{3,4\}$, while the constraint allows at most $|S|-1=1$. The ATSP model is the DFJ model with the arc distances.
oc-f-267 · level facile · notes
The metric TSP has distances satisfying the triangle inequality $d_{ij}\le d_{ik}+d_{kj}$. How does the integer linear programming model change with respect to the general TSP?
  1. Continuous variables are used, because the relaxation is exact
  2. It does not: the triangle inequality is a property of the data, not a constraint
  3. A constraint $x_{ij}\le x_{ik}+x_{kj}$ is added for every triple of cities
  4. The subtour elimination constraints are dropped, useless on metric instances
Explanation. The metric TSP has the same MTZ and DFJ models: the metric concerns the distances $d_{ij}$ of the objective, and helps approximation algorithms, not the formulation.
oc-f-287 · level facile · notes
In the MTZ and DFJ models of the TSP there is a binary variable $x_{ij}$ for every arc $(i,j)$, i.e., for every ordered pair of distinct cities, and two degree constraints per city (one arc leaves, one enters). With $n=6$ cities, how many variables $x_{ij}$ and degree constraints are there?
  1. $30$ variables and $6$ constraints
  2. $30$ variables and $12$ constraints
  3. $15$ variables and $6$ constraints
  4. $36$ variables and $12$ constraints
Explanation. The ordered pairs of distinct cities are $n(n-1)=30$; the degree constraints are $2n=12$. The unordered pairs are $15$, but the models use directed arcs.
oc-f-663 · level facile · notes
The TSP ILP models use $x_{ij}=1$ if the tour goes from city $i$ to city $j$, with the degree constraints (one outgoing and one incoming arc per city). Why are the degree constraints alone not enough?
  1. They admit arcs with $x_{ij}=\frac12$ even in the integer model
  2. They admit solutions made of several disjoint subtours
  3. They admit tours visiting a city twice
  4. They are satisfied by no tour
Explanation. With the degree constraints alone the model is an assignment: for instance $1\to2\to1$ and $3\to4\to5\to3$ satisfy them. Subtour elimination constraints (MTZ or DFJ) are needed.
oc-f-664 · level facile · notes
The TSP models on $n$ cities use the set of directed arcs $A=\{(i,j):i\ne j\}$, with one variable $x_{ij}$ per arc. How many arc variables are there?
  1. $n(n-1)$
  2. $\binom n2$
  3. $n^2$
  4. $(n-1)!/2$
Explanation. Every edge $\{i,j\}$ gives the two arcs $(i,j)$ and $(j,i)$, with the same cost in the symmetric case. $\binom n2$ is the number of edges, $(n-1)!/2$ the number of tours.
oc-f-665 · level facile · notes
The TSP has two classical ILP models: Miller-Tucker-Zemlin (MTZ), with position variables $u_i$, and Dantzig-Fulkerson-Johnson (DFJ), with one constraint per subset of cities. How do their sizes compare?
  1. Both have an exponential number of constraints
  2. MTZ has an exponential number of variables; DFJ $O(n^2)$
  3. They have the same size
  4. MTZ has $O(n^2)$ variables and constraints; DFJ has an exponential number of constraints
Explanation. DFJ writes a constraint for every proper subset of cities (about $2^n$); MTZ avoids subtours with $n$ position variables and $O(n^2)$ constraints.
oc-f-666 · level teorema · notes
On the reference TSP instance (optimal value $18$) the assignment relaxation is worth $16$, the MTZ one $17$ and the DFJ one $18$. Which general statement is consistent with these values?
  1. The DFJ relaxation always equals the optimum
  2. The three relaxations always give the same value
  3. The DFJ relaxation is stronger than the MTZ one, which is stronger than the assignment one
  4. The assignment relaxation is the strongest, because it is the smallest
Explanation. Adding constraints to a minimization relaxation can only raise its value; here DFJ closes the gap, but in general a gap remains even with DFJ.
oc-f-667 · level facile · notes
The DFJ model of the TSP has a subtour elimination constraint for every subset of cities, i.e., an exponential number of constraints. How is it used in practice?
  1. Only the assignment relaxation is solved
  2. The violated constraints are added only when needed, as cutting planes
  3. All constraints are written at the start
  4. They are replaced by the degree constraints
Explanation. One solves the model with few constraints, looks for a subtour (or a violated subset) in the solution and adds the corresponding constraint.
oc-f-812 · level ipotesi · notes
In the MTZ model of the TSP the position variables $u_i$ satisfy $u_i-u_j+n\,x_{ij}\le n-1$ for the arcs $(i,j)$ between cities different from the starting city $1$. Why do the constraints exclude the arcs touching city $1$?
  1. Along a tour positions increase by $1$ at every arc, and a cycle returning to the start would violate the constraint: imposed on city $1$ too it would exclude every tour
  2. Because city $1$ has no arcs
  3. To reduce the number of variables, with no effect on the feasible set
  4. Because $u_1$ must equal $n$
Explanation. With $x_{ij}=1$ the constraint gives $u_j\ge u_i+1$: on a closed cycle the inequalities contradict each other. Exempting city $1$ forbids only the subtours not containing it.
oc-f-1079 · level facile · notes
In the ILP models of the TSP on $n$ cities ($x_{ij}=1$ if the tour goes from $i$ to $j$) the degree constraints ask that exactly one arc leaves every city and exactly one enters it. How many degree constraints are there?
  1. $n^2$
  2. $2n$
  3. $n$
  4. $n(n-1)$
Explanation. One outgoing constraint $\sum_jx_{ij}=1$ and one incoming constraint $\sum_ix_{ij}=1$ per city. $n(n-1)$ is the number of arc variables.
oc-f-1080 · level facile · notes
The ILP models of the TSP use variables on directed arcs $x_{ij}$, even when the distances are symmetric. To how many solutions of the model does a tour of the symmetric TSP correspond?
  1. To $2$, one per direction
  2. To $1$, the same for both directions
  3. To $n$, one per start
  4. To $2n$, start and direction
Explanation. The starting city does not appear in the variables $x_{ij}$, the direction does: the tour and its reverse use opposite arcs, with the same length if $d_{ij}=d_{ji}$.
oc-f-1081 · level facile · notes
The MTZ model of the TSP on $n$ cities has the arc variables $x_{ij}$ and the position variables $u_i$ for the cities other than city $1$. How many variables does it have in total?
  1. $n^2$ arc and $n$ position variables
  2. $n(n-1)/2$ arc and $n-1$ position variables
  3. $n(n-1)$ arc and no position variables
  4. $n(n-1)$ arc and $n-1$ position variables
Explanation. The directed arcs $(i,j)$ with $i\neq j$ are $n(n-1)$; city $1$ has no position. The DFJ model uses only the $n(n-1)$ arc variables.
oc-f-1082 · level teorema · notes
In the MTZ model of the TSP the constraints $u_i-u_j+(n-1)x_{ij}\le n-2$ are written only for $i,j\neq1$. Why is city $1$ excluded?
  1. Because the constraints on $1$ are implied by the degree constraints
  2. To reduce the number of variables, for no other reason
  3. The tour returns to $1$: no cycle has always increasing positions
  4. Because city $1$ always has position $n$
Explanation. Positions grow along every travelled arc between cities other than $1$; on a closed cycle they cannot always grow. Excluding $1$ forbids every cycle not passing through $1$, i.e., every subtour.
oc-f-1083 · level facile · notes
The MTZ and DFJ models of the TSP differ in the way they eliminate subtours. Which constraints do they have in common?
  1. None: they are completely different models
  2. The degree constraints of every city
  3. The constraints on the positions $u_i$
  4. The subtour elimination constraints
Explanation. Both have the objective $\sum d_{ij}x_{ij}$ and the degree constraints; MTZ adds the positions $u_i$, DFJ one constraint per subset of cities.
oc-f-1084 · level facile · notes
In the DFJ model of the TSP there is one subtour elimination constraint for every $S\subseteq\mathscr{V}\setminus\{1\}$ with $|S|\ge2$, $2^{n-1}-n$ constraints in total. How many are there with $n=6$ cities?
  1. $26$
  2. $32$
  3. $57$
  4. $62$
Explanation. $2^5-6=26$: the $32$ subsets of $\{2,\dots,6\}$ minus the empty set and the $5$ singletons. $57=2^6-7$ would use all cities.
oc-f-1085 · level teorema · notes
In the DFJ model the subtour elimination constraint for $S$ is $\sum_{i,j\in S}x_{ij}\le|S|-1$. Why does a subtour visiting exactly the cities of $S$ violate it?
  1. Because a subtour has fewer than $|S|-1$ arcs
  2. Because a subtour violates the degree constraints
  3. Because the cities of $S$ have degree $2$
  4. A cycle on $|S|$ cities uses $|S|$ arcs inside $S$
Explanation. A cycle touching all and only the cities of $S$ has $|S|$ arcs with both endpoints in $S$, one more than the bound $|S|-1$.
oc-f-1086 · level teorema · notes
In the DFJ model the subtour elimination constraints are written only for the subsets $S$ not containing city $1$. Why are they enough?
  1. Because subsets containing city $1$ give invalid constraints
  2. Because with city $1$ the constraints are infinitely many
  3. If the solution has several subtours, at least one avoids city $1$
  4. Because subtours always pass through city $1$
Explanation. A solution of the degree constraints is a union of disjoint cycles; if there are at least two cycles, one of them avoids city $1$ and violates the constraint of its set of cities.
oc-f-1087 · level facile · notes
The assignment relaxation of the TSP has only the degree constraints and $x_{ij}\ge0$. Why does adding the upper bounds $x_{ij}\le1$ not change it?
  1. It does change it: without $x_{ij}\le1$ it is unbounded
  2. It follows from $\sum_jx_{ij}=1$ and $x\ge0$
  3. Because the optimal solution is always a tour
  4. Because the distances are positive
Explanation. Every $x_{ij}$ is a non-negative term of a sum equal to $1$. The same holds for the MTZ and DFJ relaxations.
oc-f-1088 · level facile · notes
The assignment relaxation of the TSP (degree constraints only) has an optimal solution that is a set of disjoint cycles. What is therefore obtained from its value?
  1. A lower bound, exact if the cycles form one tour
  2. An upper bound on the length of the optimal tour
  3. Always the length of the optimal tour
  4. A bound valid only for the metric TSP
Explanation. Removing the subtour constraints enlarges the region: in a minimization problem the value goes down. If the solution is already a tour, the bound is exact.
oc-f-1089 · level facile · notes
In the MTZ model of the TSP with $n=5$ cities, the constraint is $u_i-u_j+4x_{ij}\le3$ ($u$ positions in $[1,4]$). What does it impose when $x_{ij}=1$, and when $x_{ij}=0$?
  1. $u_j=u_i+1$; with $x_{ij}=0$ it imposes $u_i=u_j$
  2. $u_j\le u_i-1$; with $x_{ij}=0$ it imposes nothing
  3. $u_i+u_j\le3$; with $x_{ij}=0$ it becomes $u_i\le u_j$
  4. $u_j\ge u_i+1$; with $x_{ij}=0$ it becomes $u_i-u_j\le3$, always true
Explanation. With $x_{ij}=1$: $u_i-u_j\le-1$. With $x_{ij}=0$: $u_i-u_j\le3=n-2$, satisfied by positions in $[1,4]$; that is why $n-1$ is the smallest valid big-M.
oc-f-1090 · level teorema · notes
The MTZ model of the TSP has $O(n^2)$ variables and constraints, but its linear relaxation often gives a weak lower bound. Why?
  1. Because the MTZ relaxation is unbounded
  2. Because the MTZ constraints also cut feasible tours
  3. Many fractional solutions already satisfy the MTZ constraints
  4. Because the positions $u_i$ must be integer
Explanation. With fractional $x_{ij}$ the term $(n-1)x_{ij}$ is small and the constraints are satisfied with almost equal positions: the big-M weakens the relaxation.
oc-f-1091 · level facile · notes
In the DFJ model of the TSP, the subtour elimination constraint for a set of two cities $S=\{i,j\}$ is $x_{ij}+x_{ji}\le1$. What does it forbid?
  1. Having $i$ and $j$ in the same tour
  2. The two-arc subtour $i\to j\to i$
  3. Visiting $i$ right after $j$
  4. Using either of the two arcs
Explanation. With $|S|=2$ the bound is $|S|-1=1$ inner arc: one of the two arcs may be used, not both.
oc-f-1092 · level facile · notes
In the model $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}$ of the asymmetric TSP (distances $d_{ij}$ and $d_{ji}$ possibly different), how are a tour and the same tour travelled backwards represented?
  1. By different solutions, of generally different lengths
  2. By the same solution of the model
  3. By different solutions but always of the same length
  4. The reverse tour is infeasible in the model
Explanation. The reverse tour uses $(j,i)$ instead of $(i,j)$: it is feasible, but its length uses the distances $d_{ji}$.
oc-f-1093 · level teorema · notes
The model $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}$ is the DFJ model with different distances on the two directions of every arc. Why does the correctness proof of the DFJ model hold unchanged?
  1. Because asymmetric distances satisfy the triangle inequality
  2. Because every ATSP instance is symmetric
  3. It does not: extra constraints are needed
  4. The distances appear only in the objective
Explanation. The distances appear only in the objective; the degree and subtour elimination constraints describe the same directed tours.

14. Formulations of scheduling problems (24)

oc-f-048 · level teorema · notes
Scheduling $P\,||\,C_{\max}$ ($n$ jobs of duration $t_j$, $m$ identical machines): the model $\mathrm{ILP}_{P\|C_{\max}}$ has variables $x_{ij}$ (job $j$ on machine $i$) and $C_{\max}\ge\sum_j t_jx_{ij}$ for every machine $i$. Which statement on its LP relaxation is correct?
  1. $z(\mathrm{LP}_{P\|C_{\max}})=\max_j t_j$, and the ratio to $z(\mathrm{ILP}_{P\|C_{\max}})$ is at least $\frac1m$, reached asymptotically
  2. $z(\mathrm{LP}_{P\|C_{\max}})=\sum_j t_j/m$, and it equals $z(\mathrm{ILP}_{P\|C_{\max}})$ for every instance with $m=2$
  3. $z(\mathrm{LP}_{P\|C_{\max}})=\sum_j t_j/m$, and the ratio to $z(\mathrm{ILP}_{P\|C_{\max}})$ is at least $\frac1m$, reached asymptotically
  4. $z(\mathrm{LP}_{P\|C_{\max}})=\sum_j t_j/m$, and the ratio to $z(\mathrm{ILP}_{P\|C_{\max}})$ is at least $\frac12$ for every $m$
Explanation. Propositions 14.1–14.3: assigning every job with value $\frac1m$ to every machine gives the average load; the bound ignores the longest job, and this is why $C_{\max}\ge t_j$ is added.
oc-f-049 · level ipotesi · notes
Scheduling $P\,||\,C_{\max}$ ($n$ jobs of duration $t_j$, $m$ identical machines), model $\mathrm{ILP}_{P\|C_{\max}}$ with assignment variables and LP relaxation $\mathrm{LP}_{P\|C_{\max}}$. Which facts suffice to prove $z(\mathrm{LP}_{P\|C_{\max}})/z(\mathrm{ILP}_{P\|C_{\max}})\ge\frac1m$?
  1. $z(\mathrm{LP}_{P\|C_{\max}})=\sum_j t_j/m$; $LPT$ is a $\left(\frac43-\frac1{3m}\right)$-approximation with respect to the relaxation
  2. $z(\mathrm{LP}_{P\|C_{\max}})=\sum_j t_j/m$; all jobs on one machine is feasible, hence $z(\mathrm{ILP}_{P\|C_{\max}})\le\sum_j t_j$
  3. $z(\mathrm{LP}_{P\|C_{\max}})=\sum_j t_j/m$; $z(\mathrm{ILP}_{P\|C_{\max}})\ge\max_j t_j$ and the makespan is integer
  4. $z(\mathrm{LP}_{P\|C_{\max}})=\max_j t_j$; all jobs on one machine is feasible, hence $z(\mathrm{ILP}_{P\|C_{\max}})\le\sum_j t_j$
Explanation. The ratio is at least $\frac{\sum_j t_j/m}{\sum_j t_j}=\frac1m$: only the value of the relaxation and a trivial upper bound on the integer optimum are needed.
oc-f-050 · level facile · notes
Scheduling $P\,||\,C_{\max}$ with $m=2$ identical machines and durations $t=(10,1,1,1)$. What are the LP relaxation value $z(\mathrm{LP}_{P\|C_{\max}})$ of the model with assignment variables $x_{ij}$ and makespan $C_{\max}$, and the optimal makespan?
  1. $\frac{13}{2}$ and $10$
  2. $\frac{13}{2}$ and $7$
  3. $10$ and $10$
  4. $13$ and $10$
Explanation. The relaxation is the average load $13/2$; the job of length $10$ forces $z(I)\ge 10$, which is attained. This is why the valid inequality $C_{\max}\ge t_j$ is added.
oc-f-268 · level facile · notes
The $\mathrm{ILP}_{P\|C_{\max}}$ model of scheduling on $m$ identical machines has binary variables $x_{jh}$ (job $j$ on machine $h$) and the continuous variable $C_{\max}$, with one assignment constraint per job and one load constraint per machine. With $n=6$ jobs and $m=3$, how many variables and constraints does it have?
  1. $19$ variables and $18$ constraints
  2. $9$ variables and $19$ constraints
  3. $19$ variables and $9$ constraints
  4. $18$ variables and $9$ constraints
Explanation. The variables are $nm+1=19$; the constraints are $n=6$ assignment and $m=3$ load constraints, i.e., $9$.
oc-f-269 · level facile · notes
In scheduling $P\,||\,C_{\max}$ the largest load $\max_h L_h$ is minimized, which is not a linear function. How does the $\mathrm{ILP}_{P\|C_{\max}}$ model (with $x_{jh}=1$ if job $j$ goes on machine $h$) linearize it?
  1. It minimizes $\sum_j t_jx_{j1}$, the load of the first machine
  2. It minimizes a variable $C_{\max}$ with $C_{\max}\ge\sum_j t_jx_{jh}$ for every machine $h$
  3. It minimizes $\sum_h\sum_j t_jx_{jh}$, the sum of the loads
  4. It minimizes a variable $C_{\max}$ with $C_{\max}\le\sum_j t_jx_{jh}$ for every machine $h$
Explanation. With $C_{\max}$ at least every load, the minimum of $C_{\max}$ is the largest load. The sum of the loads is constant, $\sum_j t_j$.
oc-f-270 · level teorema · notes
In the LP relaxation of the $\mathrm{ILP}_{P\|C_{\max}}$ model (jobs divisible among the $m$ identical machines, $x_{jh}\ge 0$), which solution is optimal and what is its value?
  1. $x_{jh}=\frac1m$ for all $j,h$, with value $\frac1m\sum_j t_j$
  2. $x_{j1}=1$ for all $j$, with value $\sum_j t_j$
  3. $x_{jh}=\frac1m$ for all $j,h$, with value $\max_j t_j$
  4. $x_{jh}=\frac1n$ for all $j,h$, with value $\frac1n\sum_j t_j$
Explanation. Splitting every job equally all machines have load $\frac1m\sum_j t_j$; no solution does better, because the loads sum to $\sum_j t_j$ and the maximum is at least the average.
oc-f-271 · level facile · notes
Scheduling $P\,||\,C_{\max}$ with $m=3$ identical machines and processing times $t=(9,2,2,2)$. The LP relaxation of the model with assignment variables equals $\frac13\sum_j t_j$. What are the relaxation and the optimal makespan?
  1. $5$ and $5$
  2. $9$ and $9$
  3. $15$ and $9$
  4. $5$ and $9$
Explanation. $\frac{15}{3}=5$; but the job of length $9$ cannot be split, so the makespan is at least $9$, and $\{9\},\{2,2\},\{2\}$ attains it.
oc-f-272 · level facile · notes
In scheduling $P\,||\,C_{\max}$ with $m$ machines, the LP relaxation of the model with assignment variables equals $\frac1m\sum_j t_j$. On which kind of instance is the ratio between the relaxation and the optimal makespan close to $\frac1m$?
  1. Exactly $m$ jobs of equal length
  2. Jobs of length $1$, in a number multiple of $m$
  3. One very long job and a few short ones: the optimum is dominated by the long job
  4. Many short equal jobs: the loads balance almost perfectly
Explanation. If a job of length $T$ dominates, the optimum is about $T$ and the relaxation about $\frac Tm$. With short equal jobs the relaxation is almost exact.
oc-f-273 · level teorema · notes
In the $\mathrm{ILP}_{P\|C_{\max}}$ scheduling model the inequalities $C_{\max}\ge t_j$ for every job $j$ and $C_{\max}\ge\lceil\sum_j t_j/m\rceil$ are added. Which statement is correct?
  1. They make every vertex of the LP relaxation integer
  2. They are valid for every integer schedule and strengthen the LP relaxation
  3. They are valid only for the optimal schedule, so they may cut feasible schedules
  4. They are already implied by the LP relaxation, so the bound does not change
Explanation. In an integer schedule job $j$ sits on one machine, whose load is at least $t_j$, and the maximum of integer loads is at least the rounded-up average. The LP relaxation instead can split jobs, and is worth only $\frac1m\sum_j t_j$.
oc-f-274 · level facile · notes
In the $\mathrm{ILP}_{P\|C_{\max}}$ model of scheduling on $m$ identical machines ($x_{jh}=1$ if job $j$ goes on machine $h$), how many integer solutions correspond to the same schedule, if the schedule uses all the $m$ machines?
  1. $m!$, one per permutation of the machines
  2. $1$, because the machines are numbered
  3. $2^m$, one per subset of machines
  4. $n!$, one per order of the jobs
Explanation. The machines are identical: swapping their names gives another model solution with the same makespan. This symmetry slows down branch-and-bound, as in bin packing.
oc-f-275 · level facile · notes
In scheduling $P\,||\,C_{\max}$ with $m=4$ machines, the ratio between the LP relaxation of the model with assignment variables and the optimal makespan is always at least $\frac1m$. If the relaxation equals $12$, what do we know about the optimal makespan $z(I)$?
  1. $z(I)=12$
  2. $3\le z(I)\le 12$
  3. $z(I)\ge 48$
  4. $12\le z(I)\le 48$
Explanation. The relaxation is a lower bound, so $z(I)\ge 12$; from the ratio at least $\frac14$ we get $z(I)\le 4\cdot 12=48$, i.e., the makespan of all jobs on one machine.
oc-f-276 · level facile · notes
The $\mathrm{ILP}_{P\|C_{\max}}$ scheduling model and the $\mathrm{ILP}_{\mathrm{BPP}}$ bin packing model are both assignment models. What distinguishes them?
  1. In bin packing the variables are continuous; in scheduling they are binary
  2. In bin packing the largest load is minimized; in scheduling the number of machines
  3. In bin packing the capacity is fixed and bins are counted; in scheduling the machines are fixed and the largest load is minimized
  4. In bin packing items can be split; in scheduling jobs cannot
Explanation. The same assignment constraints appear in both; bin packing minimizes $\sum_b y_b$ with capacity $c$, scheduling minimizes $C_{\max}$ with $m$ machines.
oc-f-668 · level teorema · notes
In the LP relaxation $\mathrm{LP}_{P\|C_{\max}}$ of the $P\,||\,C_{\max}$ model ($x_{jh}$ = job $j$ on machine $h$, $\sum_hx_{jh}=1$) the bounds $x_{jh}\le1$ are added. Why does the optimal value not change with respect to the relaxation with only $x_{jh}\ge0$?
  1. Because the bounds $x_{jh}\le1$ are violated by every solution
  2. Because the makespan does not depend on the $x_{jh}$
  3. From $\sum_hx_{jh}=1$ and $x_{jh}\ge0$ it already follows that $x_{jh}\le1$
  4. Because the optimal value is always $\max_jt_j$
Explanation. The bounds are implied, so the two relaxations coincide and are worth $\sum_jt_j/m$, with the solution $x_{jh}=1/m$.
oc-f-669 · level facile · notes
The LP relaxation of $P\,||\,C_{\max}$ is worth $\sum_jt_j/m$. With $m=3$ machines and times $t=(5,5,4,4,3,3,3)$, what is it worth and what is an optimal solution?
  1. $27$, with all jobs on machine $1$
  2. $9$, with $x_{jh}=\frac13$ for every job and machine
  3. $11$, with the assignment $(1,2,3,3,1,2,1)$
  4. $5$, with every job on one machine
Explanation. $\sum_jt_j=27$ and $27/3=9$: splitting every job into equal parts among the machines balances the loads perfectly. The integer optimum is larger.
oc-f-670 · level facile · notes
For the $P\,||\,C_{\max}$ model one considers the inequalities $C_{\max}\ge t_j$ for every job and $C_{\max}\ge\lceil\sum_jt_j/m\rceil$. Why are they valid?
  1. In every integer schedule job $j$ is on a machine of load at least $t_j$, and the maximum of the $m$ integer loads is at least their average rounded up
  2. Because the LP relaxation always satisfies them
  3. Because every machine has load exactly $\sum_jt_j/m$
  4. Because the jobs all have the same duration
Explanation. Both hold for every integer solution; added to the relaxation they strengthen it (the relaxation alone may have $C_{\max}<\max_jt_j$).
oc-f-671 · level ipotesi · notes
In the $P\,||\,C_{\max}$ model the constraints $\sum_jt_jx_{jh}\ge\sum_jt_jx_{j,h+1}$ (non-increasing loads) remove equivalent renumberings of the machines. Why are they called «optimality-preserving» and not «valid»?
  1. Because every feasible assignment satisfies them
  2. Because they also hold with unrelated machines ($R\,||\,C_{\max}$)
  3. Because they remove all optimal solutions
  4. They exclude some feasible assignments, but every schedule can be renumbered to satisfy them without changing the makespan, since the machines are identical
Explanation. A valid constraint excludes no feasible solution; these exclude some, but at least one optimal solution remains. With non-identical machines the renumbering would change the times.
oc-f-1094 · level facile · notes
The ILP model of $P\,||\,C_{\max}$ has the variables $x_{jh}$ (job $j$ on machine $h$), the continuous variable $C_{\max}$, the constraints $\sum_hx_{jh}=1$ and $C_{\max}\ge\sum_jt_jx_{jh}$. With $n=4$ jobs and $m=2$ machines, how many constraints does it have, besides the domains?
  1. $6$: jobs plus machines
  2. $8$: one per variable $x_{jh}$
  3. $4$: one for every job
  4. $2$: one for every machine
Explanation. One assignment constraint per job and one load constraint per machine: $n+m=6$.
oc-f-1095 · level facile · notes
In the model of $P\,||\,C_{\max}$ ($\min C_{\max}$, $C_{\max}\ge\sum_jt_jx_{jh}$ for every machine) an assignment has loads $(9,8,10)$ and $C_{\max}=12$ is set. What can be said?
  1. It is infeasible, because $C_{\max}$ must equal a load
  2. It is optimal, because $C_{\max}$ exceeds all loads
  3. It is infeasible, because $12>\sum_jt_j/3$
  4. Feasible, not optimal: $C_{\max}$ can go down to $10$
Explanation. The constraints only ask $C_{\max}\ge$ every load; minimizing, at the optimum $C_{\max}$ equals the maximum load.
oc-f-1096 · level teorema · notes
In the model of $P\,||\,C_{\max}$ one fixes $C_{\max}=T$ (a constant) and removes the objective. Which problem is obtained?
  1. The same problem, because $T$ is the optimum
  2. A problem that is always feasible, for every $T$
  3. Is there a schedule with makespan $\le T$?
  4. Bin packing of capacity $T$ with the minimum number of bins
Explanation. The constraints $\sum_jt_jx_{jh}\le T$ and $\sum_hx_{jh}=1$ ask to place the jobs into $m$ bins of capacity $T$; for $T<z(I)$ there are no solutions.
oc-f-1097 · level facile · notes
Model of $P\,||\,C_{\max}$ with $m=2$ machines and times $t=(4,3,2)$. What is the optimum of the ILP model?
  1. $9$
  2. $5$
  3. $7$
  4. $4.5$
Explanation. $\{4\}$ and $\{3,2\}$ have loads $4$ and $5$: $C_{\max}=5$. $4.5=\sum_jt_j/m$ is the linear relaxation, $7$ the makespan of $\{4,3\},\{2\}$.
oc-f-1098 · level teorema · notes
The linear relaxation of the model of $P\,||\,C_{\max}$ (continuous variables $x_{jh}\ge0$) equals $\sum_jt_j/m$ and ignores the longest job $\max_jt_j$. Why?
  1. The jobs can be split among the machines
  2. Because the longest job always has $x_{jh}=0$
  3. Because $\max_jt_j\le\sum_jt_j/m$ in every instance
  4. Because the relaxation is unbounded
Explanation. With $x_{jh}=1/m$ every job is split into equal parts and every load equals $\sum_jt_j/m$; that is why the valid inequality $C_{\max}\ge t_j$ is added.
oc-f-1099 · level facile · notes
The second linear relaxation of $P\,||\,C_{\max}$ adds $x_{jh}\le1$ to the first one ($\sum_hx_{jh}=1$, $x_{jh}\ge0$). What is its effect?
  1. It raises the value to the maximum of $\max_jt_j$ and $\sum_jt_j/m$
  2. It makes the optimal solution integer
  3. It lowers the value, because it adds constraints
  4. None: $x_{jh}\le1$ follows from $\sum_hx_{jh}=1$ and $x\ge0$
Explanation. Every $x_{jh}$ is a non-negative term of a sum equal to $1$: the two relaxations have the same region and the same value $\sum_jt_j/m$.
oc-f-1100 · level teorema · notes
For the model of $P\,||\,C_{\max}$, $C_{\max}\ge t_j$ is a valid inequality, while the constraints on non-increasing loads $L_1\ge L_2\ge\dots\ge L_m$ preserve optimality. What is the difference?
  1. They are the same thing with two different names
  2. The first holds only in the linear relaxation
  3. The first cuts no solution; the second do, but not all optima
  4. The first cuts optimal solutions; the second do not
Explanation. Every integer schedule has makespan $\ge t_j$. A schedule with unordered loads violates the symmetry constraints, but renumbering the machines gives an equivalent one satisfying them.
oc-f-1101 · level ipotesi · notes
In the $P\,||\,C_{\max}$ instance with $m=3$ and $t=(5,5,4,4,3,3,3)$ every optimal schedule has loads $(9,9,9)$, and the model has $12$ optimal solutions. How many of them do the symmetry constraints $L_1\ge L_2\ge L_3$ on the loads eliminate?
  1. Half of them, i.e., $6$ solutions
  2. None: the loads are equal
  3. All but $2$, one per schedule
  4. All but a single one
Explanation. The constraints compare the loads; with $9\ge9\ge9$ every permutation of the machines satisfies them: they eliminate renumberings only when the loads are distinct.

15. Formulations of lot sizing problems (46)

oc-f-051 · level facile · notes
Capacitated lot sizing (CLS) over $m$ periods: $x_t$ is the production, $y_t=1$ if the setup is paid in period $t$, $cap_t$ the capacity and $D_{t,m}=\sum_{u=t}^m d_u$ the residual demand. In the big-M formulation the link is $x_t\le M_t\,y_t$. Which value of $M_t$ is the strongest?
  1. $M_t=\min\{cap_t,\ D_{t,m}\}$
  2. $M_t=\max\{cap_t,\ D_{t,m}\}$
  3. $M_t=\min\{cap_t,\ D_{1,m}\}$
  4. $M_t=\min\{cap_t,\ d_t\}$
Explanation. The production of period $t$ exceeds neither the capacity nor the residual demand $D_{t,m}$: the smallest valid value gives the strongest relaxation. With $d_t$ feasible plans producing in advance would be cut off; $D_{1,m}\ge D_{t,m}$ is valid but weaker.
oc-f-052 · level teorema · notes
In the big-M formulation of capacitated lot sizing (CLS), the production $x_t$ and the setup variable $y_t\in\{0,1\}$ are linked by $x_t\le M_t\,y_t$. Which statement on the choice of $M_t$ is correct?
  1. Every valid value gives a correct model, and the larger $M_t$, the stronger the LP relaxation
  2. The value of $M_t$ changes the optimal value of the integer model, even among valid values
  3. A value smaller than the production of a feasible plan strengthens the model without excluding solutions
  4. Every valid value gives a correct model, and the smaller $M_t$, the stronger the LP relaxation
Explanation. In the relaxation $\tilde y_t=\tilde x_t/M_t$: a small $M_t$ makes the setups more expensive. A value that is too small, however, cuts off feasible plans, and one that is too large weakens the bound.
oc-f-053 · level facile · notes
For capacitated lot sizing (CLS) there are the big-M formulation (constraints $x_t\le M_t\,y_t$) and the shortest path formulation. What distinguishes the latter from the former?
  1. It describes the plans as paths in a network, without setup variables; the integer optimal value is lower
  2. It has fewer variables than the big-M one and the same LP relaxation; the integer optimal value is the same
  3. It describes the plans as paths in a network, without big-M; its relaxation is stronger, the integer optimal value is the same
  4. It describes the plans as paths in a network, without big-M; its relaxation is weaker, the integer optimal value is the same
Explanation. The two formulations have the same optimal value; they differ in the lower bound of the relaxation and in the size of the model.
oc-f-277 · level facile · notes
Capacitated lot sizing (CLS) over $4$ periods: demands $d=(20,10,30,15)$, capacity $cap_t=50$ in every period. In the big-M formulation, $x_t\le M_t\,y_t$ links production and setup, and the strong value is $M_t=\min\{cap_t,D_{t,4}\}$ with $D_{t,4}$ the demand of periods $t$ to $4$. What is $M_3$?
  1. $30$
  2. $75$
  3. $45$
  4. $50$
Explanation. $D_{3,4}=30+15=45<50$, hence $M_3=45$: an optimal plan does not produce more than the residual demand. $75=D_{1,4}$ is the total demand, valid but weaker.
oc-f-278 · level facile · notes
In the LP relaxation of the big-M lot sizing formulation ($x_t\le M_t\,y_t$, $0\le y_t\le 1$, setup cost $sc_t$ for $y_t$), a solution produces $x_t=10$ with $M_t=40$ and $sc_t=80$. How much setup does it pay in period $t$, at least?
  1. $320$
  2. $20$
  3. $80$
  4. $0$
Explanation. The constraint gives $y_t\ge x_t/M_t=\frac14$, and the relaxation chooses the minimum: $80\cdot\frac14=20$. This is why a large $M_t$ weakens the relaxation.
oc-f-279 · level facile · notes
In lot sizing models, with production $x_t$, demand $d_t$ and stock $s_t$ at the end of period $t$ ($s_0=0$), which constraint expresses the stock balance?
  1. $s_{t-1}+x_t=d_t+s_t$
  2. $s_t+x_t=d_t+s_{t-1}$
  3. $x_t=d_t$
  4. $s_{t-1}+d_t=x_t+s_t$
Explanation. Incoming stock plus production covers the demand of the period and the outgoing stock. With $s_t\ge 0$ production cannot serve earlier periods.
oc-f-280 · level facile · notes
In the shortest-path lot sizing formulation, the variable $zv_{tk}\ge 0$ is the fraction of the demand $D_{t,k}$ of periods $t,\dots,k$ produced in period $t$, and it is an arc from $t-1$ to $k$ in a network with nodes $0,\dots,m$. What does a path from node $0$ to node $m$ represent?
  1. A lot-for-lot plan, with a setup in every period
  2. Any plan, even with late production
  3. The sequence of periods without a setup
  4. A plan producing only with zero incoming stock, one run per arc
Explanation. Every arc $(t-1,k)$ produces in $t$ the demand of periods $t$ to $k$, and the path covers every period once. Plans that are not paths are combinations of paths with fractional $zv_{tk}$.
oc-f-281 · level facile · notes
In the shortest-path formulation of capacitated lot sizing, the link with the setup is $\sum_{k\ge t}zv_{tk}\le y_t$. What makes it stronger than the big-M link $x_t\le M_t\,y_t$?
  1. It uses continuous $y_t$ variables instead of binary ones
  2. It drops the capacities $cap_t$, which weaken the relaxation
  3. It has coefficient $1$ instead of a big-M: a fractional run pays a fraction of setup equal to the fraction of the run
  4. It imposes $y_t=1$ in every period with positive demand
Explanation. The sum of the $zv_{tk}$ leaving node $t-1$ is the fraction of runs produced in $t$, and the setup covers it fully; in the big-M link a small production pays only $x_t/M_t$.
oc-f-282 · level facile · notes
In uncapacitated lot sizing (ULS), with $D_{t,m}$ the demand of periods $t$ to the last one $m$, which value of $M_t$ is the strongest in the constraint $x_t\le M_t\,y_t$?
  1. $M_t=+\infty$
  2. $M_t=D_{t,m}$
  3. $M_t=D_{1,m}$
  4. $M_t=d_t$
Explanation. Without capacities the limit comes only from the residual demand: producing more than $D_{t,m}$ in period $t$ is useless. $M_t=d_t$ would exclude runs covering several periods.
oc-f-283 · level facile · notes
In lot sizing with several products and setup times (MLS), product $p$ takes $vt_{pt}$ units of time per unit produced and $st_{pt}$ units of time for the setup ($y_{pt}=1$). Which capacity constraint is correct in period $t$?
  1. $\sum_p(st_{pt}\,y_{pt}+vt_{pt}\,x_{pt})\le cap_t$
  2. $\sum_p vt_{pt}\,x_{pt}\le cap_t$
  3. $\sum_p x_{pt}\le cap_t\,y_{pt}$
  4. $\sum_p st_{pt}\,y_{pt}\le cap_t$
Explanation. The time of the period is consumed by production and setups. Forgetting $st_{pt}\,y_{pt}$ is a typical mistake: setups would look free in terms of time.
oc-f-284 · level facile · notes
In lot sizing with several products and setup times, the strong big-M value for product $p$ in period $t$ is $M_{pt}=\min\{\lfloor(cap_t-st_{pt})/vt_{pt}\rfloor,\ sd_{ptm}\}$, with $sd_{ptm}$ the residual demand of $p$. With $cap_t=10$, $st_{pt}=2$, $vt_{pt}=2$ and $sd_{ptm}=7$, what is it?
  1. $7$
  2. $10$
  3. $5$
  4. $4$
Explanation. After the setup $10-2=8$ time units remain, i.e., $\lfloor 8/2\rfloor=4$ units of product, less than the residual demand $7$. Forgetting the setup time would give $\lfloor 10/2\rfloor=5$.
oc-f-285 · level facile · notes
In the lot sizing model with overtime (LS-OT), $\mu_t$ is the normal time used (at most $cap^{N}_t$, cost $cw_t$) and $\nu_t$ the overtime (at most $cap^{O}_t$, cost $co_t$). Which constraint links working time to production and setups?
  1. $\mu_t+\nu_t\le\sum_p x_{pt}$
  2. $\sum_p(st_{pt}\,y_{pt}+vt_{pt}\,x_{pt})\le\mu_t\,\nu_t$
  3. $\sum_p(st_{pt}\,y_{pt}+vt_{pt}\,x_{pt})\le\mu_t+\nu_t$
  4. $\sum_p vt_{pt}\,x_{pt}\le cap^{N}_t$
Explanation. The capacity becomes a decision: the time used $\mu_t+\nu_t$ must cover production and setups, and its cost $cw_t\mu_t+co_t\nu_t$ enters the objective.
oc-f-672 · level facile · notes
In single-product lot sizing models, $x_t$ is the quantity produced, $s_t$ the inventory at the end of the period and $d_t$ the demand of period $t$. Which flow balance constraint links these quantities?
  1. $s_t+x_t=d_t+s_{t-1}$
  2. $x_t=d_t$
  3. $s_{t-1}+x_t\le d_t$
  4. $s_{t-1}+x_t=d_t+s_t$
Explanation. What enters the period (previous inventory plus production) leaves as satisfied demand or final inventory. The second constraint has the inventories swapped.
oc-f-673 · level facile · notes
Capacitated lot sizing (CLS) has a big-$M$ formulation and a shortest-path formulation. What do they have in common and how do they differ?
  1. They are the same model with different names
  2. The shortest-path formulation does not admit capacities
  3. They have the same integer optimal value, but LP relaxations of different value
  4. They have equal LP relaxations but different integer optimal values
Explanation. Both describe the same plans; the shortest-path formulation has a stronger relaxation, at the price of $O(m^2)$ variables.
oc-f-674 · level teorema · notes
In the LP relaxation of the big-$M$ formulation of capacitated lot sizing ($x_t\le M_ty_t$, $0\le y_t\le1$) an optimal solution has $y_t=x_t/M_t$. Which choice of $M_t$ gives the strongest bound, among the valid ones?
  1. $M_t$ very large, so as not to exclude solutions
  2. $M_t=\min\{cap_t,D_{t,m}\}$, the smallest valid value ($D_{t,m}$ = demand of the periods from $t$ to $m$)
  3. $M_t=D_{t,m}$, the remaining demand
  4. $M_t=cap_t$, the capacity
Explanation. The smaller $M_t$, the larger $y_t$ must be for the same production, and the more setup cost the relaxation pays. On the reference instance: $99.65$, $137.5$ and $157.5$.
oc-f-675 · level ipotesi · notes
In the big-$M$ formulation of capacitated lot sizing, $x_t\le M_ty_t$. What happens if $M_t$ is chosen smaller than $\min\{cap_t,D_{t,m}\}$ ($D_{t,m}$ = demand of the periods from $t$ to $m$)?
  1. The constraint may cut off feasible plans, even optimal ones: the model is no longer correct
  2. The relaxation becomes stronger and the model stays correct
  3. The model becomes unbounded
  4. Nothing changes
Explanation. An optimal plan may produce in $t$ up to $\min\{cap_t,D_{t,m}\}$; with a smaller $M_t$ that production is forbidden. The smallest valid value gives the strongest relaxation without losing solutions.
oc-f-676 · level facile · notes
On the reference instance of capacitated lot sizing the optimal value is $180$ and the strongest big-$M$ relaxation is worth $157.5$. What is the gap $\frac{180-\LB}{\LB}$?
  1. About $12.5\%$
  2. $22.5$
  3. About $5.9\%$
  4. About $14.3\%$
Explanation. $\frac{22.5}{157.5}\approx0.143$. Dividing by $180$ instead of $\LB$ gives $12.5\%$; $5.9\%$ is the gap of the shortest-path formulation ($\LB=170$).
oc-f-677 · level teorema · notes
On the reference instance of capacitated lot sizing the relaxation of the shortest-path formulation is worth $170$, which is the optimal cost of the same problem without capacities. How is this explained?
  1. Because the integer optimal value is $170$
  2. By chance: there is no link
  3. In the relaxation the capacity constraints act only on the quantities and a convex combination of plans satisfies them
  4. Because the shortest-path formulation ignores the setup costs
Explanation. The shortest-path relaxation describes the uncapacitated part well (it is a shortest path), but the capacities remain weak.
oc-f-678 · level facile · notes
The model of lot sizing with initial inventory (LS-SI) starts from the multi-product model. What changes?
  1. The setup variables become continuous
  2. The constants $s_{p0}=0$ become variables $si_p\ge0$, with the cost $fc_p\,si_p$ in the objective
  3. The capacity constraints are removed
  4. A mandatory final inventory is added
Explanation. The initial inventory enters the balance of the first period and is paid for; the other constraints are those of the multi-product model.
oc-f-885 · level facile · notes
From which model do the ILP models of the lot sizing variants (initial inventory, overtime, unmet demand) start, and what do they add?
  1. From the uncapacitated model, removing the setups
  2. From the bin packing model
  3. From the multi-product model with setup times; they add a few variables and their costs, leaving the other constraints unchanged
  4. From a completely new model for every variant
Explanation. Every variant changes a single feature: for instance the initial inventory replaces the constant $s_{p0}=0$ with a variable paid $fc_p$ per unit.
oc-f-886 · level facile · notes
In lot sizing with unmet demand (LS-UD) the variable $\varepsilon_{pt}\in\Z_{\ge0}$ is the unmet demand of product $p$ in period $t$, with penalty $cu_{pt}$ per unit. How does the flow balance constraint change?
  1. $s_{pt}=\varepsilon_{pt}$
  2. $s_{p,t-1}+x_{pt}+\varepsilon_{pt}=d_{pt}+s_{pt}$
  3. $s_{p,t-1}+x_{pt}=d_{pt}+s_{pt}+\varepsilon_{pt}$
  4. $x_{pt}+\varepsilon_{pt}\le cap_t$
Explanation. The demand $d_{pt}$ is covered by inventory, production and an unmet part, paid $cu_{pt}\varepsilon_{pt}$ in the objective.
oc-f-887 · level ipotesi · notes
In lot sizing with unmet demand the penalty $cu_{pt}$ per lost unit enters the objective. What happens if the penalty is smaller than the cost of producing and holding that unit?
  1. The optimal plan prefers to leave that demand unmet
  2. The model becomes infeasible
  3. The penalty has no effect
  4. The optimal plan still produces all the demand
Explanation. The model chooses the cheapest way to cover every unit: with a low penalty giving up is cheaper; in practice $cu_{pt}$ is set high enough.
oc-f-1102 · level facile · notes
The big-$M$ models of lot sizing have, for every period $t$, the production $x_t$, the stock $s_t$ and the setup $y_t$. Of which type are these variables?
  1. All continuous and non-negative
  2. $x_t$ and $s_t$ integer, $y_t$ binary
  3. All binary, like the setups
  4. $x_t$ binary, $s_t$ and $y_t$ integer
Explanation. Quantities and stocks are numbers of units (non-negative integers); the setup is a yes/no decision.
oc-f-1103 · level facile · notes
In lot sizing models the flow balance is $s_{t-1}+x_t=d_t+s_t$. With $s_2=3$, $x_3=4$ and $d_3=5$, what is $s_3$?
  1. $2$
  2. $7$
  3. $12$
  4. $-2$
Explanation. $s_3=s_2+x_3-d_3=3+4-5=2$: the incoming stock plus the production covers the demand, and the rest goes to the next period.
oc-f-1104 · level facile · notes
For capacitated lot sizing there are the big-$M$ formulation and the shortest path formulation. What does the second one replace?
  1. The setup variables, with continuous variables
  2. The capacity constraint, with a path constraint
  3. The objective function, with the length of a tour
  4. The production and stock variables, with the arcs of a network
Explanation. The variables $zv_{tk}$ are arcs from node $t-1$ to node $k$: producing in $t$ the demand of periods $t,\dots,k$. The setups $y_t$ remain.
oc-f-1105 · level facile · notes
The big-$M$ model of capacitated lot sizing over $m$ periods has balance constraints, capacity constraints and linking constraints $x_t\le M_ty_t$. How many does it have in each family?
  1. $m^2$ linking, $m$ for the others
  2. One per family
  3. $m$ in each family
  4. $m$ balance, a single capacity, $m$ linking
Explanation. Every period has its own balance, its own capacity and its own link between production and setup.
oc-f-1106 · level teorema · notes
In the big-$M$ model of capacitated lot sizing the strong value $M_t=\min\{cap_t,D_{t,m}\}$ is used ($D_{t,m}$ demand of periods $t$ to $m$). What happens to the capacity constraint $x_t\le cap_t$?
  1. It must be rewritten as $x_t\le D_{t,m}$
  2. It becomes redundant
  3. It becomes tighter
  4. It must become an equality
Explanation. $x_t\le M_ty_t\le cap_t$: with $M_t\le cap_t$ and $y_t\le1$ the link already implies the capacity; keeping it is useful only with values of $M_t$ larger than $cap_t$.
oc-f-1107 · level teorema · notes
In single-product lot sizing, why can the quantities $x_t$ be made integer without changing the optimal cost, once the setups $y_t$ are fixed?
  1. A minimum-cost flow remains, with integer optimum
  2. Because the demands are always even
  3. Because the stocks are zero at the optimum
  4. Because the linear relaxation is always integer
Explanation. With the setup periods fixed, balances and capacities are the constraints of a network with integer data; with several products and times $vt_{pt}>1$ the argument no longer holds.
oc-f-1108 · level facile · notes
In the big-$M$ formulation of lot sizing the link between production and setup is $x_t\le M_ty_t$, with $y_t\in\{0,1\}$. What does it impose?
  1. $x_t=0\Rightarrow y_t=0$ in every period
  2. $y_t=1\Rightarrow x_t=M_t$ in every period
  3. $x_t=M_ty_t$ in every period
  4. $y_t=0\Rightarrow x_t=0$; otherwise $x_t\le M_t$
Explanation. Without setup there is no production; with the setup one produces up to $M_t$. The converse ($x_t=0\Rightarrow y_t=0$) is not imposed, but holds at the optimum because the setup costs.
oc-f-1109 · level facile · notes
