  3. To show that Ext-Greedy is optimal on those instances
  4. To prove the first proposition
Explanation. A guarantee is tight if it cannot be lowered; a family of instances whose ratio tends to $2$ proves it.
oc-f-1142 · level teorema · notes
Knapsack with large $c$ and two items: $(p,w)=(2,1)$ and $(c,c)$. Which ratio $z/GR$ does greedy $GR$ (by efficiency, takes what fits) obtain, and what does it show?
  1. $c/2$: the ratio of $GR$ is unbounded
  2. $2$: it is exactly the worst case of $GR$
  3. $1$: here $GR$ finds the optimum
  4. $c$: because $GR$ is worth only $1$
Explanation. $GR$ takes $(2,1)$, more efficient, and then $(c,c)$ does not fit: $GR=2$, $z=c$. For $c\to\infty$ the ratio grows without bound.
oc-f-1143 · level facile · notes
For the algorithm $H^2$ of the knapsack $z(I)/H^2(I)\le\frac43$ holds. On an instance with $z(I)=120$, which minimum value does $H^2$ guarantee?
  1. $80$
  2. $60$
  3. $100$
  4. $90$
Explanation. $H^2\ge\frac34\cdot120=90$. $60$ is the guarantee of Ext-Greedy ($\frac12z$); $80$ would use the factor $\frac23$.
oc-f-1144 · level facile · notes
For the algorithm $H^{\ell}$ of the knapsack $z(I)/H^{\ell}(I)\le\frac{\ell+2}{\ell+1}$ holds (tight). Which guarantee does $\ell=4$ give?
  1. $\frac43$
  2. $\frac76$
  3. $\frac65$
  4. $\frac54$
Explanation. $\frac{4+2}{4+1}=\frac65$. With $\ell=2$ one gets back $\frac43$, the ratio of $H^2$.
oc-f-1145 · level facile · notes
The family $H^{\varepsilon}$ (i.e., $H^{\ell}$ with $\ell(\varepsilon)=\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil-2$) is a PTAS for the knapsack, with time $O(n^{\ell+1})$. With $\varepsilon=0.1$, what are $\ell$ and the exponent of the time?
  1. $\ell=1$, time $O(n^2)$
  2. $\ell=8$, time $O(n^9)$
  3. $\ell=10$, time $O(n^{11})$
  4. $\ell=8$, time $O(n^2/\varepsilon)$
Explanation. $\lceil10\rceil-2=8$, hence $O(n^9)$: polynomial for fixed $\varepsilon$, but the exponent grows with $1/\varepsilon$; that is why it is not an FPTAS.
oc-f-1146 · level teorema · notes
Theorem: if a polynomial algorithm $\mathscr{A}$ for the knapsack had absolute guarantee $k$ ($z-\mathscr{A}\le k$), it would solve the problem to optimality. What is the idea of the proof?
  1. Multiply the profits by $k+1$
  2. Divide the profits by $k$ and round
  3. Remove $k$ items from the instance
  4. Increase the capacity by $k$
Explanation. On the instance with profits $(k+1)p_j$ two different values differ by at least $k+1>k$: the solution of $\mathscr{A}$ is optimal, also for the original instance.
oc-f-1147 · level facile · notes
The 0/1 knapsack is NP-hard. If $P\neq NP$, which kind of guarantee does it admit in polynomial time?
  1. Only absolute, with constant error $k$
  2. Both, relative and absolute
  3. No guarantee of any kind
  4. Only relative, up to an FPTAS
Explanation. A constant absolute guarantee would give the optimum in polynomial time; relative guarantees instead exist (Ext-Greedy, $H^{\ell}$, FPTAS).

36. Approximation algorithms for bin packing (42)

oc-f-122 · level teorema · notes
In bin packing (BPP), Next Fit (NF), Worst Fit (WF), First Fit (FF) and Best Fit (BF) pack the items one at a time in the given order. What are their worst-case performance ratios $r(\cdot)$?
  1. $r(NF)=2$ and $r(WF)=r(FF)=r(BF)=\frac{17}{10}$
  2. $r(NF)=r(WF)=r(FF)=r(BF)=2$
  3. $r(NF)=\frac{17}{10}$ and $r(FF)=r(BF)=\frac32$
  4. $r(NF)=r(WF)=2$ and $r(FF)=r(BF)=\frac{17}{10}$
Explanation. All Any Fit algorithms have the half-full property, hence they are $2$-approximation algorithms; WF asymptotically attains $2$ as NF does, while FF and BF have $\frac{17}{10}$.
oc-f-123 · level ipotesi · notes
In bin packing (capacity $c$, weights $w_i$, optimum $z(I)$), a solution with $k$ bins has the half-full property if at most one bin has total weight at most $c/2$. Which facts are needed to prove that an algorithm with this property is a $2$-approximation?
  1. Every item weighs more than $c/2$; every solution with $z(I)$ bins has $\sum_i w_i\le z(I)\,c$; $k$ is an integer
  2. The items are sorted by non-increasing weight; $z(I)\ge\lceil\sum_i w_i/c\rceil$; $k$ is an integer
  3. The property gives $\sum_i w_i>(k-1)\frac c2$; every solution with $z(I)$ bins has $\sum_i w_i\le z(I)\,c$; $k$ is an integer
  4. The property gives $\sum_i w_i>(k-1)\frac c2$; the LP relaxation equals $\sum_i w_i/c$ and its dual has an integer solution
Explanation. From the two inequalities $(k-1)\frac c2<z(I)\,c$, i.e., $k<2z(I)+1$, and by integrality $k\le 2z(I)$.
oc-f-124 · level ipotesi · notes
In bin packing, an algorithm is Any Fit if it opens a new bin only when the current item fits in none of the bins already open. Which fact is used to prove that its solutions have the half-full property (at most one bin with weight at most $c/2$)?
  1. The number of bins is at most $\frac{17}{10}z(I)$, hence few bins are empty
  2. The content of two bins never fits into one, whatever the bin selection rule
  3. The rule always chooses the bin with minimum residual capacity, which fills up first
  4. The items are sorted by non-increasing weight, hence the first bins are full
Explanation. If two bins both had weight at most $c/2$ they could be merged, but the Any Fit condition excludes it. NF is not Any Fit, but it still has guarantee $2$.
oc-f-125 · level facile · notes
In bin packing, Next Fit (NF) keeps a single bin open and, if the item does not fit, closes it and opens a new one. An algorithm is Any Fit if it opens a new bin only when the item fits in none of the previous ones. Why is NF not Any Fit?
  1. It may open a bin for an item that would fit into a closed bin
  2. It sorts the items by non-increasing weight before packing them
  3. It always chooses the bin with maximum residual capacity
  4. It may exceed the capacity of the open bin
Explanation. An Any Fit algorithm opens a new bin only if the item fits into none of the bins opened so far; NF keeps a single open bin.
oc-f-503 · level facile · notes
Bin packing with capacity $c=10$ and items of weight $6,5,4,3,2$ in this order. Next Fit (NF) keeps a single bin open and opens a new one when the item does not fit; First Fit (FF) puts each item into the first open bin where it fits. How many bins do they use?
  1. NF $3$, FF $3$
  2. NF $4$, FF $2$
  3. NF $3$, FF $2$
  4. NF $2$, FF $2$
Explanation. NF: $\{6\}$, $\{5,4\}$, $\{3,2\}$. FF: $\{6,4\}$, $\{5,3,2\}$: the item of weight $4$ goes back to the first bin, which NF has already closed.
oc-f-504 · level facile · notes
In bin packing with $n$ items, Next Fit (NF) keeps a single bin open at a time. How much time does it take, and why?
  1. $O(2^n)$: all partitions are tried
  2. $O(n)$: every item is compared only with the open bin
  3. $O(n^2)$: every item is compared with all bins
  4. $O(n\log n)$: the items must be sorted
Explanation. One check per item: if it fits it goes into the open bin, otherwise a new bin is opened. The speed is paid with poorly filled bins.
oc-f-505 · level facile · notes
Bin packing with capacity $c=10$: three open bins have residual capacities $2$, $5$ and $3$, and an item of weight $3$ arrives. Where do First Fit (first that fits), Best Fit (smallest sufficient residual) and Worst Fit (largest residual) put it?
  1. FF in the $2$nd, BF in the $3$rd, WF in the $2$nd
  2. FF in the $1$st, BF in the $1$st, WF in the $2$nd
  3. FF in the $3$rd, BF in the $3$rd, WF in the $2$nd
  4. FF in the $2$nd, BF in the $2$nd, WF in the $3$rd
Explanation. The first bin (residual $2$) is not enough. FF takes the second, BF the smallest sufficient residual ($3$, the third), WF the largest ($5$, the second). All three are Any Fit algorithms.
oc-f-506 · level facile · notes
In bin packing a solution has the half-full property if at most one bin has total weight at most $c/2$. With $c=10$, a solution has loads $(4,4,7)$. Can it have been produced by an Any Fit algorithm (which opens a new bin only if the item fits in none of the previous ones)?
  1. Yes: every feasible solution is obtained with some order of the items
  2. Yes, but only with Worst Fit
  3. No, because the total load $15$ is not a multiple of $c$
  4. No: two bins have load at most $5$, and the content of the second would have fitted into the first
Explanation. Any Fit solutions have the half-full property: when the second lightly loaded bin was opened, its first item fitted into the other one. The loads $4$ and $4$ violate the property.
oc-f-507 · level ipotesi · notes
Next Fit (NF) is not an Any Fit algorithm, yet it has $NF(I)\le 2\,z(I)$ in bin packing. Which fact is used in the proof?
  1. NF sorts the items by non-increasing weight
  2. The content of any two bins does not fit into one
  3. Two consecutive NF bins together weigh more than $c$
  4. Every NF bin weighs more than $c/2$
Explanation. NF opens bin $b+1$ only because its first item did not fit into bin $b$: consecutive pairs exceed $c$, and adding up gives the guarantee $2$.
oc-f-508 · level facile · notes
In bin packing, a solution with $k$ bins and the half-full property (at most one bin with weight at most $c/2$) satisfies $\sum_j w_j>(k-1)\frac c2$. With $\sum_j w_j=23$ and $c=10$, how many bins can an Any Fit algorithm use at most?
  1. $3$
  2. $5$
  3. $6$
  4. $4$
Explanation. $23>(k-1)\cdot 5$ gives $k-1\le 4$, i.e., $k\le 5$. The weight bound gives $z(I)\ge\lceil 2.3\rceil=3$, consistent with the guarantee $k\le 2z(I)$.
oc-f-509 · level facile · notes
First Fit, Best Fit and Worst Fit are all Any Fit algorithms for bin packing, so they have the half-full property and ratio at most $2$. What does the fact that $r(WF)=2$ while $r(FF)=r(BF)=\frac{17}{10}$ teach?
  1. The Any Fit condition alone gives only the guarantee $2$: the bin selection rule matters
  2. Worst Fit is not an Any Fit algorithm
  3. First Fit and Best Fit violate the half-full property
  4. The guarantees depend only on the order of the items
Explanation. The half-full property holds for every Any Fit rule and gives $2$; going down to $\frac{17}{10}$ requires knowing which bin is chosen, the first or the fullest.
oc-f-510 · level facile · notes
Next Fit (NF) for bin packing has worst-case ratio $r(NF)=2$. Which kind of instance approaches it?
  1. Items all of weight $c$: every algorithm uses one bin per item
  2. Items sorted by non-increasing weight
  3. Items all of weight $1$, with large $c$
  4. Items alternating weight about $c/2$ and very small weight: NF closes every bin half empty
Explanation. With weights $\frac c2,\epsilon,\frac c2,\epsilon,\dots$ NF puts one large and one small item into every bin, while the optimum pairs the large items and gathers the small ones in few bins.
oc-f-785 · level facile · notes
In the chapter on bin packing approximation a solution is a partition of the items into packing patterns, $z(I)$ is the minimum number of bins and $\mathscr{A}(I)$ the number used by a heuristic. Which performance ratio is used and what is its minimum value?
  1. $\mathscr{A}(I)/z(I)\ge1$
  2. $z(I)/\mathscr{A}(I)\ge1$
  3. $\mathscr{A}(I)-z(I)\ge1$
  4. $\mathscr{A}(I)/z(I)\le1$
Explanation. Bin packing is a minimization problem: the heuristic solution uses at least $z(I)$ bins, and the ratio has the heuristic in the numerator.
oc-f-786 · level facile · notes
A bin packing algorithm is Any Fit if it opens a new bin only when the item fits in no open bin. Which of Next Fit, First Fit, Best Fit and Worst Fit is NOT Any Fit, and why?
  1. First Fit: it chooses the first bin
  2. Best Fit: it chooses the fullest bin
  3. Worst Fit: it chooses the emptiest bin
  4. Next Fit: it closes the bin as soon as an item does not fit, even if the item would fit in an earlier one
Explanation. FF, BF and WF differ only in the choice rule among the bins where the item fits, which Any Fit leaves free; NF keeps a single bin open.
oc-f-787 · level teorema · notes
In a solution produced by an Any Fit algorithm for bin packing, any two bins have together weight greater than $c$. Why?
  1. Because the items are sorted by weight
  2. It is not true for Worst Fit
  3. The first item of the bin opened later did not fit into the other one, whose load never decreased
  4. Because every bin is more than half full by construction of the choice rule
Explanation. Only the Any Fit condition is used, not the choice rule: this is why the property, and the guarantee $\mathscr{A}(I)\le2z(I)$, also holds for WF.
oc-f-788 · level facile · notes
Bin packing with $c=10$ and items, in order, of weight $(6,5,4,3)$. How many bins does First Fit use and with which loads?
  1. $4$, with loads $(6,5,4,3)$
  2. $2$, with loads $(10,8)$
  3. $3$, with loads $(6,9,3)$
  4. $2$, with loads $(9,9)$
Explanation. $6$ opens bin $1$; $5$ does not fit ($11$) and opens bin $2$; $4$ fits into bin $1$ ($10$); $3$ does not fit into bin $1$ and fits into bin $2$ ($8$).
oc-f-789 · level facile · notes
Bin packing with $c=10$: the open bins have loads $(5,8,3)$ and an item of weight $2$ arrives. Into which bin does Best Fit put it (minimum residual capacity among those where it fits)?
  1. Into bin $2$, which becomes full
  2. Into bin $1$, the first where it fits
  3. Into bin $3$, the emptiest
  4. Into a new bin
Explanation. Residuals $5,2,7$: the item fits everywhere, and the minimum residual is $2$, in bin $2$. First Fit would put it into bin $1$, Worst Fit into bin $3$.
oc-f-790 · level facile · notes
Worst Fit for bin packing puts every item into the open bin with maximum residual capacity among those where it fits. Which worst-case guarantee does it have, compared to First Fit?
  1. Ratio $\frac{17}{10}$, as First Fit
  2. Ratio $\frac32$
  3. No constant guarantee
  4. Ratio $2$, tight; First Fit has asymptotic ratio $\frac{17}{10}$
Explanation. WF is Any Fit, hence $WF(I)\le2z(I)$, and there are instances with $WF(I_n)/z(I_n)\to2$; FF and BF only reach $\frac{17}{10}$.
oc-f-791 · level teorema · notes
For Worst Fit there are instances $I_n$ with $WF(I_n)/z(I_n)\to2$. What does it mean for the class of Any Fit algorithms, which guarantee $\mathscr{A}(I)\le2z(I)$?
  1. That Worst Fit is not Any Fit
  2. That First Fit has ratio $2$
  3. The bound $2$ cannot be improved for the class as a whole; better choice rules can improve it for single algorithms
  4. That no Any Fit algorithm has ratio below $2$
Explanation. The Any Fit condition alone gives $2$; FF and BF, with better choice rules, go down to $\frac{17}{10}$.
oc-f-792 · level facile · notes
First Fit and Best Fit for bin packing satisfy $\mathscr{A}(I)\le\frac{17}{10}z(I)$ (Dósa and Sgall; the first version, from 1974, had a $+2$), and the factor $\frac{17}{10}$ is tight. On an instance with $z(I)=100$, at most how many bins can First Fit use according to this guarantee?
  1. $150$
  2. $170$
  3. $172$
  4. $200$
Explanation. $\frac{17}{10}\cdot100=170$; $172$ is the weaker 1974 bound. The bound $2z(I)=200$ of the Any Fit condition alone is weaker still.
oc-f-793 · level ipotesi · notes
The Any Fit condition alone guarantees the half-full property and hence $\mathscr{A}(I)\le2z(I)$. What happens to the guarantee if the Any Fit condition is dropped, as Next Fit does?
  1. Next Fit still keeps $NF(I)\le2z(I)$, because two consecutive bins together exceed $c$
  2. Next Fit loses every constant guarantee
  3. Next Fit becomes optimal
  4. Next Fit has guarantee $\frac{17}{10}$
Explanation. For NF the property holds only for pairs of consecutive bins, but it is enough for the guarantee $2$; what the Any Fit condition adds is the property for every pair.
oc-f-1153 · level facile · notes
Bin packing with capacity $c=10$. Next Fit (NF) scans the items in the given order, keeps a single bin open and, if the item does not fit, closes it and opens a new one. With weights, in order, $(4,7,2,5,6,3)$, which vector $bin$ ($bin_i$ = bin of item $i$) does NF return?
  1. $(1,2,2,3,4,4)$
  2. $(1,2,1,3,4,1)$
  3. $(1,2,2,3,3,4)$
  4. $(1,2,2,3,4,5)$
Explanation. $4$ in bin $1$; $7$ does not fit (residual $6$): bin $2$, then $2$ (residual $1$); $5$ opens bin $3$; $6$ does not fit (residual $5$): bin $4$, where $3$ also fits. $(1,2,1,3,4,1)$ is First Fit, which goes back to earlier bins.
oc-f-1154 · level facile · notes
In bin packing ($c=10$), an algorithm returns $bin=(1,1,2,3,3,3)$ ($bin_i$ = bin of item $i$) with weights $w=(5,4,8,3,3,2)$. The load pattern $P_b$ is the set of items with $bin_i=b$. What are $P_3$ and its total weight?
  1. $P_3=\{3\}$, weight $8$
  2. $P_3=\{3,4,5\}$, weight $14$
  3. $P_3=\{6\}$, weight $2$
  4. $P_3=\{4,5,6\}$, weight $8$
Explanation. $bin_4=bin_5=bin_6=3$, hence $P_3=\{4,5,6\}$ with weight $3+3+2=8$. $\{3\}$ confuses the bin index with the item index: item $3$ is in bin $2$.
oc-f-1155 · level facile · notes
In the pseudocode of Next Fit for bin packing, $rc$ is the residual capacity of the open bin and a new bin is opened if $w[i]>rc$. What does NF do when an item arrives whose weight $w[i]$ equals $rc$ exactly?
  1. It puts it into the first closed bin where it fits
  2. It discards it and moves to the next item
  3. It puts it into the open bin, which is left with $rc=0$
  4. It opens a new bin and puts it there
Explanation. The condition for opening a bin is $w[i]>rc$, strict: with $w[i]=rc$ the item fits and fills the bin exactly. NF never goes back to closed bins.
oc-f-1156 · level facile · notes
First Fit (FF) is run on six items of weight $5,7,3,4,2,6$, scanned in this order, with bins of capacity $10$: every item goes into the first bin, in order of opening, that can take it, otherwise into a new one. What is the result?
  1. $4$, with loads $(10,7,4,6)$
  2. $3$, with loads $(10,7,10)$
  3. $3$, with loads $(9,10,8)$
  4. $4$, with loads $(5,10,6,6)$
Explanation. $5\to1$, $7\to2$, $3\to1$ (residual $5$), $4\to3$ (residuals $2$ and $3$), $2\to1$, $6\to3$ (residual $6$). $(9,10,8)$ is Best Fit, $(5,10,6,6)$ is Next Fit; $(10,7,4,6)$ forgets to check bin $3$ for the item $6$.
oc-f-1157 · level facile · notes
In bin packing an Any Fit algorithm opens a new bin only if the item fits in none of the open ones, and leaves free the choice among the bins where it fits. What does First Fit fix?
  1. The first bin (in order of opening) where it fits
  2. The order of the items, scanned by non-increasing weight
  3. The bin with minimum residual capacity
  4. Always the last bin opened so far
Explanation. FF scans the items in the given order and chooses the first suitable bin. Sorting the weights in non-increasing order is something else (First Fit Decreasing); the minimum residual is Best Fit; the last bin is the idea of Next Fit.
oc-f-1158 · level facile · notes
Bin packing with $c=10$ and weights, in order, $(5,7,3,3,4)$. Best Fit (BF) puts every item, among the open bins where it fits, into the one with minimum residual capacity (ties: the first opened), and opens a new bin only if it fits in none. Which vector $bin$ ($bin_i$ = bin of item $i$) does it return?
  1. $(1,2,1,2,3)$
  2. $(1,2,2,3,3)$
  3. $(1,2,1,3,3)$
  4. $(1,2,2,1,3)$
Explanation. The first $3$ fits in bins $1$ (residual $5$) and $2$ (residual $3$): BF chooses bin $2$, which becomes full. The second $3$ goes into bin $1$ (residual $2$), and $4$ opens bin $3$. $(1,2,1,2,3)$ is First Fit (and here also Worst Fit), $(1,2,2,3,3)$ is Next Fit.
oc-f-1159 · level facile · notes
Bin packing with $c=10$: four open bins have residual capacities $(4,2,4,7)$ and an item of weight $3$ arrives. Best Fit chooses, among the bins where the item fits, the one with minimum residual capacity, and on ties the first opened. Where does the item go?
  1. Into bin $3$
  2. Into bin $4$
  3. Into bin $1$
  4. Into bin $2$
Explanation. The item fits in bins $1$, $3$, $4$ (residuals $4,4,7$); the minimum $4$ is tied between $1$ and $3$, and the first opened wins. Bin $2$ has the smallest residual but the item does not fit; bin $4$ is the choice of Worst Fit.
oc-f-1160 · level facile · notes
Bin packing with $c=10$ and weights, in order, $(6,5,3,4,2)$. First Fit (FF) uses the first bin where the item fits; Worst Fit (WF) the one with maximum residual capacity among those where it fits; both open a bin only if the item fits in none. How many bins do they use?
  1. Both $3$
  2. FF $3$, WF $2$
  3. FF $2$, WF $3$
  4. Both $2$
Explanation. After $6$ and $5$ the residuals are $(4,5)$. FF puts $3$ into the first ($\to(1,5)$), then $4$ into the second ($\to(1,1)$) and opens a third for $2$. WF puts $3$ into the second ($\to(4,2)$), then $4$ into the first and $2$ into the second: $(10,10)$. A worse guarantee ($r(WF)=2$) does not prevent winning on a single instance.
oc-f-1161 · level facile · notes
In bin packing, Worst Fit puts every item, among the open bins where it fits, into the one with maximum residual capacity. What is the idea of this rule?
  1. Avoid residuals too small for future items
  2. Fill every open bin as much as possible
  3. Close every bin as soon as an item does not fit
  4. Scan the heaviest items before the others
Explanation. By putting the item into the emptiest bin, WF spreads the free space and avoids unusable residuals. Filling as much as possible is the opposite idea, of Best Fit; closing bins is Next Fit; the order by weight is not part of WF.
oc-f-1162 · level facile · notes
Bin packing with $c=10$ and weights, in order, $(2,9,2,9,2,9)$. Next Fit keeps a single bin open. A solution has the half-full property if at most one bin has load $\le c/2$. How many bins does NF use, and does its solution have the property?
  1. $6$, and it does: two consecutive bins exceed $10$
  2. $4$, and it does: a single bin has load $\le5$
  3. $3$, and it does: every bin weighs $11$
  4. $6$, and it does not: three bins have load $2$
Explanation. No item fits together with the previous one ($2+9=11>10$), so NF opens $6$ bins, and three have load $2\le5$. Two consecutive bins exceeding $c$ is a different property. $4$ bins are those of First Fit, $(6,9,9,9)$.
oc-f-1163 · level facile · notes
In bin packing with capacity $c$, a solution has the half-full property if at most one bin has total weight at most $c/2$. Which condition is equivalent?
  1. Every bin, without exception, weighs more than $c/2$
  2. At most one bin is not completely filled
  3. For every pair of bins, at least one weighs more than $c/2$
  4. For every pair of bins, together they weigh more than $c$
Explanation. If two bins both weighed at most $c/2$ the property would fail, and conversely. «Together more than $c$» is the stronger property of Any Fit solutions; «every bin» does not allow the exception.
oc-f-1164 · level facile · notes
In bin packing with $c=10$, a solution has two bins with loads $6$ and $1$. Does it have the half-full property (at most one bin with load $\le c/2$)? Can the two bins be merged into one?
  1. No, it does not; and they cannot be merged
  2. Yes, it does; and yes, they can be merged
  3. Yes, it does; hence they cannot be merged
  4. No, it does not; and yes, they can be merged
Explanation. Only the bin with load $1$ is $\le5$: the property holds; but $6+1=7\le10$, so they merge. The property does not prevent merging: it serves to prove the guarantee $2$.
oc-f-1165 · level teorema · notes
In bin packing, for a solution with $k$ bins and the half-full property one gets $(k-1)\frac c2<\sum_iw_i\le z(I)\,c$ ($z(I)$ = optimal number of bins). How does one conclude $k\le2z(I)$?
  1. From $k-1<2z(I)$, since $k$ and $z(I)$ are integers
  2. From $k<2z(I)$, dividing by $\frac c2$
  3. From $z(I)\ge2$, which holds for every instance
  4. From $\sum_iw_i\le c$, which holds for every instance
Explanation. Dividing by $\frac c2$ gives $k-1<2z(I)$, i.e. $k<2z(I)+1$; integrality gives $k\le2z(I)$. One does not get $k<2z(I)$ directly.
oc-f-1166 · level ipotesi · notes
In bin packing, does the proposition «if an algorithm always produces solutions with the half-full property, then $\mathscr{A}(I)\le2z(I)$» apply to an algorithm that is NOT Any Fit but always produces solutions with that property?
  1. No: the proof uses the Any Fit condition
  2. Yes, but only in the limit $z(I)\to\infty$
  3. No: the items must also be sorted by weight
  4. Yes: the proof uses only the property of the solution
Explanation. The proof counts the bins filled beyond half and uses $\sum_iw_i\le z(I)c$: it does not look at how the solution was built. The Any Fit condition only serves to guarantee the property.
oc-f-1167 · level facile · notes
In bin packing, the instance $I_n$ has $c=n$ and $n$ items (with $n$ a multiple of $4$) of alternating weight $\frac n2$ (odd indices) and $2$ (even indices). Next Fit uses $\frac n2$ bins and the optimum is $\frac n4+1$. With $n=20$, what are $NF$, $z$ and the ratio?
  1. $NF=20$, $z=6$, ratio $\frac{10}3$
  2. $NF=10$, $z=10$, ratio $1$
  3. $NF=10$, $z=6$, ratio $\frac53$
  4. $NF=10$, $z=5$, ratio $2$
Explanation. $NF=\frac{20}2=10$ and $z=\frac{20}4+1=6$: the $10$ large items two by two and all small ones ($10\cdot2=20$) in one bin. $z=5$ forgets the bin of the small items. The ratio tends to $2$ only for $n\to\infty$.
oc-f-1168 · level facile · notes
In bin packing, two consecutive bins of Next Fit together weigh more than $c$; summing over disjoint pairs gives $z(I)\ge\lfloor k/2\rfloor+1$, where $k$ is the number of NF bins and $z(I)$ the optimum. If NF uses $k=7$ bins, what is the least value of $z(I)$?
  1. $2$
  2. $4$
  3. $3$
  4. $7$
Explanation. $\lfloor7/2\rfloor+1=4$: the $3$ pairs weigh more than $3c$, so more than $3$ bins are needed. $3$ forgets the $+1$; indeed $k\le2z(I)-1=7$.
oc-f-1169 · level teorema · notes
In bin packing, the instance $I_n$ has $c=n$ and alternating weights $\frac n2,2,\frac n2,2,\dots$; Worst Fit (bin with maximum residual among those where the item fits) uses $\frac n2$ bins on it. Why does WF never put two items of weight $\frac n2$ into the same bin?
  1. Every small item goes into the new bin, left with residual $\frac n2-2$
  2. Because two items of weight $\frac n2$ together exceed the capacity $c=n$
  3. Because Worst Fit does not satisfy the Any Fit condition
  4. Because the small items all end up in the first opened bin
Explanation. The newly opened bin has the maximum residual $\frac n2$, so it receives the small item and drops to $\frac n2-2<\frac n2$. Two large items would fit together ($\frac n2+\frac n2=n$): it is the WF rule that prevents it.
oc-f-1170 · level facile · notes
In bin packing Next Fit and Worst Fit have the same worst-case ratio, $r(NF)=r(WF)=2$. Are they therefore equivalent?
  1. Yes: the same ratio means the same solutions
  2. No: WF uses fewer bins than NF on every instance
  3. Yes: both keep a single bin open at a time
  4. No: only NF can leave many bins half full or less
Explanation. WF is Any Fit, hence it has the half-full property; NF can leave many bins with load $\le c/2$. The worst-case ratio looks only at the worst instance; «always fewer» is too strong.
oc-f-1171 · level facile · notes
For First Fit and Best Fit in bin packing, Johnson, Demers, Ullman, Garey and Graham (1974) proved $\mathscr{A}(I)\le\frac{17}{10}z(I)+2$; Dósa and Sgall (2013, 2014) proved $\mathscr{A}(I)\le\frac{17}{10}z(I)$. What changes between the two?
  1. The result now also holds for Worst Fit
  2. The result now holds only with sorted items
  3. The additive constant $+2$ was removed
  4. The factor went down from $2$ to $\frac{17}{10}$
Explanation. The factor $\frac{17}{10}$ was already there in 1974; the second result removes the $+2$, so it also holds for small $z(I)$. Worst Fit has $r(WF)=2$.
oc-f-1172 · level teorema · notes
In bin packing an Any Fit algorithm opens a new bin only if the item fits in none of the open ones. It is known that no Any Fit algorithm has worst-case ratio below $\frac{17}{10}$, and every Any Fit has ratio at most $2$. A new Any Fit chooses the bin at random: what is known about its ratio?
  1. Nothing: the Any Fit condition gives no guarantee
  2. It lies between $\frac{17}{10}$ and $2$
  3. It is exactly $2$, like Worst Fit
  4. It is at most $\frac{17}{10}$, like First Fit
Explanation. The Any Fit condition gives the half-full property, hence at most $2$; Johnson's lower bound $\frac{17}{10}$ holds for the whole class. The extremes are attained by FF/BF and by WF.
oc-f-1173 · level facile · notes
In bin packing First Fit and Best Fit have worst-case ratio $\frac{17}{10}$, Worst Fit $2$; all three scan the items in the given order and are Any Fit (they open a bin only if the item fits nowhere else). What explains the whole gap between $\frac{17}{10}$ and $2$?
  1. The rule for choosing among the bins where the item fits
  2. The order in which the items are scanned
  3. The number of bins kept open at the same time
  4. The additive constant $+2$ of the First Fit bound
Explanation. The three algorithms have the same order and keep all bins open; they differ only in the choice rule (first, minimum residual, maximum residual).

37. Vertex coloring: limits of approximation (25)

oc-f-126 · level teorema · notes
In the vertex coloring problem (VCP) on a graph $G$ with $n$ vertices the number of colors is minimized. If $P\neq NP$, which statement on the approximation of the VCP is correct?
  1. It has no polynomial $\alpha$-approximation for any constant $\alpha\ge 1$
  2. It has a polynomial $\frac43$-approximation, but none below $\frac43$
  3. It has a polynomial $2$-approximation, the greedy coloring
  4. It has a $(\Delta(G)+1)$-approximation for every graph, $DSATUR$
Explanation. The $\frac43$ theorem excludes the ratios below $\frac43$; Zuckerman's result also excludes $n^{1-\varepsilon}$, hence any constant. The bound $GC(I)\le\Delta(G)+1$ does not compare with $\chi(G)$.
oc-f-127 · level ipotesi · notes
In vertex coloring, let $\chi(G)$ be the chromatic number. The proof that no polynomial algorithm $\mathscr{A}$ has ratio $\mathscr{A}(I)/\chi(G)$ smaller than $\frac43$ on every graph (if $P\neq NP$) uses:
  1. that deciding whether $\chi(G)\le 2$ is NP-complete, and that the number of colors is an integer
  2. that deciding whether $\chi(G)\le 4$ is NP-complete, and that planar graphs have $\chi(G)\le 4$
  3. that the greedy coloring uses at most $\Delta(G)+1$ colors, and that the number of colors is an integer
  4. that deciding whether $\chi(G)\le 3$ is NP-complete, and that the number of colors is an integer
Explanation. With ratio $<\frac43$, a graph with $\chi\le 3$ would get at most $3$ colors and one with $\chi\ge 4$ at least $4$: 3-colorability would be decided in polynomial time. With $2$ colors the argument says nothing, because that test is easy.
oc-f-128 · level facile · notes
In an interval graph every vertex $v$ is an interval $[a_v,b_v]$ of the line, and two vertices are adjacent if the intervals intersect. With which vertex order is the greedy coloring (smallest free color) optimal?
  1. By non-increasing length $b_v-a_v$
  2. With any vertex order
  3. By non-decreasing left endpoint $a_v$
  4. By non-increasing right endpoint $b_v$
Explanation. With the intervals sorted by left endpoint, when an interval receives color $q$ there are $q$ intervals intersecting at $a_v$: the coloring uses $\omega(G)$ colors, hence it is optimal.
oc-f-129 · level facile · notes
A graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges is bipartite if and only if its chromatic number is $\chi(G)\le 2$. How much does it cost to decide whether $G$ is bipartite and, if so, to find a coloring with $2$ colors?
  1. $O(nm)$, with a shortest path from every vertex
  2. $O(n+m)$, with a breadth-first search
  3. $O(n^3)$, with linear programming
  4. $O(2^n)$: the problem is NP-complete
Explanation. A breadth-first search colors alternating two colors and finds an odd cycle if the graph is not bipartite. Already with $3$ colors the problem is NP-complete.
oc-f-511 · level ipotesi · notes
The proof that no polynomial algorithm for coloring has ratio $\mathscr{A}(I)/\chi(G)<\frac43$ on every graph (if $P\neq NP$) uses a hypothetical algorithm with ratio $<\frac43$. What would it do on a graph with $\chi(G)=3$?
  1. It would use exactly $4$ colors, which says nothing
  2. It would use $2$ colors, contradicting $\chi(G)=3$
  3. It would not terminate, because the problem is NP-hard
  4. It would use fewer than $4$ colors, i.e., $3$: it would decide in polynomial time whether $\chi(G)\le 3$
Explanation. With ratio $<\frac43$ and $\chi(G)=3$ the number of colors is $<4$, hence $3$; if $\chi(G)\ge 4$ it is at least $4$. 3-colorability, NP-complete, would be decided: only the integrality of $\chi$ is used.
oc-f-512 · level facile · notes
The same argument excluding ratios below $\frac43$ for coloring (distinguishing $3$ colors from $4$) does not exclude ratios below $\frac32$ by distinguishing $2$ colors from $3$. Why?
  1. Because $\frac32>\frac43$
  2. Because with $2$ colors the greedy coloring is always optimal
  3. Deciding whether $\chi(G)\le 2$ is polynomial (bipartite graphs), so no contradiction arises
  4. Because no graph has $\chi(G)=2$
Explanation. The argument needs an NP-complete decision problem; 2-colorability is decided by breadth-first search in $O(n+m)$.
oc-f-513 · level facile · notes
For vertex coloring, giving every vertex a different color is always feasible. Which ratio does this trivial algorithm guarantee, and what does Zuckerman's theorem say (if $P\neq NP$)?
  1. Ratio at most $\log n$; an algorithm with constant ratio exists
  2. Ratio at most $n$; no polynomial algorithm guarantees $n^{1-\varepsilon}$ for any $\varepsilon>0$
  3. Ratio at most $2$; no polynomial algorithm guarantees less than $2$
  4. Ratio at most $\Delta+1$; no polynomial algorithm guarantees less than $\frac43$
Explanation. $n$ colors against $\chi(G)\ge 1$ give ratio at most $n$. The theorem says one cannot do substantially better: in particular the problem has no constant ratio.
oc-f-514 · level facile · notes
Every planar graph with $n\ge 3$ vertices has at most $3n-6$ edges and hence a vertex of degree at most $5$. How many edges does a planar graph with $n=10$ vertices have at most?
  1. $24$
  2. $30$
  3. $45$
  4. $27$
Explanation. $3\cdot 10-6=24$. The sum of the degrees is at most $48<6n$, so some vertex has degree at most $5$: it is the key step of the five color theorem.
oc-f-515 · level facile · notes
On planar graphs, the algorithm $PL$ colors with at most $5$ colors in polynomial time (Heawood's theorem). Which guarantee does it have with respect to the chromatic number $\chi(G)$, if the graph has at least one edge?
  1. Relative: $PL(I)/\chi(G)\le\frac43$
  2. None: planar graphs are as hard as all others
  3. Additive: $PL(I)-\chi(G)\le 0$, i.e., $PL$ is exact
  4. Additive: $PL(I)-\chi(G)\le 2$, recognizing separately the graphs with $\chi(G)\le 2$
Explanation. With at least one edge $\chi(G)\ge 2$; bipartite graphs are recognized and colored in $O(n+m)$, and on the others $\chi(G)\ge 3$, hence $5-\chi(G)\le 2$. With the four color theorem the error drops to $1$.
oc-f-516 · level facile · notes
The greedy coloring uses at most $\Delta(G)+1$ colors, with $\Delta(G)$ the maximum degree. On graphs of maximum degree at most $3$ with at least one edge, which ratio with respect to $\chi(G)$ does it guarantee?
  1. At most $\frac43$, because $\chi(G)\ge 3$
  2. Exactly $1$: on these graphs it is optimal
  3. At most $2$, because it uses at most $4$ colors and $\chi(G)\ge 2$
  4. At most $4$, because it uses at most $4$ colors and $\chi(G)\ge 1$
Explanation. $\frac{\Delta+1}{\chi(G)}\le\frac42=2$: on bounded-degree graphs the greedy coloring has a constant ratio, while on general graphs no polynomial algorithm has one.
oc-f-517 · level facile · notes
Interval graph with vertices $[1,4]$, $[2,5]$, $[3,6]$, $[7,8]$ (two vertices adjacent if the intervals intersect). The greedy coloring with the vertices by non-decreasing left endpoint uses $\omega(G)$ colors. How many colors are needed?
  1. $1$
  2. $3$
  3. $4$
  4. $2$
Explanation. The first three intervals overlap at the point $3.5$ and form a clique, so $\omega=3$; $[7,8]$ intersects none and reuses color $1$. The greedy gives $3=\chi(G)$.
oc-f-518 · level facile · notes
Zuckerman's theorem excludes, if $P\neq NP$, the ratios $n^{1-\varepsilon}$ for coloring. Why does it also exclude every constant ratio $\alpha$?
  1. On graphs with large enough $n$, $\alpha<n^{1-\varepsilon}$: an $\alpha$-approximation would have ratio below the forbidden threshold
  2. Because every constant is below $\frac43$
  3. Because constant ratios hold only on planar graphs
  4. It does not: $\alpha$-approximations with large $\alpha$ exist
Explanation. For fixed $\varepsilon$, when $n>\alpha^{1/(1-\varepsilon)}$ we have $\alpha<n^{1-\varepsilon}$; the small graphs, finitely many, are solved optimally in constant time.
oc-f-794 · level facile · notes
In the chapter on the limits of coloring approximation, $\mathscr{A}(I)$ is the number of colors of an algorithm and $\chi(G)$ the chromatic number. Which ratio is studied?
  1. $\mathscr{A}(I)/\chi(G)\ge1$
  2. $\chi(G)/\mathscr{A}(I)\ge1$
  3. $\mathscr{A}(I)-\chi(G)$, always $\le1$
  4. $\omega(G)/\mathscr{A}(I)$
Explanation. Coloring is a minimization problem: the algorithm uses at least $\chi(G)$ colors, and the ratio has the algorithm in the numerator.
oc-f-795 · level facile · notes
The Petersen graph has $n=10$, $m=15$, maximum degree $\Delta=3$ and contains cycles of length $5$. Which consequences does this have for coloring?
  1. It is bipartite, hence $\chi=2$
  2. $\chi=\Delta+1=4$ always
  3. $\chi=n/2=5$
  4. It is not bipartite, hence $\chi\ge3$; the bound $\Delta+1$ gives $\chi\le4$
Explanation. An odd cycle prevents $2$-coloring; greedy coloring guarantees at most $\Delta+1=4$ colors. Actually $\chi=3$.
oc-f-898 · level facile · notes
The VCP is not approximable in general, but on some graph classes it is solved exactly in polynomial time. Which of these is one of those classes, and with which method?
  1. Bipartite graphs: a breadth-first search finds a $2$-coloring or an odd cycle
  2. Complete graphs: $2$ colors are needed
  3. Graphs with a triangle: $3$ colors suffice
  4. All graphs with $n\le100$
Explanation. A graph with at least one edge is $2$-colorable if and only if it has no odd cycle, and the search decides it in linear time. Complete graphs need $n$ colors.
oc-f-1174 · level facile · notes
Vertex coloring (VCP, minimum number of colors $\chi(G)$) is not approximable in general. On which of the classes bipartite, bounded maximum degree, planar, interval graphs is it solved exactly in polynomial time, and on which is there only a guarantee?
  1. Exact on bipartite and interval; guarantee on bounded degree and planar
  2. Exact on all four classes
  3. Exact on bipartite and planar; guarantee on interval and bounded degree
  4. Exact on bounded degree and interval; guarantee on bipartite and planar
Explanation. Bipartite: breadth-first search; interval: greedy by left endpoint, optimal. Bounded degree: $\Delta+1$ colors; planar: additive error at most $2$ (or $1$ with four colors). Deciding $\chi\le3$ stays NP-complete on planar graphs.
oc-f-1175 · level facile · notes
If $P\neq NP$ no polynomial algorithm for vertex coloring has ratio $\mathscr{A}(I)/\chi(G)<\frac43$ on all graphs. Why does this not prevent an exact polynomial algorithm on bipartite graphs?
  1. Because on bipartite graphs the chromatic number is $\chi(G)=1$
  2. Because the theorem holds only under $P=NP$
  3. Because on bipartite graphs coloring becomes a maximization problem
  4. The theorem is about all graphs; the hard ones are not bipartite
Explanation. A bound on the worst case over all graphs does not hold on a restricted class: the reductions use graphs with $\chi\ge3$. A bipartite graph with an edge has $\chi=2$.
oc-f-1176 · level facile · notes
To decide whether $\chi(G)\le2$ one runs a breadth-first search from vertex $1$ and colors every vertex by the parity of its level $\ell(v)$. Graph with edges $\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{2,4\},\{3,5\},\{4,5\},\{4,6\},\{5,6\}$: which edge joins two levels of equal parity, and what does it certify?
  1. None: the graph is bipartite and $\chi=2$
  2. $\{5,6\}$: a closed walk of length $4$, hence $\chi\ge3$
  3. $\{4,5\}$: a closed walk of length $5$, hence $\chi\ge3$
  4. $\{4,6\}$: a closed walk of length $6$, hence $\chi\ge3$
Explanation. Levels: $1\to0$; $2,3\to1$; $4,5\to2$; $6\to3$. Only $\{4,5\}$ joins two even levels: with the tree paths it gives $\ell(4)+\ell(5)+1=5$, the cycle $1,2,4,5,3$. The edges $\{4,6\}$ and $\{5,6\}$ join levels of different parity.
oc-f-1177 · level facile · notes
A graph $G$ is bipartite if $\chi(G)\le2$, i.e. if its vertices split into two stable sets; by König this happens if and only if $G$ has no cycles of odd length. What is $\chi(G)$ for a graph with at least one edge and no odd cycles?
  1. It depends on the maximum degree $\Delta(G)$
  2. Exactly $2$
  3. $1$ or $2$, depending on the graph
  4. Exactly $3$
Explanation. Without odd cycles $\chi\le2$; an edge requires two colors, hence $\chi=2$. $\chi=1$ holds only for graphs without edges.
oc-f-1178 · level facile · notes
The greedy coloring $GC$ scans the vertices in a given order and gives each one the smallest color not used by its already colored neighbors; it uses at most $\Delta(G)+1$ colors ($\Delta$ = maximum degree). On the star with one center and $9$ leaves, how many colors does $GC$ use and what is $\Delta+1$?
  1. $2$ colors with every order; $\Delta+1=10$
  2. $10$ colors with every order; $\Delta+1=10$
  3. From $2$ to $10$ colors depending on the order; $\Delta+1=10$
  4. $2$ colors with every order; $\Delta+1=9$
Explanation. The leaves are pairwise non-adjacent: they all take the same color and the center the other one, in any order. The bound $\Delta+1$ does not compare $GC$ with $\chi$: here it is $10$ against $\chi=2$.
oc-f-1179 · level teorema · notes
Greedy coloring uses at most $\Delta(G)+1$ colors on every graph ($\Delta$ = maximum degree). On which connected graphs is the bound attained with any order, and what does Brooks' theorem say about the others?
  1. Trees and even cycles; for the others $\chi(G)\le\Delta(G)-1$
  2. Planar graphs; for the others $\chi(G)\le4$
  3. Bipartite graphs; for the others $\chi(G)=\Delta(G)+1$
  4. Complete graphs and odd cycles; for the others $\chi(G)\le\Delta(G)$
Explanation. $K_n$ has $\chi=n=\Delta+1$ and an odd cycle has $\chi=3=\Delta+1$. Brooks (1941): a connected graph that is neither complete nor an odd cycle has $\chi\le\Delta$, and such a coloring is found in linear time.
oc-f-1180 · level teorema · notes
On planar graphs the four-color algorithm gives a coloring with additive error $\mathscr{A}(I)-\chi(G)\le1$. Deciding whether a planar graph has $\chi(G)\le3$ is NP-complete. What follows, if $P\neq NP$?
  1. The minimum possible additive error on planar graphs is $2$
  2. On planar graphs no algorithm has a constant ratio
  3. The error $1$ cannot drop to $0$ and $\frac43$ is the best ratio on planar graphs
  4. On planar graphs there is an exact algorithm, but not polynomial in $n$
Explanation. An exact algorithm would decide $\chi\le3$; and a ratio $<\frac43$ would distinguish $3$ colors from $4$. The four-color theorem still gives the ratio $\frac43$.
oc-f-1181 · level ipotesi · notes
Heawood's theorem (every planar graph can be colored with $5$ colors) is proved by induction: remove a vertex $v$, color $G-v$ and put $v$ back. Why is $v$ chosen of degree at most $5$?
  1. Because every planar graph has maximum degree at most $5$
  2. Its neighbors use at most $5$ colors; if all, a swap frees one
  3. Because the vertices of degree at most $5$ form a stable set
  4. Because the graph $G-v$ then becomes bipartite
Explanation. It exists by the lemma $m\le3n-6$. With at most $4$ colors among the neighbors the fifth is free; with $5$, swapping two colors in a component (Kempe chain) frees one. The maximum degree of a planar graph can be large (a star).
oc-f-1182 · level facile · notes
In an interval graph every vertex $v$ is a closed interval $[a_v,b_v]$ and two vertices are adjacent if the intervals intersect. Greedy coloring (each vertex gets the smallest color not used by its already colored neighbors) is optimal if it scans the vertices in which order?
  1. By non-decreasing left endpoint $a_v$
  2. In any order: on interval graphs it is always optimal
  3. By non-increasing length $b_v-a_v$
  4. By non-increasing number of intersections (degree)
Explanation. With the order by $a_v$, the already colored neighbors of $v$ all contain the point $a_v$: with $v$ they form a clique, so the colors are at most $\omega(G)$. With other orders greedy can use one more color.
oc-f-1183 · level facile · notes
Interval graph with $[1,4],[2,6],[3,5],[5,8],[7,10],[9,12]$ (vertices $1,\dots,6$, adjacent if the intervals intersect). Greedy coloring uses $3$ colors in the order $1,2,3,4,5,6$ and $4$ colors in the order $1,2,3,5,4,6$. What does the example show?
  1. The chromatic number of this graph is $\chi(G)=4$
  2. The given graph is not an interval graph
  3. Greedy coloring is never optimal on these graphs
  4. Optimality is guaranteed only with the left-endpoint order
Explanation. $\{1,2,3\}$ contains the point $3$, hence $\omega=\chi=3$: the left-endpoint order is optimal, the other uses one more color (vertex $4$ has neighbors $2,3,5$ with colors $1,2,3$).

38. Maximum clique: limits of approximation (21)

oc-f-130 · level teorema · notes
In the strong product $G\boxtimes H$ the vertices are the pairs $(u,x)$, and two distinct pairs are adjacent if each component is equal or adjacent in its own graph. With $\omega$ the cardinality of a maximum clique, which statement is correct?
  1. $\omega(G\boxtimes H)=\max\{\omega(G),\omega(H)\}$
  2. $\omega(G\boxtimes H)=\omega(G)^{\omega(H)}$
  3. $\omega(G\boxtimes H)=\omega(G)\,\omega(H)$
  4. $\omega(G\boxtimes H)=\omega(G)+\omega(H)$
Explanation. The product of two cliques is a clique of the strong product, and a clique of the product has at most $|p(K)|\cdot\max_u|K_u|$ vertices: the clique number multiplies.
oc-f-131 · level ipotesi · notes
In the maximum clique problem (MCP), with $\omega(G)$ the cardinality of a maximum clique and $G\boxtimes G$ the strong product of $G$ with itself, the theorem «a constant $\alpha$-approximation for the MCP would give a $\beta$-approximation for every $\beta>1$» is proved using:
  1. $\omega(G)=\alpha(\overline{G})$; from a stable set of $\overline{G}$ one extracts a clique of $G$; the half-full property
  2. $\omega(G\boxtimes G)=\omega(G)^2$; from a clique $K$ of the product one extracts a clique of $G$ with at least $\sqrt{|K|}$ vertices; a constant number of products
  3. $\omega(G\boxtimes G)=2\,\omega(G)$; from a clique $K$ of the product one extracts a clique of $G$ with at least $|K|/2$ vertices; a constant number of products
  4. $\omega(G\boxtimes G)=\omega(G)^2$; from a clique $K$ of the product one extracts a clique of $G$ with at least $\sqrt{|K|}$ vertices; $\log n$ products
Explanation. Applying the algorithm to $G\boxtimes G$ gives ratio $\sqrt\alpha$ on $G$; repeating a constant number of times brings the ratio below any $\beta>1$. A number of products growing with $n$ would not be polynomial.
oc-f-132 · level facile · notes
For the maximum clique problem (MCP) and the maximum stable set problem (MSSP) on a graph $G$ with $n$ vertices, with $\omega(G)$ the cardinality of a maximum clique, which statement on planar graphs is correct?
  1. $\omega(G)\le 4$ and the MCP is solved in $O(n^4)$, while the MSSP stays NP-hard
  2. $\omega(G)\le 4$ and the MCP is solved in $O(n^4)$; so is the MSSP, through the complement
  3. $\omega(G)\le 4$, but the MCP stays NP-hard like the MSSP
  4. $\omega(G)\le 5$ and the MCP is solved in $O(n^5)$, while the MSSP stays NP-hard
Explanation. A clique of a planar graph has at most $4$ vertices, so it is enough to enumerate the subsets of at most $4$ vertices. The complement of a planar graph is not planar: the easy case does not transfer to the MSSP.
oc-f-133 · level facile · notes
A graph has $n=24$ vertices and maximum degree $\Delta(G)=5$. A stable set is maximal if no vertex can be added to it. At least how many vertices does every maximal stable set have?
  1. $5$
  2. $6$
  3. $20$
  4. $4$
Explanation. A maximal stable set $S$ has $|S|\ge\frac{n}{\Delta(G)+1}=\frac{24}{6}=4$: every vertex is in $S$ or adjacent to a vertex of $S$, and every vertex of $S$ covers at most $\Delta+1$ vertices.
oc-f-519 · level facile · notes
In the strong product $G\boxtimes H$ the vertices are the pairs $(u,x)$ with $u$ a vertex of $G$ and $x$ of $H$. How many vertices does $G\boxtimes G$ have if $G$ has $5$ vertices, and what is its maximum clique if $\omega(G)=2$?
  1. $25$ vertices, $\omega(G\boxtimes G)=8$
  2. $25$ vertices, $\omega(G\boxtimes G)=4$
  3. $10$ vertices, $\omega(G\boxtimes G)=4$
  4. $25$ vertices, $\omega(G\boxtimes G)=2$
Explanation. The vertices are $5\cdot 5=25$, and $\omega(G\boxtimes H)=\omega(G)\,\omega(H)$: $2\cdot 2=4$. The product is built in polynomial time.
oc-f-520 · level facile · notes
From a clique $K$ of the strong product $G\boxtimes G$ a clique of $G$ is obtained: either the projection $p(K)$ (the first components) or the largest fibre (the second components with the same first one). If $|K|=16$, how many vertices does the obtained clique of $G$ have at least?
  1. $4$
  2. $8$
  3. $16$
  4. $2$
Explanation. $|K|\le|p(K)|\cdot\max_u|K_u|$, so the larger of the two factors is at least $\sqrt{|K|}=4$. It is the constructive step of the amplification.
oc-f-521 · level facile · notes
In the maximum clique problem, an algorithm with ratio $\omega(G)/\mathscr{A}(I)\le\alpha$ applied to $G\boxtimes G$ gives a clique $K$ of the product, from which a clique of $G$ with at least $\sqrt{|K|}$ vertices is obtained. Which ratio follows on $G$ with $\alpha=4$?
  1. $4$
  2. $16$
  3. $\frac43$
  4. $2$
Explanation. $|K|\ge\omega(G)^2/\alpha$, so the obtained clique has at least $\omega(G)/\sqrt\alpha$ vertices: ratio $\sqrt 4=2$. Repeating the products the ratio drops below every constant larger than $1$.
oc-f-522 · level facile · notes
In the maximum clique problem, a single vertex is always a clique. Which ratio $\omega(G)/\mathscr{A}(I)$ does the algorithm returning one vertex guarantee, and what does the Håstad–Zuckerman theorem say (if $P\neq NP$)?
  1. At most $\Delta+1$; a polynomial algorithm with ratio $\frac43$ exists
  2. At most $\sqrt n$; a PTAS exists
  3. At most $n$; no polynomial algorithm guarantees $n^{1-\varepsilon}$ for any $\varepsilon>0$
  4. At most $2$; no polynomial algorithm guarantees less than $2$
Explanation. $\omega(G)\le n$, so one vertex gives ratio at most $n$; the theorem says one cannot do substantially better, and in particular excludes every constant ratio.
oc-f-523 · level facile · notes
In the maximum clique problem on graphs of maximum degree $\Delta$, a maximum clique is found exactly in $O(n\,2^{\Delta}\Delta^2)$ time, examining the subsets of the neighbours of every vertex. When is this time polynomial in $n$?
  1. Only on planar graphs
  2. For every fixed $\Delta$, and even when $\Delta\le\log_2 n$
  3. Only for $\Delta\le 3$
  4. Never: $2^{\Delta}$ is always exponential
Explanation. With $\Delta\le\log_2 n$ we have $2^{\Delta}\le n$, and the time is $O(n^2\log^2 n)$. A clique contains a vertex and some of its neighbours, so examining the $2^{\Delta}$ subsets of the neighbourhood is enough.
oc-f-524 · level facile · notes
For the maximum stable set on a graph with maximum degree $\Delta(G)$, the greedy adding vertices while possible finds a maximal stable set $S$ with $|S|\ge\frac{n}{\Delta(G)+1}$. Which ratio $\alpha(G)/|S|$ does it guarantee with $\Delta(G)=3$?
  1. At most $4$
  2. At most $3$
  3. At most $\frac43$
  4. No constant ratio
Explanation. $\alpha(G)\le n$ and $|S|\ge\frac n4$ give $\alpha(G)/|S|\le 4=\Delta+1$. Every added vertex excludes at most $\Delta$ neighbours.
oc-f-525 · level facile · notes
The maximum clique on $G$ is the maximum stable set on the complement $\overline G$, so the two problems have the same approximation limits on general graphs. Why are the easy special cases of the clique (planar graphs, bounded degree) not easy for the stable set?
  1. Because the maximum stable set is always polynomial
  2. Because the complement of a planar graph is still planar
  3. Because on planar graphs $\alpha(G)=\omega(G)$
  4. The complement of a planar or bounded-degree graph is dense: on the original class the stable set stays NP-hard
Explanation. Passing to the complement changes the class of graphs. On planar graphs the maximum stable set stays NP-hard, but it is approximable (it even has a PTAS).
oc-f-526 · level facile · notes
In the maximum clique problem on a planar graph with $n$ vertices, why is it enough to examine the subsets of at most $4$ vertices?
  1. Because every planar graph is bipartite
  2. Because planar graphs have at most $4n$ edges
  3. Every planar graph has $\omega(G)\le 4$ ($K_5$ is not planar): $O(n^4)$ subsets are checked
  4. Because every planar graph has maximum degree at most $4$
Explanation. A clique of $5$ vertices would be a $K_5$, which is not planar; the subsets of at most $4$ vertices are $O(n^4)$ and each is checked in constant time.
oc-f-796 · level facile · notes
In the chapter on the limits of maximum clique approximation, $\mathscr{A}(I)$ is the number of vertices of the clique returned by an algorithm and $\omega(G)$ the clique number. Which relations hold?
  1. $\mathscr{A}(I)\le\omega(G)$ and $\omega(G)/\mathscr{A}(I)\ge1$
  2. $\mathscr{A}(I)\ge\omega(G)$
  3. $\mathscr{A}(I)/\omega(G)\ge1$
  4. $\mathscr{A}(I)=\omega(G)$
Explanation. Maximum clique is a maximization problem: the optimum goes in the numerator so that the ratio is at least $1$.
oc-f-797 · level facile · notes
The graph $G$ is the cycle $1,2,\dots,7,1$ with the chord $\{1,3\}$, with $\omega(G)=3$. The strong product $G\boxtimes G$ has $49$ vertices. What is $\omega(G\boxtimes G)$, and by which clique is it attained?
  1. $6$, by $\{1,2,3\}\times\{1,2\}$
  2. $3$, by $\{1,2,3\}\times\{1\}$
  3. $49$, by all vertices
  4. $9$, by $\{1,2,3\}\times\{1,2,3\}$
Explanation. In the strong product $\omega(G\boxtimes H)=\omega(G)\,\omega(H)$: the product of two cliques is a clique. It is the tool that amplifies a constant approximation ratio.
oc-f-1184 · level facile · notes
In maximum clique, an $\alpha$-approximation algorithm ($\omega(G)/\mathscr{A}(I)\le\alpha$) applied to the strong product $G\boxtimes G$ gives a $\sqrt\alpha$-approximation; repeating $t$ times gives the ratio $\alpha^{1/2^t}$ on a graph with $n^{2^t}$ vertices. With $\alpha=16$, what is the minimum $t$ reaching ratio $2$?
  1. $t=2$, on a graph with $n^4$ vertices
  2. $t=1$, on a graph with $n^2$ vertices
  3. $t=3$, on a graph with $n^8$ vertices
  4. $t=2$, on a graph with $2n^2$ vertices
Explanation. $16^{1/2}=4$, $16^{1/4}=2$: $2$ steps are needed, and the graph has $n^{2^2}=n^4$ vertices. With $t=1$ the ratio is $4$; $t=3$ suffices but is not the minimum.
oc-f-1185 · level facile · notes
For maximum clique ($\omega(G)$ = maximum cardinality of a clique, $n$ vertices), the theorem of Håstad (1999) and Zuckerman (2007) excludes the ratio $\omega(G)/\mathscr{A}(I)\le n^{1-\varepsilon}$ for every $\varepsilon>0$. What distinguishes the two contributions?
  1. The bound: $n^{1/2}$ for Håstad, $n^{1-\varepsilon}$ for Zuckerman
  2. The problem: clique for Håstad, stable set for Zuckerman
  3. The class: planar graphs for Håstad, all graphs for Zuckerman
  4. The assumption: $NP\neq ZPP$ for Håstad, $P\neq NP$ for Zuckerman
Explanation. The bound $n^{1-\varepsilon}$ is the same; Håstad obtains it assuming that NP problems cannot be solved in randomized polynomial time, Zuckerman under $P\neq NP$ alone.
oc-f-1186 · level teorema · notes
For maximum clique the following hold, if $P\neq NP$: (i) no polynomial algorithm has ratio $\omega(G)/\mathscr{A}(I)\le n^{1-\varepsilon}$ (Håstad, Zuckerman); (ii) a constant ratio would give every constant ratio (strong product). What follows?
  1. The problem has ratio $2$ but not a PTAS
  2. The problem has ratio $n^{1/2}$ but not a constant one
  3. The problem has neither a constant ratio nor a PTAS
  4. The problem has a PTAS but not an FPTAS
Explanation. (i) excludes every constant (for $n>\alpha^2$ one would have $\alpha<n^{1/2}$); a PTAS would in particular give a constant ratio. Also $n^{1/2}=n^{1-1/2}$ is excluded by (i).
oc-f-1187 · level facile · notes
Every planar graph with $n\ge3$ vertices has at most $3n-6$ edges. In maximum clique, why does this imply that a planar graph contains no clique with $5$ vertices?
  1. $K_5$ has more than $3\cdot5=15$ edges
  2. $K_5$ has $10$ edges, more than $3\cdot5-6=9$
  3. $K_5$ has no vertex of degree at most $5$
  4. $K_5$ has $5$ vertices of degree $4$, more than $3$
Explanation. A subgraph of a planar graph is planar, and $K_5$ violates the bound: $10>9$. Its vertices have degree $4\le5$, and $10<15$.
oc-f-1188 · level facile · notes
In maximum clique on a graph with $n$ vertices and maximum degree $\Delta$, enumerating the subsets of $N(v)$ for every vertex $v$ takes time $O(n\,2^{\Delta}\Delta^2)$. When is this time polynomial in $n$?
  1. For fixed $\Delta$, and also for $\Delta\le\log_2n$
  2. Only for graphs with $\Delta\le3$, like cubic ones
  3. Never: the factor $2^{\Delta}$ stays exponential
  4. For every graph with $\Delta\le\sqrt n$
Explanation. With $\Delta\le\log_2n$ one has $2^\Delta\le n$, and the time is $O(n^2\log^2n)$. With $\Delta=\sqrt n$ the factor $2^{\sqrt n}$ is not polynomial.
oc-f-1189 · level facile · notes
In maximum clique on bounded-degree graphs, for every vertex $v$ one examines all $2^{\deg(v)}$ subsets $S$ of $N(v)$ (neighbors of $v$) and keeps the largest $\{v\}\cup S$ that is a clique. On a graph with degrees $3,2,2,3,1,1$, how many subsets are examined in total?
  1. $64$
  2. $12$
  3. $18$
  4. $28$
Explanation. $2^3+2^2+2^2+2^3+2^1+2^1=8+4+4+8+2+2=28$. $64=2^6$ are the subsets of all vertices, $12$ the sum of the degrees.
oc-f-1190 · level facile · notes
In the strong product $G\boxtimes G$, for a clique $K$ the projection $p(K)$ (first components) and every fiber $K_u$ (second components with first component $u$) are cliques of $G$. An algorithm returns $K=\{1,2,3\}\times\{4,5\}$, with $|K|=6$. Which clique of $G$ is obtained, and why is it enough?
  1. $K$ itself: it is already a clique of $G$
  2. $\{1,2,3,4,5\}$: it joins projection and fiber
  3. $p(K)=\{1,2,3\}$: it has $3\ge\sqrt6$ vertices
  4. The fiber $\{4,5\}$: it has $2\ge\sqrt6$ vertices
Explanation. The largest among projection and fibers has at least $\sqrt{|K|}$ vertices, because the product of the two sizes is at least $|K|$: here $3\ge\sqrt6\approx2.45$, while $2<\sqrt6$. $K$ is made of pairs, not of vertices of $G$.

39. The TSP: the general case and the metric case (28)

oc-f-134 · level teorema · notes
For the TSP (shortest tour visiting all cities), $DT$ is the double tree algorithm and $CH$ Christofides' algorithm; the TSP is metric if the triangle inequality holds. If $P\neq NP$, which statement is correct?
  1. The general TSP has no constant approximation; on the metric TSP $DT$ has ratio $\frac32$ and $CH$ ratio $2$
  2. The general TSP has a $2$-approximation, $DT$; on the metric TSP $CH$ has ratio $\frac32$
  3. The general TSP has no constant approximation; on the metric TSP the nearest neighbour has ratio $\frac32$
  4. The general TSP has no constant approximation; on the metric TSP $DT$ has ratio $2$ and $CH$ ratio $\frac32$
Explanation. A constant guarantee on the general TSP would decide the Hamiltonian cycle problem; with the triangle inequality $DT$ and $CH$ have ratios $2$ and $\frac32$, both tight.
oc-f-135 · level ipotesi · notes
In the metric TSP, the double tree algorithm $DT$ doubles a minimum spanning tree $T$ (of length $d(T)$), follows an Eulerian circuit of it and skips the cities already visited. With $z(I)$ the length of the optimal tour, which facts are needed to prove $DT(I)\le 2\,z(I)$?
  1. $d(T)\le z(I)/2$; the Eulerian circuit of the doubled tree has length $2d(T)$; distances are symmetric
  2. The nearest neighbour tour has length at most $2z(I)$; every city has even degree; distances are symmetric
  3. $d(T)\le z(I)$; the Eulerian circuit of the doubled tree has length $2d(T)$; shortcuts do not lengthen the walk
  4. $d(T)\le z(I)$; the minimum perfect matching on the odd-degree cities costs at most $z(I)/2$; shortcuts do not lengthen the walk
Explanation. Removing an edge from the optimal tour gives a spanning tree, hence $d(T)\le z(I)$; shortcutting uses the triangle inequality. The matching is needed for $CH$.
oc-f-136 · level ipotesi · notes
In the metric TSP, Christofides' algorithm $CH$ adds to a minimum spanning tree $T$ a minimum perfect matching $M$ on the odd-degree cities of $T$, follows an Eulerian circuit of $T\cup M$ and skips the cities already visited. Which facts are needed to prove $CH(I)\le\frac32\,z(I)$?
  1. $d(T)\le z(I)$; the doubled tree circuit has length $2d(T)$; distances are symmetric
  2. $d(T)\le z(I)$; $d(M)\le z(I)/2$; shortcuts do not lengthen the Eulerian circuit of $T\cup M$
  3. $d(T)\le z(I)/2$; $d(M)\le z(I)$; shortcuts do not lengthen the Eulerian circuit of $T\cup M$
  4. $d(T)\le z(I)$; $d(M)\le d(T)$; the odd-degree cities of $T$ are odd in number
Explanation. The Eulerian circuit of $T\cup M$ has length $d(T)+d(M)\le z(I)+\frac{z(I)}2$; the odd-degree cities of a tree are even in number, so the perfect matching exists.
oc-f-527 · level ipotesi · notes
The proof that the general TSP has no polynomial $\alpha$-approximation (if $P\neq NP$) starts from a graph $G$ asking whether a Hamiltonian cycle exists. Which TSP instance is built?
  1. Euclidean distances between the vertices of $G$ drawn in the plane
  2. Distance $2$ on the edges and $1$ on non-adjacent pairs
  3. Distance $1$ on the edges of $G$ and $\alpha n+1$ on non-adjacent pairs: an $\alpha$-approximation would separate tours of length $n$ from the others
  4. Distance $1$ on all pairs: every tour is optimal
Explanation. If $G$ is Hamiltonian the optimum is $n$ and the algorithm returns at most $\alpha n$, hence only edges of $G$; otherwise every tour uses a non-adjacent pair and exceeds $\alpha n$. An NP-complete problem would be decided.
oc-f-528 · level facile · notes
A TSP instance is metric if $d_{ij}\le d_{ik}+d_{kj}$ for all triples. Which of the following families of instances is always metric?
  1. Instances with distances drawn at random in $[1,100]$
  2. Cities in the plane with Euclidean distances
  3. Instances with arbitrary integer distances
  4. Instances with $d_{ij}\in\{1,2\}$ and $d_{ij}\ne d_{ji}$
Explanation. The Euclidean distance satisfies the triangle inequality. Symmetric distances $1$ and $2$ are metric, but here they are asymmetric; random distances can violate it.
oc-f-529 · level facile · notes
The general TSP has no constant approximation (if $P\neq NP$), the metric TSP does. What is known about the complexity of the metric TSP?
  1. It stays NP-hard, but admits algorithms with constant ratio such as $2$ or $\frac32$
  2. It is polynomial, because the triangle inequality allows shortcuts
  3. It is polynomial on Euclidean instances, NP-hard on the others
  4. It has no constant approximation either
Explanation. The metric does not make the problem easy, but it allows turning closed walks into tours without making them longer: it is the basis of the double tree and Christofides.
oc-f-530 · level facile · notes
In the metric TSP, the double tree algorithm $DT$ computes a minimum spanning tree $T$, doubles its edges, follows an Eulerian circuit and skips the cities already visited. If $d(T)=7$, what is known about the $DT$ tour and the optimal tour $z(I)$?
  1. $DT(I)=14$ and $z(I)=7$
  2. $DT(I)\le 7$ and $z(I)\ge 14$
  3. $DT(I)\le\frac{21}{2}$ and $z(I)\ge 7$
  4. $DT(I)\le 14$ and $z(I)\ge 7$
Explanation. The Eulerian circuit of the doubled tree has length $2d(T)=14$ and shortcuts do not lengthen it; removing an edge from the optimal tour gives a tree, so $d(T)\le z(I)$.
oc-f-531 · level facile · notes
In the Christofides algorithm for the metric TSP, a minimum perfect matching on the cities of odd degree in the minimum spanning tree $T$ is added to $T$. In a star with a centre and $3$ leaves (degree of the centre $3$, of the leaves $1$), how many such cities are there?
  1. $1$
  2. $0$
  3. $4$
  4. $3$
Explanation. The centre has degree $3$ and the three leaves degree $1$: all four are odd. In every graph the number of odd-degree vertices is even, so the perfect matching exists.
oc-f-532 · level ipotesi · notes
For every TSP instance, metric or not, the length $d(T)$ of a minimum spanning tree is at most the length $z(I)$ of the optimal tour. Which argument proves it?
  1. Doubling the tree gives the optimal tour
  2. Removing an edge from the optimal tour gives a path through all cities, i.e., a spanning tree, of length at most $z(I)$
  3. The triangle inequality allows shortening the tree
  4. The optimal tour always contains the minimum spanning tree
Explanation. The path is a spanning tree, and $T$ is the shortest spanning tree; distances are positive, so removing an edge does not lengthen. The metric is not needed.
oc-f-533 · level ipotesi · notes
In the metric TSP, let $O$ be an even set of cities and $M$ a minimum perfect matching of $O$. Why is $d(M)\le z(I)/2$?
  1. The optimal tour, shortcut to the cities of $O$ only, splits into two perfect matchings of $O$ with alternate edges; the shorter one has length at most $z(I)/2$
  2. Because $M$ has half the edges of the optimal tour
  3. Because every edge of $M$ is shorter than every edge of the tour
  4. Because $M$ is contained in the minimum spanning tree
Explanation. By the triangle inequality the tour restricted to $O$ is not longer than $z(I)$; its edges, taken alternately, form two perfect matchings, and the cheaper one is at most half.
oc-f-534 · level facile · notes
In the metric TSP, the Christofides algorithm uses a minimum spanning tree $T$ with $d(T)=10$ and a minimum perfect matching $M$ with $d(M)=4$, and returns a tour of length $CH(I)=14$. What is known about the optimal tour $z(I)$?
  1. $z(I)=14$
  2. $\frac{28}{3}\le z(I)\le 10$
  3. $z(I)\ge 14$
  4. $10\le z(I)\le 14$
Explanation. The $CH$ tour is feasible, so $z(I)\le 14$; $d(T)\le z(I)$ gives $z(I)\ge 10$ (stronger than $14/\frac32\approx 9.33$ and than $2d(M)=8$).
oc-f-535 · level facile · notes
In the metric TSP there are instances $I_n$, with $n\ge 5$ odd, on which the double tree $DT$ has ratio exactly $\frac{2n}{n+2}$. What is it with $n=7$, and what does it tend to?
  1. $\frac{7}{9}$, and it tends to $1$
  2. $2$ for every $n$
  3. $\frac{14}{9}$, and it tends to $2$
  4. $\frac{14}{9}$, and it tends to $\frac32$
Explanation. $\frac{2\cdot 7}{7+2}=\frac{14}{9}\approx 1.56$; as $n\to+\infty$ the ratio tends to $2$, so the guarantee $2$ of $DT$ cannot be improved.
oc-f-798 · level teorema · notes
In the metric TSP a closed walk $W$ visiting every city at least once is turned into a tour $\sigma$ by skipping the cities already visited (shortcuts). Why does $L(\sigma)$ not exceed the length of $W$?
  1. Because $\sigma$ has fewer cities than $W$
  2. Because the distances are all equal
  3. It holds for every TSP instance, even non-metric
  4. By the triangle inequality every shortcut $d_{u_0u_q}$ is at most the length of the stretch of $W$ it replaces
Explanation. $d_{u_0u_q}\le d_{u_0u_1}+d_{u_1u_q}\le\dots$; without the triangle inequality a shortcut may lengthen the tour. It is the key step of the double tree and of Christofides.
oc-f-799 · level facile · notes
In the metric TSP, the double tree algorithm and Christofides' algorithm both start from a minimum spanning tree $T$. How do they make the multigraph Eulerian?
  1. Double tree: adds a matching; Christofides: doubles $T$
  2. Neither uses an Eulerian multigraph
  3. Double tree: it doubles the edges of $T$; Christofides: it adds a minimum-cost perfect matching on the odd-degree cities of $T$
  4. Both double the edges of $T$
Explanation. Doubling costs $2d(T)\le2z$; the matching costs at most $z/2$, which gives the guarantees $2$ and $\frac32$. In both cases the Eulerian walk is shortened by shortcuts.
oc-f-800 · level teorema · notes
For Christofides' algorithm there are metric instances $I_n$ ($n$ odd) with $CH(I_n)/z(I_n)\to\frac32$. In the construction the MST is the path $1,2,\dots,n$, the odd-degree cities are only $1$ and $n$, and the matching is the long edge $\{1,n\}$. What does it show?
  1. That shortcuts may lengthen the tour
  2. That the guarantee $\frac32$ of Christofides is tight: the matching may cost almost half the optimal tour
  3. That Christofides is always optimal
  4. That the double tree is better than Christofides
Explanation. The cycle $1,\dots,n,1$ costs about $\frac32 z(I_n)$, while the optimal tour advances two cities at a time. No better ratio holds for all instances.
oc-f-801 · level ipotesi · notes
The guarantee $CH(I)\le\frac32z(I)$ of Christofides uses the triangle inequality. What happens for the general TSP, without this assumption?
  1. No polynomial algorithm has a constant ratio, if P $\ne$ NP
  2. Christofides stays a $\frac32$-approximation
  3. Christofides becomes a $2$-approximation
  4. The general TSP becomes polynomial
Explanation. Without the triangle inequality shortcuts may cost a lot, and a constant guarantee would allow deciding the existence of a Hamiltonian cycle.
oc-f-1191 · level facile · notes
To show that the TSP has no polynomial $\alpha$-approximation, from a graph $G$ with $n$ vertices one builds an instance with $d_{ij}=1$ if $\{i,j\}$ is an edge of $G$ and $d_{ij}=\lceil\alpha n\rceil+1$ otherwise. With $\alpha=2$ and $n=10$, how long is every tour at least if $G$ has no Hamiltonian cycle?
  1. $20$
  2. $29$
  3. $30$
  4. $21$
Explanation. Every tour uses at least one non-adjacent pair ($21$) and $9$ other edges of length at least $1$: $9+21=30>\alpha n=20$. If $G$ is Hamiltonian, $z=10$ and the algorithm would give at most $20$.
oc-f-1192 · level ipotesi · notes
The proof that the general TSP has no constant ratio (if $P\neq NP$) uses distances $1$ on the edges of a graph $G$ and $\lceil\alpha n\rceil+1$ on the other pairs. Why does it say nothing about the metric TSP (triangle inequality $d_{ij}\le d_{ik}+d_{kj}$)?
  1. Because in the metric TSP distances can be $0$
  2. The instances built violate the triangle inequality
  3. Because the metric TSP is solved in polynomial time
  4. Because Hamiltonian cycle is easy on metric graphs
Explanation. If $\{i,k\},\{k,j\}\in E$ and $\{i,j\}\notin E$, then $d_{ij}=\lceil\alpha n\rceil+1>2=d_{ik}+d_{kj}$. The proof needs such large distances; the metric TSP stays NP-hard.
oc-f-1193 · level facile · notes
A TSP instance is metric if $d_{ij}\le d_{ik}+d_{kj}$ for every triple of distinct cities. In the reference instance $d_{15}=9$, $d_{12}=5$ and $d_{25}=4$. Does the triple $(1,2,5)$ violate the condition?
  1. No: $9\le5+4$ holds, equality being allowed
  2. Yes: $d_{15}$ is not strictly smaller than $d_{12}+d_{25}$
  3. Yes: $d_{15}$ is the largest distance of the instance
  4. No: the condition concerns only nearby cities
Explanation. The triangle inequality is $\le$, not $<$: $9=5+4$ satisfies it. Going from $1$ to $5$ through $2$ costs no less than the direct link, and shortcuts remain no longer.
oc-f-1194 · level facile · notes
In the metric TSP (distances satisfying the triangle inequality) the double tree and the Christofides algorithms have a constant ratio. What role does the triangle inequality play in their guarantees?
  1. It makes the TSP solvable in polynomial time
  2. It guarantees that the minimum spanning tree is already a tour
  3. It guarantees that the optimal tour has length at most $2n$
  4. Shortcuts (skipping already visited cities) do not lengthen the walk
Explanation. Skipping the inner cities of a stretch replaces the stretch by a single edge, not longer by the triangle inequality. The metric TSP stays NP-hard.
oc-f-1195 · level facile · notes
Metric TSP with $4$ cities: $d_{12}=2$, $d_{13}=3$, $d_{14}=4$, $d_{23}=3$, $d_{24}=5$, $d_{34}=2$. Kruskal's algorithm scans the edges by non-decreasing distance (ties by index pair) and takes those that close no cycle. Which minimum spanning tree $T$ does it find?
  1. $\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{2,3\}$, with $d(T)=8$
  2. $\{1,2\},\{3,4\}$, with $d(T)=4$
  3. $\{1,2\},\{3,4\},\{1,3\}$, with $d(T)=7$
  4. $\{1,2\},\{3,4\},\{1,4\}$, with $d(T)=8$
Explanation. It takes $\{1,2\}$ and $\{3,4\}$ ($2$), then $\{1,3\}$ ($3$, before $\{2,3\}$ by the tie rule), which connects everything. $\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{2,3\}$ is a cycle; two edges do not span $4$ cities.
oc-f-1196 · level facile · notes
In the metric TSP, the double tree and Christofides turn a closed walk $W$ into a tour by shortcuts: follow $W$ and keep every city only at its first occurrence. From $W=(1,2,1,3,4,3,1)$ which tour is obtained?
  1. $(1,2,1,3,4)$
  2. $(1,2,3,4)$
  3. $(1,2,4,3)$
  4. $(1,3,4,2)$
Explanation. The first occurrences, in order, are $1,2,3,4$; the repetitions of $1$ and $3$ are skipped and the tour returns to $1$. $(1,2,1,3,4)$ is not a tour: it repeats city $1$.
oc-f-1197 · level facile · notes
Metric TSP with $d_{12}=2$, $d_{13}=3$, $d_{14}=4$, $d_{23}=3$, $d_{24}=5$, $d_{34}=2$ and minimum spanning tree $T=\{\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{3,4\}\}$. The double tree visits $T$ depth-first from city $1$ (children in increasing order) and keeps the cities in order of first visit. Which tour does it give, and how long is it?
  1. $(1,2,3,4)$, of length $11$
  2. $(1,2,3,4)$, of length $14$
  3. $(1,3,4,2)$, of length $12$
  4. $(1,2,4,3)$, of length $12$
Explanation. Visit: $1,2,1,3,4,3,1$ (length $2d(T)=14$); the first occurrences give $(1,2,3,4)$: $2+3+2+4=11\le14$. $14$ is the circuit without shortcuts.
oc-f-1198 · level facile · notes
In the double tree for the metric TSP the edges of the minimum spanning tree are doubled and an Eulerian circuit is followed with Fleury's rule (avoid a bridge of the unused edges, if there is an alternative). Why is the circuit a depth-first visit of the tree?
  1. Because Kruskal's algorithm always returns a path
  2. Because in the doubled tree every city has degree $2$
  3. Because Fleury always chooses the farthest neighbor
  4. The last copy of the edge to the parent is a bridge, used last
Explanation. As long as a child remains to be visited, going back to the parent would cross a bridge: Fleury goes down into the children first. The tour is therefore the preorder of the tree.
oc-f-1199 · level facile · notes
Metric TSP with $d_{12}=2$, $d_{13}=3$, $d_{14}=4$, $d_{23}=3$, $d_{24}=5$, $d_{34}=2$, minimum tree $T=\{\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{3,4\}\}$. Christofides adds a minimum perfect matching $M$ on the cities of odd degree in $T$ and follows an Eulerian circuit from $1$ (neighbor of minimum index). Which tour does it give?
  1. $(1,3,4,2)$, of length $15$
  2. $(1,2,1,3,4)$, of length $14$
  3. $(1,2,4,3)$, of length $12$
  4. $(1,2,3,4)$, of length $11$
Explanation. Odd degrees: $2$ and $4$, hence $M=\{\{2,4\}\}$ ($5$). $T\cup M$ is the cycle $1,2,4,3,1$, of length $7+5=12$, with no shortcut. The optimal tour $(1,2,3,4)$ has length $11$: here Christofides does not find it, the double tree does.
oc-f-1200 · level facile · notes
In the Christofides algorithm for the metric TSP, $O$ is the set of cities of odd degree in the minimum spanning tree $T$, and a perfect matching of $O$ is sought. Why is $|O|$ always even?
  1. Because the blossom algorithm requires it
  2. The degrees of a graph sum to twice the number of edges
  3. Because $T$ has $n-1$ edges and $n$ is odd
  4. Because the leaves of a tree are always even in number
Explanation. The degree sum is even, so the cities of odd degree are even in number; in the complete graph a perfect matching of $O$ exists. A tree can have an odd number of leaves (star with $3$ leaves).
oc-f-1201 · level facile · notes
In a metric TSP instance the minimum spanning tree weighs $d(T)=20$ and a minimum perfect matching of an even set of cities weighs $d(M)=9$. The bounds $d(T)\le z(I)$ and $d(M)\le z(I)/2$ hold ($z(I)$ = length of the optimal tour). Which lower bound on $z(I)$ follows?
  1. $z(I)\ge20$
  2. $z(I)\ge29$
  3. $z(I)\ge18$
  4. $z(I)\ge14.5$
Explanation. The two bounds give $z\ge20$ and $z\ge18$: the stronger one, $20$, holds. Adding them ($29$) is a mistake: $T$ and $M$ are not disjoint parts of a tour.
oc-f-1202 · level teorema · notes
For the double tree in the metric TSP there are instances $I_n$ ($n$ odd): city $1$ is at distance $a=n$ from all, two leaves are at distance $b=n+1$ if consecutive on a path $P$ and $2a$ otherwise. Why is $DT(I_n)=2(n-1)a$?
  1. Because the minimum tree is the path $P$, traversed twice
  2. Because the shortcuts save $b-a$ at every single step
  3. Because the optimum has length $(n-1)a$ and $DT$ doubles it
  4. The MST is the star; leaves consecutive in preorder are not joined by $P$
Explanation. Every edge weighs at least $a$ and only those from the center equal $a$: the MST is the star. The preorder is $(1,2,\dots,n)$ and consecutive indices are never consecutive on $P$: $a+(n-2)2a+a$. The optimum is $(n+2)(n-1)$.

40. Approximation for $P\|C_{\max}$ (19)

oc-f-137 · level ipotesi · notes
In scheduling $P\,||\,C_{\max}$ ($m$ machines, durations $t_j$, optimal makespan $z(I)$), $LIST$ assigns every job of the list to the least loaded machine. Let $\ell$ be a job finishing last, with start $S_\ell$. Which facts are needed to prove $LIST(I)\le\left(2-\frac1m\right)z(I)$?
  1. $\ell$ is the longest job; $z(I)=\frac1m\sum_j t_j$; $z(I)\ge t_\ell$
  2. The jobs are sorted by non-increasing duration; $z(I)\ge t_\ell$; $S_\ell\le z(I)$
  3. $S_\ell\le\frac1m\sum_{j\ne\ell}t_j$; $z(I)\ge\frac1m\sum_j t_j$; $z(I)\ge t_\ell$
  4. $S_\ell\le\frac1m\sum_{j\ne\ell}t_j$; $z(I)\ge\frac1m\sum_j t_j$; $z(I)\ge 2t_\ell$
Explanation. $LIST(I)=S_\ell+t_\ell\le\frac1m\sum_j t_j+\left(1-\frac1m\right)t_\ell\le\left(2-\frac1m\right)z(I)$. Sorting is needed only for the better guarantee of $LPT$.
oc-f-138 · level facile · notes
In scheduling $P\,||\,C_{\max}$, $LPT$ sorts the jobs by non-increasing duration and assigns each to the least loaded machine; its guarantee is $\frac43-\frac1{3m}$. What is it with $m=2$ machines?
  1. $\frac54$
  2. $\frac76$
  3. $\frac32$
  4. $\frac43$
Explanation. $\frac43-\frac1{3m}=\frac43-\frac16=\frac76$. With any list $LIST$ guarantees $2-\frac12=\frac32$.
oc-f-139 · level teorema · notes
In scheduling $P\,||\,C_{\max}$ with $m$ machines, $LIST$ (any list, least loaded machine) guarantees $2-\frac1m$ and $LPT$ (list by non-increasing duration) guarantees $\frac43-\frac1{3m}$. Which statement is correct?
  1. Both are tight: for every $m\ge 2$ some instances reach exactly the two ratios
  2. Both are tight only for $m=2$; for $m\ge 3$ the ratios are lower
  3. The guarantee of $LIST$ is tight, that of $LPT$ is not: its true ratio is lower
  4. Neither is reached: the ratios are only approached as $n$ grows
Explanation. Graham's instance families reach exactly the two ratios for every $m\ge 2$ (for $LPT$: $2m+1$ jobs, two of every duration from $2m-1$ down to $m$ plus one of duration $m$).
oc-f-536 · level facile · notes
Scheduling $P\,||\,C_{\max}$ with $m=3$ machines. $LIST$ assigns every job, in list order, to the least loaded machine (ties: smallest index); $LPT$ does the same with the list sorted by non-increasing time. With the list $t=(2,3,4,6,2,2)$, what are the makespans of $LIST$ and $LPT$?
  1. $7$ and $7$
  2. $8$ and $8$
  3. $9$ and $7$
